When her days to give birth are completed, look — there are twins in her womb.
The first comes out red, all his body like a hairy cloak. So they call his name Esau.
Afterward his brother comes out, with his hand gripping Esau’s heel. So his name is called Jacob. Isaac is sixty years old when she bears them.
When the boys grow up, Esau is a skilful hunter, a man of the open country. Jacob is a quiet man, dwelling in tents.
Isaac loves Esau because he eats of his game, but Rebekah loves Jacob.
Once when Jacob is cooking stew, Esau comes in from the open country, and he is exhausted.
“Let me eat some of that red stew — that red stuff there — for I am exhausted,” Esau says to Jacob. (That is why his name is called Edom.)
“Sell me your birthright first,” Jacob says.
“Look — I am about to die,” Esau says. “What use is a birthright to me?”
“Swear to me first,” Jacob says. So he swears to him and sells his birthright to Jacob.
Then Jacob gives Esau bread and lentil stew. He eats and drinks and rises and goes. So Esau despises his birthright.
Now there is a famine in the land — besides the former famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac goes to Gerar, to Abimelech king of the Philistines.
And YHWH appears to him and says, “Do not go down to Egypt. Dwell in the land of which I shall tell you.
Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you — for to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father.
I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and will give to your offspring all these lands. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed —
because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.”
So Isaac settles in Gerar.

When the men of the place ask him about his wife, he says, “She is my sister” — for he is afraid to say “My wife,” thinking, “lest the men of the place kill me because of Rebekah,” because she is beautiful in appearance.
When he has been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looks out of a window and sees — and look, Isaac is laughing with Rebekah his wife.
So Abimelech calls Isaac and says, “Look — she really is your wife. How then could you say, ‘She is my sister’?”
“Because I thought, ‘Lest I die because of her,’” Isaac says to him.
“What is this you have done to us?” Abimelech says. “One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us.”
So Abimelech warns all the people: “Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death.”
And Isaac sows in that land and reaps in the same year a hundredfold. And YHWH blesses him.
And the man becomes rich and gains more and more until he becomes very wealthy.
He has possessions of flocks and herds and many servants, so that the Philistines envy him.
Now all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines have stopped them up and filled them with earth.
And Abimelech says to Isaac, “Move away from us, for you are much mightier than we.”
So Isaac departs from there and camps in the valley of Gerar and settles there.

And Isaac digs again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father — which the Philistines had stopped up after the death of Abraham — and he gives them the names that his father had given them.
But when Isaac’s servants dig in the valley and find there a well of spring water,
the herdsmen of Gerar quarrel with Isaac’s herdsmen, saying, “The water is ours.” So he calls the name of the well Esek — because they contended with him.
Then they dig another well, and they quarrel over that also. So he calls its name Sitnah.
And he moves from there and digs another well, and they do not quarrel over it. So he calls its name Rehoboth, saying, “For now YHWH has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land.”
From there he goes up to Beersheba.
And YHWH appears to him that night and says:
“I am the God of Abraham your father.
Do not be afraid, for I am with you.
I will bless you and multiply your offspring
for the sake of Abraham my servant.”
So he builds an altar there and calls on the name of YHWH and pitches his tent there. And there Isaac’s servants dig a well.
When Abimelech comes to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army,
Isaac says to them, “Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have sent me away from you?”
They say, “We see plainly that YHWH has been with you. So we say, let there be a sworn oath between us — between you and us — and let us make a covenant with you,
that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you and have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace. You are now the blessed of YHWH.”
So he makes them a feast and they eat and drink.
In the morning they rise early and exchange oaths. And Isaac sends them on their way, and they depart from him in peace.
That same day Isaac’s servants come and tell him about the well they have dug and say to him, “We have found water.”
He calls it Shibah. Therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.
When Esau is forty years old, he takes Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
And they make life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac is old and his eyes are dim so that he cannot see, he calls Esau his older son and says to him, “My son.”
“Here I am,” he says.
“Look — I am old. I do not know the day of my death.
Now then, take your weapons — your quiver and your bow — and go out to the open country and hunt game for me,
and prepare for me delicious food, such as I love, and bring it to me so that I may eat, that my soul may bless you before I die.”
Now Rebekah is listening when Isaac speaks to Esau his son. So when Esau goes to the open country to hunt for game and bring it,
Rebekah says to her son Jacob, “Look, I heard your father speak to your brother Esau:
‘Bring me game and prepare for me delicious food, that I may eat it and bless you before YHWH before my death.’
Now therefore, my son, listen to my voice as I command you.
Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats, so that I may prepare from them delicious food for your father, such as he loves.
And you shall bring it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before his death.”
“But my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man,” Jacob says to Rebekah his mother.
“Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall seem to be mocking him and bring a curse upon myself and not a blessing.”
“Let your curse be on me, my son,” his mother says to him. “Only listen to my voice and go, bring them to me.”
So he goes and takes them and brings them to his mother. And his mother prepares delicious food, such as his father loved.
Then Rebekah takes the best garments of Esau her older son, which were with her in the house, and puts them on Jacob her younger son.
And the skins of the young goats she puts on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.
And she puts the delicious food and the bread she has prepared into the hand of her son Jacob.
So he goes in to his father and says, “My father.”
“Here I am. Who are you, my son?” he says.
“I am Esau your firstborn,” Jacob says to his father. “I have done as you told me. Now sit up and eat of my game, so that your soul may bless me.”
“How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?” Isaac says.
“Because YHWH your God granted me success,” he says.
“Come near, that I may feel you, my son — whether you are really my son Esau or not.”
So Jacob goes near to Isaac his father, who feels him and says, “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.”
And he does not recognise him, because his hands are hairy like his brother Esau’s hands. So he blesses him.
“Are you really my son Esau?” he says.
“I am,” he says.
“Bring it near to me, that I may eat of my son’s game and bless you.” He brings it near to him, and he eats. He brings him wine, and he drinks.
Then his father Isaac says to him, “Come near and kiss me, my son.”
So he comes near and kisses him. And Isaac smells the smell of his garments and blesses him and says:
“See, the smell of my son
is like the smell of a field
that YHWH has blessed.
May God give you of the dew of heaven
and of the fatness of the earth
and plenty of grain and wine.
Let peoples serve you,
and nations bow down to you.
Be lord over your brothers,
and may your mother’s sons bow down to you.
Cursed be everyone who curses you,
and blessed be everyone who blesses you!”
As soon as Isaac has finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob has barely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother comes in from his hunting.
He also prepares delicious food and brings it to his father. And he says to his father, “Let my father arise and eat of his son’s game, so that you may bless me.”
“Who are you?” his father Isaac says to him.
“I am your son, your firstborn, Esau,” he says.
Then Isaac trembles violently and says, “Who was it then who hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate it all before you came, and I blessed him? Yes, and he shall be blessed.”
When Esau hears the words of his father, he cries out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and says to his father, “Bless me, even me also, my father!”
“Your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing,” he says.

“Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times. He took away my birthright, and look, now he has taken away my blessing!” And he says, “Have you not reserved a blessing for me?”
“Look, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants, and with grain and wine I have sustained him,” Isaac answers Esau. “What then can I do for you, my son?”
“Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, my father!” Esau lifts up his voice and weeps.
Then Isaac his father answers him:
“Behold, away from the fatness of the earth
shall your dwelling be,
and away from the dew of heaven on high.
By your sword you shall live,
and you shall serve your brother.
But when you grow restless,
you shall break his yoke from your neck.”
Now Esau hates Jacob because of the blessing with which his father has blessed him. And Esau says to himself, “The days of mourning for my father are approaching. Then I will kill my brother Jacob.”
But the words of Esau her older son are told to Rebekah. So she sends and calls Jacob her younger son and says to him, “Look — your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you.
Now therefore, my son, listen to my voice. Arise, flee to my brother Laban in Haran
and stay with him a while, until your brother’s fury turns away —
until your brother’s anger against you turns away and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and bring you from there. Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?”
And Rebekah says to Isaac, “I loathe my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women like these, one of the women of the land, what good will my life be to me?”
Then Isaac calls Jacob and blesses him and charges him: “You shall not take a wife from the Canaanite women.
Arise, go to Paddan-aram, to the house of Bethuel your mother’s father, and take as your wife from there one of the daughters of Laban your mother’s brother.
God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, that you may become a company of peoples.
May he give the blessing of Abraham to you and to your offspring with you, that you may take possession of the land of your sojournings that God gave to Abraham.”
So Isaac sends Jacob away, and he goes to Paddan-aram, to Laban the son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, Jacob’s and Esau’s mother.
Now Esau sees that Isaac has blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he charged him, “You shall not take a wife from the Canaanite women,”
and that Jacob had listened to his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram.
So when Esau sees that the Canaanite women do not please Isaac his father,
Esau goes to Ishmael and takes as his wife, besides the wives he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, the sister of Nebaioth.
Jacob leaves Beersheba and goes toward Haran.
And he comes to a certain place and stays there that night, because the sun has set. Taking one of the stones of the place, he puts it under his head and lies down in that place to sleep.
And he dreams — and look, a ladder is set up on the earth, and its top reaches to heaven. And look, the angels of God are ascending and descending on it.
And look — YHWH stands above it and says:
“I am YHWH, the God of Abraham your father
and the God of Isaac.
The land on which you lie I will give to you
and to your offspring.
Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth,
and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east
and to the north and to the south.
And in you and in your offspring
shall all the families of the earth be blessed.
Look — I am with you and will keep you
wherever you go,
and will bring you back to this land.
For I will not leave you
until I have done what I have promised you.”
Then Jacob wakes from his sleep and says, “Surely YHWH is in this place — and I did not know it.”
And he is afraid and says, “How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
So Jacob rises early in the morning and takes the stone that he had put under his head and sets it up as a pillar and pours oil on the top of it.
He calls the name of that place Bethel — though the name of the city was Luz at first.
Then Jacob makes a vow, saying, “If God will be with me and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,
so that I come again to my father’s house in peace, then YHWH shall be my God,
and this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, shall be God’s house. And of all that you give me I will give a full tenth to you.”
Then Jacob lifts his feet and goes to the land of the people of the east.
He looks and sees a well in the open country, and look — three flocks of sheep lying beside it. For out of that well the flocks were watered. The stone on the mouth of the well is large.
When all the flocks are gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, then put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
“My brothers, where do you come from?” Jacob says to them.
“We are from Haran,” they say.
“Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?” he says to them.
“We know him,” they say.
“Is it well with him?” he says.
“It is well,” they say. “And look — Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep!”
“Look — the sun is still high. It is not time for the animals to be gathered. Water the sheep and go, pasture them.”
“We cannot,” they say, “until all the flocks are gathered and the stone is rolled from the mouth of the well. Then we water the sheep.”
While he is still speaking with them, Rachel comes with her father’s sheep — for she is a shepherdess.

Now when Jacob sees Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother’s brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother’s brother, Jacob goes up and rolls the stone from the mouth of the well and waters the flock of Laban his mother’s brother.
Then Jacob kisses Rachel and weeps aloud.
And Jacob tells Rachel that he is her father’s kinsman, and that he is Rebekah’s son. And she runs and tells her father.
As soon as Laban hears the news about Jacob his sister’s son, he runs to meet him. He embraces him and kisses him and brings him to his house. Jacob tells Laban all these things,
and Laban says to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.”
And he stays with him a month.
“Should you serve me for nothing, just because you are my kinsman?” Laban says to Jacob. “Tell me — what shall your wages be?”
Now Laban has two daughters. The name of the older is Leah, and the name of the younger is Rachel.
Leah’s eyes are weak, but Rachel is beautiful in form and beautiful in appearance.
Jacob loves Rachel. And he says, “I will serve you seven years for Rachel your younger daughter.”
“It is better that I give her to you than I should give her to any other man,” Laban says. “Stay with me.”
So Jacob serves seven years for Rachel. And they seem to him like a few days because of his love for her.
“Give me my wife,” Jacob says to Laban, “for my time is completed, that I may go in to her.”
So Laban gathers together all the people of the place and makes a feast.
But in the evening he takes his daughter Leah and brings her to Jacob, and he goes in to her.
Laban gives Leah his servant Zilpah as a servant.
And in the morning — look, it is Leah! And Jacob says to Laban, “What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?”
“It is not done so in our place — to give the younger before the firstborn,” Laban says.
“Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also in return for serving me another seven years.”
Jacob does so and completes her week. Then Laban gives him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
Laban gives his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant.
So Jacob goes in to Rachel also, and he loves Rachel more than Leah. And he serves Laban for another seven years.
And when YHWH sees that Leah is hated, he opens her womb. But Rachel is barren.
And Leah conceives and bears a son. She calls his name Reuben — for she says, “Because YHWH has seen my affliction. For now my husband will love me.”
She conceives again and bears a son and says, “Because YHWH has heard that I am hated, he has given me this son also.” And she calls his name Simeon.
Again she conceives and bears a son and says, “Now this time my husband will be attached to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name is called Levi.
And she conceives again and bears a son and says, “This time I will praise YHWH.” Therefore she calls his name Judah. Then she stops bearing.
When Rachel sees that she bears Jacob no children, Rachel envies her sister. And she says to Jacob, “Give me children — or I will die!”
“Am I in the place of God?” Jacob says, angered by Rachel. “It is he who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb.”
“Here is my servant Bilhah,” she says. “Go in to her, so that she may give birth on my knees, and even I may have children through her.”
So she gives him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob goes in to her.
And Bilhah conceives and bears Jacob a son.
Then Rachel says, “God has judged me, and has also heard my voice and given me a son.” Therefore she calls his name Dan.
Rachel’s servant Bilhah conceives again and bears Jacob a second son.
Then Rachel says, “With mighty wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister and have prevailed.” And she calls his name Naphtali.
When Leah sees that she has stopped bearing children, she takes her servant Zilpah and gives her to Jacob as a wife.
Then Leah’s servant Zilpah bears Jacob a son.
And Leah says, “Good fortune has come!” So she calls his name Gad.
Leah’s servant Zilpah bears Jacob a second son.
And Leah says, “Happy am I! For women will call me happy.” So she calls his name Asher.
In the days of wheat harvest, Reuben goes and finds mandrakes in the field and brings them to his mother Leah. Then Rachel says to Leah, “Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”
But she says to her, “Is it a small matter that you have taken away my husband? Would you take away my son’s mandrakes also?”
“Then he may lie with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes,” Rachel says.
When Jacob comes in from the field in the evening, Leah goes out to meet him and says, “You must come in to me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” And he lies with her that night.
And God listens to Leah, and she conceives and bears Jacob a fifth son.
Leah says, “God has given me my wages because I gave my servant to my husband.” So she calls his name Issachar.
And Leah conceives again and bears Jacob a sixth son.
Then Leah says, “God has endowed me with a good endowment. Now my husband will honor me, because I have borne him six sons.” So she calls his name Zebulun.
Afterward she bears a daughter and calls her name Dinah.
Then God remembers Rachel, and God listens to her and opens her womb.
She conceives and bears a son and says, “God has taken away my reproach.”
And she calls his name Joseph, saying, “May YHWH add to me another son!”
As soon as Rachel has borne Joseph, Jacob says to Laban, “Send me away, that I may go to my own home and country.
Give me my wives and my children for whom I have served you, and let me go. For you know the service I have given you.”
“If I have found favour in your sight, I have learned by divination that YHWH has blessed me because of you,” Laban says.
“Name your wages, and I will give them.”
“You yourself know how I have served you, and how your livestock has fared with me,” Jacob says.
“For you had little before I came, and it has increased abundantly. And YHWH has blessed you wherever I turned. But now — when shall I provide for my own household also?”
“What shall I give you?” Laban says.
“You shall not give me anything,” Jacob says. “If you will do this for me, I will again pasture your flock and keep it.
Let me pass through all your flock today, removing from it every speckled and spotted sheep and every black lamb, and the spotted and speckled among the goats. These shall be my wages.

So my honesty will answer for me later, when you come to look into my wages with you. Every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats and black among the lambs, if found with me, shall be counted stolen.”
“Good,” Laban says. “Let it be as you have said.”

But that day Laban removes the male goats that are striped and spotted, and all the female goats that are speckled and spotted, every one that has white on it, and every lamb that is black, and puts them in the charge of his sons.
And he sets a distance of three days’ journey between himself and Jacob, and Jacob pastures the rest of Laban’s flock.
Then Jacob takes fresh sticks of poplar and almond and plane trees, and peels white streaks in them, exposing the white of the sticks.
He sets the sticks that he has peeled in front of the flocks in the troughs, so that the flocks would see them when they came to drink.
The flocks breed in front of the sticks and so the flocks produce young that are striped, speckled, and spotted.
And Jacob separates the lambs and sets the faces of the flocks toward the striped and all the black in the flock of Laban. He puts his own droves apart and does not put them with Laban’s flock.
Whenever the stronger of the flock are breeding, Jacob lays the sticks in the troughs before the eyes of the flock, that they may breed among the sticks.
But for the feebler of the flock he does not lay them there. So the feebler would be Laban’s and the stronger Jacob’s.
Thus the man increases greatly and has large flocks, female servants and male servants, and camels and donkeys.
Now Jacob hears that the sons of Laban are saying, “Jacob has taken all that was our father’s, and from what was our father’s he has gained all this wealth.”
And Jacob sees that Laban’s face toward him is not as it had been before.
Then YHWH says to Jacob, “Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you.”
So Jacob sends and calls Rachel and Leah into the field where his flock is
and says to them, “I see that your father’s face toward me is not as it was before. But the God of my father has been with me.
You know that I have served your father with all my strength.
Yet your father has cheated me and changed my wages ten times. But God did not allow him to harm me.
If he said, ‘The speckled shall be your wages,’ then all the flock bore speckled. And if he said, ‘The striped shall be your wages,’ then all the flock bore striped.
Thus God has taken away the livestock of your father and given them to me.
In the breeding season of the flock I lifted up my eyes and saw in a dream that the male goats that mated with the flock were striped, speckled, and mottled.
Then the angel of God said to me in the dream, ‘Jacob.’ And I said, ‘Here I am.’
And he said, ‘Lift up your eyes and see: all the male goats that mate with the flock are striped, speckled, and mottled — for I have seen all that Laban is doing to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and made a vow to me. Now arise, go out from this land and return to the land of your kindred.’”
Then Rachel and Leah answer him: “Is there any portion or inheritance left for us in our father’s house?
Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us and has indeed devoured our money.
All the wealth that God has taken away from our father belongs to us and to our children. Now then, whatever God has said to you, do.”
So Jacob arises and sets his sons and his wives on camels.
He drives away all his livestock and all his property that he had gained — the livestock in his possession that he had acquired in Paddan-aram — to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.
Now Laban has gone to shear his sheep. And Rachel steals her father’s household gods.
And Jacob tricked Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was fleeing.
He fled with all that he had and arose and crossed the Euphrates and set his face toward the hill country of Gilead.
When it is told Laban on the third day that Jacob had fled,
he takes his kinsmen with him and pursues him for seven days and overtakes him in the hill country of Gilead.
But God comes to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and says to him, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob — either good or bad.”
And Laban overtakes Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban with his kinsmen camped in the hill country of Gilead.
“What have you done?” Laban says to Jacob. “You have tricked me and driven away my daughters like captives taken by the sword.
Why did you flee secretly and trick me, and did not tell me, so that I might have sent you away with mirth and songs, with tambourine and lyre?
And why did you not permit me to kiss my sons and my daughters farewell? Now you have done foolishly.
It is in my power to do you harm. But the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, ‘Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.’
And now you have gone away because you longed greatly for your father’s house. But why did you steal my gods?”
“Because I was afraid,” Jacob answers Laban, “for I thought you would take your daughters from me by force.
Anyone with whom you find your gods shall not live. In the presence of our kinsmen, point out what I have that is yours and take it.”
For Jacob does not know that Rachel had stolen the gods.
So Laban goes into Jacob’s tent and into Leah’s tent and into the tent of the two female servants, but he does not find them. And he goes out of Leah’s tent and enters Rachel’s tent.
Now Rachel has taken the household gods and put them in the camel’s saddle and sits on them. Laban feels all about the tent but does not find them.
“Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me.” So he searches but does not find the household gods.
Then Jacob becomes angry and quarrels with Laban. Jacob says to Laban, “What is my offence? What is my sin, that you have hotly pursued me?
For you have felt through all my goods. What have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, that they may decide between us two.
These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your female goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flocks.
What was torn by wild beasts I did not bring to you. I bore the loss of it myself. From my hand you required it — whether stolen by day or stolen by night.
There I was: by day the heat consumed me and the cold by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes.
These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times.

If the God of my father — the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac — had not been on my side, surely now you would have sent me away empty-handed. God saw my affliction and the labour of my hands and rebuked you last night.”

“The daughters are my daughters, and the children are my children, and the flocks are my flocks — all that you see is mine,” Laban answers. “But what can I do today for these daughters of mine, or for their children whom they have borne?
Come, let us make a covenant, you and I. And let it be a witness between us.”
So Jacob takes a stone and sets it up as a pillar.
And Jacob says to his kinsmen, “Gather stones.” And they take stones and make a heap, and they eat there by the heap.
Laban calls it Jegar-sahadutha, but Jacob calls it Galeed.
“This heap is a witness between you and me today,” Laban says. That is why he named it Galeed —
and also Mizpah, for he says, “May YHWH watch between you and me when we are out of one another’s sight.
If you oppress my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters — although no one is with us — see, God is witness between you and me.”
Then Laban says to Jacob, “See this heap and the pillar, which I have set between you and me.
This heap is a witness and the pillar is a witness that I will not pass over this heap to you and you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, to do harm.
The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor — the God of their father — judge between us.”
And Jacob swears by the Fear of his father Isaac.
And Jacob offers a sacrifice in the hill country and calls his kinsmen to eat bread. They eat bread and spend the night in the hill country.
Early in the morning Laban arises and kisses his grandchildren and his daughters and blesses them. Then Laban departs and returns home.
Jacob goes on his way, and the angels of God meet him.
And when Jacob sees them he says, “This is God’s camp!” And he calls the name of that place Mahanaim.
And Jacob sends messengers before him to Esau his brother in the land of Seir, the country of Edom,
instructing them: “Thus you shall say to my lord Esau: Thus says your servant Jacob. I have sojourned with Laban and stayed until now.
I have oxen, donkeys, flocks, male servants, and female servants. I have sent to tell my lord, in order to find favour in your sight.”
And the messengers return to Jacob, saying, “We came to your brother Esau, and he is coming to meet you — and there are four hundred men with him.”
Then Jacob is greatly afraid and distressed. He divides the people who are with him, and the flocks and herds and camels, into two camps,
thinking, “If Esau comes to the one camp and attacks it, then the camp that is left will escape.”
And Jacob says, “O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, O YHWH who said to me, ‘Return to your country and to your kindred, and I will do you good’ —
I am not worthy of the least of all the steadfast love and all the faithfulness that you have shown to your servant. For with only my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.
Please deliver me from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau. For I fear him, lest he come and attack me — the mothers with the children.
But you said, ‘I will surely do you good, and make your offspring as the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude.’”
So he stays there that night, and from what he has with him he takes a present for his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty milking camels and their calves, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
These he hands over to his servants, every drove by itself, and says to his servants, “Pass on before me and put a space between drove and drove.”
He instructs the first: “When Esau my brother meets you and asks you, ‘To whom do you belong? Where are you going? And whose are these before you?’
then you shall say, ‘They belong to your servant Jacob. It is a present sent to my lord Esau. And moreover, he is behind us.’”
He likewise instructs the second and the third and all who follow the droves: “You shall say the same thing to Esau when you find him,

and you shall say, ‘Moreover, your servant Jacob is behind us.’” For he thinks, “I will appease him with the present that goes before me, and afterward I will see his face. Perhaps he will accept me.”
So the present passes on before him, and he himself stays that night in the camp.
The same night he arises and takes his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven children, and crosses the ford of the Jabbok.
He takes them and sends them across the stream, and everything else that he has.
And Jacob is left alone.
And a man wrestles with him until the breaking of the day.
When the man sees that he does not prevail against Jacob, he touches the socket of his hip. And the socket of Jacob’s hip is put out of joint as he wrestles with him.
“Let me go, for the day is breaking,” the man says.
“I will not let you go unless you bless me,” Jacob says.
“What is your name?” the man says.
“Jacob,” he says.
“Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel — for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
“Tell me your name,” Jacob says.
“Why is it that you ask my name?” he says. And he blesses him there.
So Jacob calls the name of the place Peniel — saying, “For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered.”
The sun rises upon him as he passes Penuel, limping because of his hip.
Therefore to this day the people of Israel do not eat the sinew of the thigh that is on the hip socket, because he touched the socket of Jacob’s hip on the sinew of the thigh.
And Jacob lifts up his eyes and looks — and look, Esau is coming, and four hundred men with him. So he divides the children among Leah and Rachel and the two female servants.
He puts the servants with their children in front, then Leah with her children, and Rachel and Joseph last of all.
He himself goes on before them, bowing himself to the ground seven times, until he comes near to his brother.
But Esau runs to meet him and embraces him and falls on his neck and kisses him — and they weep.
And when Esau lifts up his eyes and sees the women and children, he says, “Who are these with you?”
“The children with whom God has graciously given your servant,” Jacob says.
Then the servants draw near, they and their children, and bow down.
Leah likewise and her children draw near and bow down. And last Joseph and Rachel draw near and bow down.
“What do you mean by all this company that I met?” Esau says.
“To find favour in the sight of my lord,” Jacob says.
“I have enough, my brother. Keep what you have for yourself.”
“No, please,” Jacob says. “If I have found favour in your sight, then accept my present from my hand. For I have seen your face, which is like seeing the face of God — and you have accepted me.
Please accept my blessing that is brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.”
And he urges him, and he takes it.
“Let us journey on our way,” Esau says, “and I will go ahead of you.”
“My lord knows that the children are tender, and the nursing flocks and herds are a care to me,” Jacob says. “If they are driven hard for one day, all the flocks will die.
Let my lord pass on ahead of his servant, and I will lead on slowly, at the pace of the livestock that are ahead of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir.”
“Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me,” Esau says.
“What need is there? Let me find favour in the sight of my lord.”
So Esau returns that day on his way to Seir.
But Jacob journeys to Succoth and builds himself a house and makes booths for his livestock. That is why the place is called Succoth.
And Jacob comes safely to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he comes from Paddan-aram. And he camps before the city.
And he buys for a hundred pieces of money the piece of land on which he has pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father.
There he erects an altar and calls it El-Elohe-Israel.
Now Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she had borne to Jacob, goes out to see the women of the land.
And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, sees her, he seizes her and lies with her and violates her.
And his soul is drawn to Dinah the daughter of Jacob. He loves the young woman and speaks tenderly to her.
So Shechem speaks to his father Hamor: “Get me this girl as my wife.”
Now Jacob hears that he has defiled his daughter Dinah — but his sons are with his livestock in the field, so Jacob holds his peace until they come.
And Hamor the father of Shechem goes out to Jacob to speak with him.

The sons of Jacob come in from the field when they hear it, and the men are indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter — for such a thing must not be done.
“My son Shechem’s heart longs for your daughter,” Hamor says to them. “Please give her to him as his wife.
Make marriages with us. Give your daughters to us and take our daughters for yourselves.
You shall dwell with us, and the land shall be open to you. Dwell and trade in it and get property in it.”
Shechem also says to her father and to her brothers, “Let me find favour in your eyes, and whatever you say to me I will give.
Ask me for as great a bride-price and gift as you will, and I will give whatever you say to me. Only give me the young woman as my wife.”
The sons of Jacob answer Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully — because he had defiled their sister Dinah.
They say to them, “We cannot do this thing — to give our sister to one who is uncircumcised. For that would be a disgrace to us.
Only on this condition will we consent to you: if you will become as we are by circumcising every male among you.
Then we will give our daughters to you and take your daughters to ourselves and dwell with you and become one people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, then we will take our daughter and go.”
Their words please Hamor and Hamor’s son Shechem.
And the young man does not delay to do the thing, because he delights in Jacob’s daughter. Now he was the most honored of all his father’s house.
So Hamor and his son Shechem come to the gate of their city and speak to the men of their city:
“These men are at peace with us. Let them dwell in the land and trade in it — the land is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters as wives, and let us give them our daughters.
Only on this condition will the men consent to dwell with us to become one people — when every male among us is circumcised as they are circumcised.
Will not their livestock, their property, and all their beasts be ours? Only let us consent for them, and they will dwell with us.”
And all who went out of the gate of his city listen to Hamor and his son Shechem. And every male is circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his city.
On the third day, when they are in pain, two of the sons of Jacob — Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers — take each his sword and come against the city while it feels secure and kill every male.
They kill Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword and take Dinah out of Shechem’s house and go.
The sons of Jacob come upon the slain and plunder the city, because they had defiled their sister.
They take their flocks and their herds, their donkeys, and whatever was in the city and in the field.
All their wealth, all their little ones and their wives, all that was in the houses, they capture and plunder.

“You have brought trouble on me by making me stink to the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites,” Jacob says to Simeon and Levi. “My numbers are few, and if they gather themselves against me and attack me, I shall be destroyed, both I and my household.”
“Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?” they say.
God says to Jacob, “Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.”
So Jacob says to his household and to all who are with him, “Put away the foreign gods that are among you and purify yourselves and change your garments.
Then let us arise and go up to Bethel, so that I may make there an altar to the God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone.”
So they give to Jacob all the foreign gods they had and the rings that were in their ears. And Jacob buries them under the terebinth tree that was near Shechem.
And as they journey, a terror from God falls upon the cities that were around them, so that they do not pursue the sons of Jacob.
And Jacob comes to Luz (that is, Bethel), which is in the land of Canaan, he and all the people who were with him.
And there he builds an altar and calls the place El-Bethel — because there God had revealed himself to him when he fled from his brother.
And Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, dies, and she is buried under an oak below Bethel. So it is called Allon-bacuth.
God appears to Jacob again when he comes from Paddan-aram and blesses him.
“Your name is Jacob. Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.”
So he calls his name Israel.
And God says to him:
“I am El Shaddai.
Be fruitful and multiply.
A nation and a company of nations
shall come from you,
and kings shall come from your own body.
The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac
I will give to you,
and I will give the land to your offspring
after you.”
Then God goes up from him in the place where he had spoken with him.
And Jacob sets up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him — a pillar of stone. He pours a drink offering on it and pours oil on it.
So Jacob calls the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
Then they journey from Bethel. When they are still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel goes into labour and she has hard labour.
And when her labour is at its hardest, the midwife says to her, “Do not fear, for you have another son.”
And as her soul is departing — for she is dying — she calls his name Ben-oni. But his father calls him Benjamin.
So Rachel dies, and she is buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).
And Jacob sets up a pillar over her tomb. It is the pillar of Rachel’s tomb, which is there to this day.
Israel journeys on and pitches his tent beyond the tower of Eder.
While Israel dwells in that land, Reuben goes and lies with Bilhah his father’s concubine. And Israel hears of it.
Now the sons of Jacob are twelve:
the sons of Leah — Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun;
the sons of Rachel — Joseph and Benjamin;
the sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s servant — Dan and Naphtali;
the sons of Zilpah, Leah’s servant — Gad and Asher.
These are the sons of Jacob who are born to him in Paddan-aram.
And Jacob comes to his father Isaac at Mamre, at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned.
Now the days of Isaac were 180 years.
And Isaac breathes his last and dies and is gathered to his people, old and full of years. And his sons Esau and Jacob bury him.
These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom).
Esau takes his wives from the Canaanite women — Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite,
and Basemath, Ishmael’s daughter, the sister of Nebaioth.
And Adah bears to Esau, Eliphaz. And Basemath bears Reuel.
And Oholibamah bears Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who are born to him in the land of Canaan.

Then Esau takes his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the members of his household, his livestock, all his beasts, and all his property that he has acquired in the land of Canaan. He goes into a land away from his brother Jacob.
For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together. The land of their sojournings could not support them because of their livestock.
So Esau settles in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
These are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir.

The sons of Esau: Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, and Reuel the son of Basemath the wife of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz. (Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau’s son; she bore Amalek to Eliphaz.) These are the sons of Adah, Esau’s wife. The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife. The sons of Oholibamah: Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau’s wife Oholibamah.
These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau: the chiefs Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz,
Korah, Gatam, and Amalek — these are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom. These are the sons of Adah.
These are the sons of Reuel, Esau’s son: the chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah — these are the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
These are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau’s wife: the chiefs Jeush, Jalam, and Korah — these are the chiefs of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau’s wife.
These are the sons of Esau (that is, Edom), and these are their chiefs.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan — these are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites:

Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, the name of his city being Dinhabah. Bela dies, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigns in his place. Jobab dies, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigns in his place. Husham dies, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigns in his place, the name of his city being Avith. Hadad dies, and Samlah of Masrekah reigns in his place. Samlah dies, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigns in his place. Shaul dies, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigns in his place. Baal-hanan the son of Achbor dies, and Hadar reigns in his place, the name of his city being Pau; his wife’s name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.
These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their clans and their dwelling places, by their names: the chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,
Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon,
Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,
Magdiel, and Iram — these are the chiefs of Edom, according to their dwelling places in the land of their possession. He is Esau, the father of Edom.
Jacob settles in the land of his father’s sojournings, in the land of Canaan.
These are the generations of Jacob.

Joseph, being seventeen years old, is pasturing the flock with his brothers. He is a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. And Joseph brings a bad report about them to their father.
Now Israel loves Joseph more than any of his other sons, because he is the son of his old age. And he makes him a long robe with sleeves.
But when his brothers see that their father loves him more than all his brothers, they hate him and cannot speak peaceably to him.
Now Joseph dreams a dream and tells it to his brothers, and they hate him even more.
He says to them, “Hear this dream that I have dreamed:
behold, we are binding sheaves in the field, and look — my sheaf rises and stands upright. And look — your sheaves gather around and bow down to my sheaf.”
“Are you indeed to reign over us? Are you indeed to rule over us?” his brothers say to him. And they hate him even more for his dreams and for his words.
Then he dreams another dream and tells it to his brothers: “Look — I have dreamed another dream. The sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”

But when he tells it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebukes him and says to him, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow down to the ground before you?”
And his brothers are jealous of him, but his father keeps the saying in mind.
Now his brothers go to pasture their father’s flock near Shechem.
And Israel says to Joseph, “Are not your brothers pasturing the flock near Shechem? Come — I will send you to them.”
“Here I am,” he says.
“Go now, see if it is well with your brothers and well with the flock, and bring me word.” So he sends him from the Valley of Hebron, and he comes to Shechem.
And a man finds him wandering in the fields. The man asks him, “What are you seeking?”
“I am seeking my brothers,” he says. “Tell me — where are they pasturing the flock?”
“They have moved on from here,” the man says. “I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’”
So Joseph goes after his brothers and finds them at Dothan.
They see him from afar, and before he comes near to them they conspire against him to kill him.
“Here comes this dreamer,” they say to one another.
“Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will become of his dreams.”
But when Reuben hears it, he rescues him out of their hands, saying, “Let us not take his life.”
“Do not shed blood,” Reuben says to them. “Throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him” — that he might rescue him out of their hand to restore him to his father.
So when Joseph comes to his brothers, they strip him of his robe — the long robe with sleeves that he is wearing.
And they take him and throw him into the pit. The pit is empty — there is no water in it.
Then they sit down to eat. And looking up, they see a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, going down to Egypt.
“What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?” Judah says to his brothers.
“Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him — for he is our brother, our own flesh.”
And his brothers listen to him.
Then Midianite traders pass by. And they pull Joseph up and lift him out of the pit and sell him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. They take Joseph to Egypt.
When Reuben returns to the pit and sees that Joseph is not in the pit, he tears his clothes
and returns to his brothers and says, “The boy is gone — and I, where shall I go?”
Then they take Joseph’s robe and slaughter a male goat and dip the robe in the blood.
And they send the long robe with sleeves and bring it to their father and say, “This we have found. Please identify whether it is your son’s robe or not.”
And he identifies it and says, “It is my son’s robe. A fierce animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces.”
Then Jacob tears his garments and puts sackcloth on his loins and mourns for his son many days.
All his sons and all his daughters rise up to comfort him, but he refuses to be comforted and says, “I shall go down to my son mourning, to Sheol.”
And his father weeps for him.
Meanwhile the Midianites had sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.
It happens at that time that Judah goes down from his brothers and turns aside to a certain Adullamite, whose name is Hirah.
There Judah sees the daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name is Shua. He takes her and goes in to her.
She conceives and bears a son, and he calls his name Er.
She conceives again and bears a son, and she calls his name Onan.
Yet again she bears a son, and she calls his name Shelah. Judah is in Chezib when she bears him.
And Judah takes a wife for Er his firstborn. Her name is Tamar.
But Er, Judah’s firstborn, is wicked in the sight of YHWH, and YHWH puts him to death.
Then Judah says to Onan, “Go in to your brother’s wife and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
But Onan knows that the offspring would not be his. So whenever he goes in to his brother’s wife he wastes the semen on the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother.
And what he does is wicked in the sight of YHWH, and he puts him to death also.
Then Judah says to Tamar his daughter-in-law, “Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up” — for he thinks, “Lest he die also, like his brothers.”
So Tamar goes and dwells in her father’s house.
In the course of time the wife of Judah, Shua’s daughter, dies. And when Judah is comforted, he goes up to Timnah to his sheepshearers, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
And it is told to Tamar, “Look — your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”

So she takes off her widow’s garments and covers herself with a veil, wrapping herself up, and sits at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah — for she sees that Shelah is grown up, and she has not been given to him as a wife.
When Judah sees her, he thinks she is a prostitute — for she has covered her face.
He turns aside to her at the road and says, “Come, let me come in to you.” For he does not know that she is his daughter-in-law.
“What will you give me, that you may come in to me?” she says.
“I will send you a young goat from the flock,” he says.
“If you give me a pledge until you send it —” she says.
“What pledge shall I give you?” he says.
“Your signet and your cord and your staff that is in your hand,” she says.
So he gives them to her and goes in to her, and she conceives by him.
Then she arises and goes away and takes off her veil and puts on her widow’s garments.
When Judah sends the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to take back the pledge from the woman’s hand, he does not find her.
And he asks the men of the place, “Where is the cult prostitute who was at Enaim at the road?”
“There has been no cult prostitute here,” they say.
So he returns to Judah and says, “I have not found her. And also the men of the place said, ‘There has been no cult prostitute here.’”
“Let her keep the things as her own,” Judah says. “Otherwise we shall be laughed at. Look — I sent this young goat, and you did not find her.”
About three months later Judah is told, “Tamar your daughter-in-law has been immoral. Moreover, she is pregnant by immorality.”
“Bring her out and let her be burned,” Judah says.
As she is being brought out, she sends word to her father-in-law: “By the man to whom these belong I am pregnant.”
And she says, “Please identify whose these are — the signet and the cord and the staff.”
Then Judah identifies them and says, “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.”
And he did not know her again.
When the time of her labour comes, there are twins in her womb.
And when she is in labour, one puts out a hand. And the midwife takes and ties a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, “This one came out first.”
But as he draws back his hand, look — his brother comes out. And she says, “What a breach you have made for yourself!” Therefore his name is called Perez.
Afterward his brother comes out with the scarlet thread on his hand, and his name is called Zerah.
Now Joseph has been brought down to Egypt. And Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, buys him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there.
And YHWH is with Joseph, and he becomes a successful man. He is in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master sees that YHWH is with him and that YHWH causes all that he does to succeed in his hands.
So Joseph finds favour in his sight and attends him, and he makes him overseer of his house and puts him in charge of all that he has.

From the time that he makes him overseer in his house and over all that he has, YHWH blesses the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. The blessing of YHWH is on everything that he has, in house and field.
So he leaves all that he has in Joseph’s charge, and because of him he has no concern about anything but the food he eats.
Now Joseph is handsome in form and appearance.
And after a time his master’s wife casts her eyes on Joseph and says, “Lie with me.”
But he refuses and says to his master’s wife, “Look — because of me my master has no concern about anything in the house, and he has put everything that he has in my charge.
He is not greater in this house than I am, and he has withheld nothing from me except you — because you are his wife. How then could I do this great wickedness and sin against God?”
And as she speaks to Joseph day after day, he does not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her.
But one day, when he goes into the house to do his work and none of the men of the house are there in the house,
she seizes him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me.” But he leaves his garment in her hand and flees and gets outside.
And as soon as she sees that he has left his garment in her hand and has fled outside,
she calls to the men of her household and says to them, “See, he has brought among us a Hebrew man to laugh at us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried out with a loud voice.
And as soon as he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled and got outside.”
Then she lays up his garment by her until his master comes home,
and she tells him the same story: “The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought among us, came in to me to laugh at me.
But as soon as I lifted up my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled outside.”
As soon as his master hears the words that his wife speaks to him — “This is what your servant did to me” — his anger burns.
And Joseph’s master takes him and puts him into the prison — the place where the king’s prisoners are confined. And he is there in prison.
But YHWH is with Joseph and shows him steadfast love and gives him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.
And the keeper of the prison puts Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who are in the prison. Whatever is done there, he is the one doing it.
The keeper of the prison pays no attention to anything that is in Joseph’s charge, because YHWH is with him. And whatever he does, YHWH makes it succeed.
Some time after this, the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and his baker offend against their lord the king of Egypt.
And Pharaoh is angry with his two officers — the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
And he puts them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph is confined.
The captain of the guard appoints Joseph to attend to them, and he attends them. They are in custody for some time.
And they both dream — the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who are confined in the prison — each his own dream, and each dream with its own interpretation, on the same night.
When Joseph comes to them in the morning, he sees that they are troubled.
So he asks Pharaoh’s officers who are with him in custody in his master’s house, “Why are your faces downcast today?”
“We have dreamed dreams,” they say to him, “and there is no one to interpret them.”
“Do not interpretations belong to God?” Joseph says to them. “Tell them to me, please.”
So the chief cupbearer tells his dream to Joseph and says to him, “In my dream there is a vine before me,
and on the vine there are three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms shot forth, and the clusters ripened into grapes.
Pharaoh’s cup is in my hand, and I take the grapes and press them into Pharaoh’s cup and place the cup in Pharaoh’s hand.”
“This is its interpretation,” Joseph says to him. “The three branches are three days.
In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your position. And you shall place Pharaoh’s cup in his hand as formerly, when you were his cupbearer.
Only remember me, when it is well with you, and please do me the kindness of mentioning me to Pharaoh, and so get me out of this house.
For I was indeed stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the pit.”
When the chief baker sees that the interpretation is favourable, he says to Joseph, “I also had a dream: there are three cake baskets on my head,
and in the uppermost basket there are all sorts of baked food for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating it out of the basket on my head.”
“This is its interpretation,” Joseph says. “The three baskets are three days.
In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head — from you — and hang you on a tree. And the birds will eat the flesh from you.”
On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he makes a feast for all his servants and lifts up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants.
He restores the chief cupbearer to his position, and the cupbearer places the cup in Pharaoh’s hand.
But the chief baker he hangs, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
Yet the chief cupbearer does not remember Joseph — he forgets him.
After two whole years, Pharaoh dreams that he is standing by the Nile.
And look — out of the Nile there come up seven cows, attractive and fat, and they feed in the reed grass.
And look — seven other cows, ugly and thin, come up out of the Nile after them and stand by the other cows on the bank of the Nile.
And the ugly, thin cows eat up the seven attractive, fat cows. And Pharaoh wakes.
Then he falls asleep and dreams a second time. And look — seven ears of grain, fat and good, are growing on a single stalk.
And look — seven ears, thin and blighted by the east wind, are sprouting up after them.
And the thin ears swallow up the seven fat, full ears. And Pharaoh wakes — and look, it is a dream.

So in the morning his spirit is troubled. He sends and calls for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men. And Pharaoh tells them his dreams, but there is no one who can interpret them to Pharaoh.
Then the chief cupbearer speaks to Pharaoh: “I remember my sins today.
When Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put me and the chief baker in custody in the house of the captain of the guard,
we dreamed on the same night, he and I — each of us with a dream with its own interpretation.
A young Hebrew man was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. When we told him, he interpreted our dreams to us — giving an interpretation to each man according to his dream.
And as he interpreted to us, so it was: I was restored to my position and he was hanged.”
Then Pharaoh sends and calls Joseph. And they quickly bring him out of the pit. And he shaves himself and changes his clothes and comes in to Pharaoh.
“I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it,” Pharaoh says to Joseph. “I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it.”
“It is not in me,” Joseph answers Pharaoh. “God will give Pharaoh a favourable answer.”
Then Pharaoh says to Joseph, “In my dream I am standing on the bank of the Nile.
Seven cows, fat and attractive, come up out of the Nile and feed in the reed grass.
Seven other cows come up after them — poor and very ugly and thin. I had never seen such ugly ones in all the land of Egypt.
And the thin, ugly cows ate up the first seven fat cows.
But when they had eaten them no one would have known they had eaten them — they were just as ugly as at the beginning. Then I woke.
I also saw in my dream: seven ears growing on a single stalk, full and good.
Seven ears, withered, thin, and blighted by the east wind, sprouted up after them.
And the thin ears swallowed up the seven good ears. I told it to the magicians, but there was no one who could tell me what it meant.”
“The dreams of Pharaoh are one,” Joseph says to Pharaoh. “God has revealed to Pharaoh what he is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years — the dreams are one.
The seven lean and ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and the seven empty ears blighted by the east wind are seven years of famine.
It is as I told Pharaoh: God has shown to Pharaoh what he is about to do.
There will come seven years of great abundance throughout all the land of Egypt.
After them seven years of famine will arise, and all the abundance will be forgotten in the land of Egypt. The famine will consume the land.
The abundance will be unknown in the land by reason of the famine that will follow, for it will be very severe.
And the doubling of Pharaoh’s dream means that the thing is fixed by God, and God will shortly bring it about.
Now therefore let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man and set him over the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh proceed to appoint overseers over the land and take one-fifth of the produce of the land of Egypt during the seven plentiful years.
And let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming and store up grain under the authority of Pharaoh for food in the cities and let them keep it.
That food shall be a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine that are to occur in the land of Egypt, so that the land may not perish through the famine.”
This proposal pleases Pharaoh and all his servants.
“Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?” Pharaoh says to his servants.
Then Pharaoh says to Joseph, “Since God has shown you all this, there is none so discerning and wise as you are.
You shall be over my house, and all my people shall order themselves as you command. Only as regards the throne will I be greater than you.”
And Pharaoh says to Joseph, “See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt.”
Then Pharaoh takes his signet ring from his hand and puts it on Joseph’s hand and clothes him in garments of fine linen and puts a gold chain about his neck.
And he makes him ride in his second chariot. And they call out before him, “Abrek!” And he sets him over all the land of Egypt.
“I am Pharaoh,” Pharaoh says to Joseph, “and without your consent no one shall lift up hand or foot in all the land of Egypt.”
And Pharaoh calls Joseph’s name Zaphenath-paneah. And he gives him in marriage Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On. So Joseph goes out over all the land of Egypt.
Joseph is thirty years old when he stands before Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh and went through all the land of Egypt.
During the seven plentiful years the earth produces abundantly.
And he gathers up all the food of these seven years, which occur in the land of Egypt, and puts the food in the cities. He puts in every city the food from the fields around it.
And Joseph stores up grain in great abundance, like the sand of the sea, until he stops measuring it, for it cannot be measured.
Before the year of famine comes, two sons are born to Joseph. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On, bears them to him.
Joseph calls the name of the firstborn Manasseh — “For God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s house.”
The name of the second he calls Ephraim — “For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
The seven years of plenty that occurred in the land of Egypt came to an end,
and the seven years of famine begin to come, as Joseph had said. There is famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there is bread.
When all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cry to Pharaoh for bread. And Pharaoh says to all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do.”
So when the famine has spread over all the land, Joseph opens all the storehouses and sells to the Egyptians. The famine is severe in the land of Egypt.
Moreover, all the earth comes to Egypt to Joseph to buy grain, because the famine is severe over all the earth.
When Jacob sees that there is grain in Egypt, Jacob says to his sons, “Why do you look at one another?”
“I have heard that there is grain in Egypt. Go down and buy grain for us there, that we may live and not die.”
So ten of Joseph’s brothers go down to buy grain in Egypt.
But Jacob does not send Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, with his brothers — for he fears that harm might happen to him.
Thus the sons of Israel come to buy among the others who come — for the famine is in the land of Canaan.
Now Joseph is governor over the land. He is the one who sells to all the people of the land. And Joseph’s brothers come and bow themselves before him with their faces to the ground.
Joseph sees his brothers and recognises them, but he treats them like strangers and speaks roughly to them. “Where do you come from?” he says to them.
“From the land of Canaan, to buy food,” they say.
And Joseph recognises his brothers, but they do not recognise him.
And Joseph remembers the dreams that he had dreamed about them and says to them, “You are spies. You have come to see the nakedness of the land.”
“No, my lord — your servants have come to buy food,” they say.
“We are all sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants have never been spies.”
“No,” he says to them. “You have come to see the nakedness of the land.”
“We, your servants, are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan. And look — the youngest is this day with our father, and one is no more.”
“It is as I said to you — you are spies.”
“By this you shall be tested: as Pharaoh lives, you shall not go from this place unless your youngest brother comes here.
Send one of you, and let him bring your brother, while you remain confined, that your words may be tested, whether there is truth in you. Or else, as Pharaoh lives, surely you are spies.”
And he puts them all together in custody for three days.
On the third day Joseph says to them, “Do this and you will live, for I fear God.
If you are honest men, let one of your brothers remain confined where you are in custody, and let the rest go and carry grain for the famished of your households.
And bring your youngest brother to me. So your words will be verified, and you shall not die.”
And they do so.
Then they say to one another, “In truth we are guilty concerning our brother. We saw the distress of his soul when he begged us, and we did not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us.”
“Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy?” Reuben answers them. “But you did not listen. So now there comes a reckoning for his blood.”
They do not know that Joseph understands them, for there is an interpreter between them.
And he turns away from them and weeps. Then he returns to them and speaks to them. And he takes Simeon from them and binds him before their eyes.
And Joseph gives orders to fill their bags with grain and to restore every man’s money in his sack and to give them provisions for the journey. This is done for them.
Then they load their donkeys with grain and depart.
And as one of them opens his sack to give his donkey fodder at the lodging place, he sees his money in the mouth of his sack.
“My money has been put back — here it is in my sack!” he says to his brothers. And their hearts fail them and they turn trembling to one another, saying, “What is this that God has done to us?”
When they come to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan, they tell him all that has happened to them:
“The man, the lord of the land, spoke roughly to us and took us to be spies of the land.
But we said to him, ‘We are honest men. We have never been spies.
We are twelve brothers, sons of our father. One is no more, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Canaan.’
Then the man, the lord of the land, said to us, ‘By this I shall know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain for the famished of your households, and go.
And bring your youngest brother to me. Then I shall know that you are not spies but honest men, and I will deliver your brother to you, and you shall trade in the land.’”
As they empty their sacks, look — every man’s bundle of money is in his sack. And when they and their father see their bundles of money, they are afraid.
“You have bereaved me of my children,” Jacob says to them. “Joseph is no more, and Simeon is no more, and now you would take Benjamin. All this has come against me.”
“Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you,” Reuben says to his father. “Put him in my charge, and I will bring him back to you.”

“My son shall not go down with you,” Jacob says, “for his brother is dead, and he is the only one left. If harm should happen to him on the journey that you are to make, you would bring down my grey hairs with sorrow to Sheol.”
Now the famine is severe in the land.
And when they have eaten up the grain that they brought from Egypt, their father says to them, “Go again, buy us a little food.”
But Judah says to him, “The man solemnly warned us, saying, ‘You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.’
If you will send our brother with us, we will go down and buy you food.
But if you will not send him, we will not go down — for the man said to us, ‘You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.’”
“Why did you treat me so badly as to tell the man that you had another brother?” Israel says.

“The man questioned us carefully about ourselves and our kindred,” they say. “‘Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?’ We answered him according to these questions. Could we in any way know that he would say, ‘Bring your brother down’?”
And Judah says to Israel his father, “Send the boy with me, and we will arise and go, that we may live and not die — both we and you and also our little ones.
I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame before you forever.
If we had not delayed, we could have been there and back twice by now.”

Then their father Israel says to them, “If it must be so, then do this: take some of the choice fruits of the land in your bags and carry a present down to the man — a little balm and a little honey, gum, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds.
Take double the money with you. Carry back with you the money that was returned in the mouth of your sacks — perhaps it was an oversight.
Take also your brother, and arise and go again to the man.
May El Shaddai grant you mercy before the man, and may he send back your other brother and Benjamin. And as for me — if I am bereaved, I am bereaved.”
So the men take this present, and they take double the money with them, and Benjamin. They arise and go down to Egypt and stand before Joseph.
When Joseph sees Benjamin with them, he says to the steward of his house, “Bring the men into the house and slaughter an animal and prepare it — for the men are to dine with me at noon.”
The man does as Joseph told him and brings the men to Joseph’s house.

And the men are afraid because they are brought to Joseph’s house. They say, “It is because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time that we are brought in — so that he may assault us and fall upon us and take us as servants and seize our donkeys.”
So they go up to the steward of Joseph’s house and speak with him at the door of the house
and say, “Oh, my lord, we came down the first time to buy food.
And when we came to the lodging place we opened our sacks, and there was each man’s money in the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight. So we have brought it back with us.
And we have brought other money down with us to buy food. We do not know who put our money in our sacks.”
“Peace to you, do not be afraid,” the steward says. “Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your money.”
And he brings Simeon out to them.
And when the man brings the men into Joseph’s house and gives them water, and they wash their feet, and he gives their donkeys fodder,
they prepare the present for Joseph’s coming at noon — for they hear that they shall eat bread there.
When Joseph comes home, they bring into the house to him the present that they have, and bow down to him to the ground.
And he asks them about their welfare and says, “Is your father well — the old man of whom you spoke? Is he still alive?”
“Your servant our father is well. He is still alive.” And they bow their heads down and prostrate themselves.
And he lifts up his eyes and sees his brother Benjamin, his mother’s son, and says, “Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me? God be gracious to you, my son.”
Then Joseph hurries out — for his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he seeks a place to weep. And he goes into his chamber and weeps there.
Then he washes his face and comes out. He restrains himself and says, “Serve the food.”

They serve him by himself, and them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves — because the Egyptians could not eat with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians.
And they sit before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth. And the men look at one another in amazement.
Portions are taken and sent to them from Joseph’s table, and Benjamin’s portion is five times as much as any of theirs. And they drink and are merry with him.
Then he commands the steward of his house: “Fill the men’s sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man’s money in the mouth of his sack.
And put my cup, the silver cup, in the mouth of the sack of the youngest, with his money for the grain.”
And he does as Joseph told him.
As soon as the morning is light, the men are sent away with their donkeys.
They have gone out of the city and are not yet far away when Joseph says to his steward, “Up, follow the men. And when you overtake them, say to them, ‘Why have you repaid evil for good?
Is it not from this that my lord drinks, and by this that he practises divination? You have done evil in doing this.’”
When he overtakes them, he speaks to them these same words.
They say to him, “Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing!
Look — the money that we found in the mouths of our sacks we brought back to you from the land of Canaan. How then could we steal silver or gold from your lord’s house?
Whichever of your servants is found with it shall die, and we also will be my lord’s servants.”
“Let it be as you say,” he says. “The one with whom it is found shall be my servant, but the rest of you shall be blameless.”
Then each man quickly lowers his sack to the ground, and each man opens his sack.
He searches, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest. And the cup is found in Benjamin’s sack.
Then they tear their garments, and every man loads his donkey, and they return to the city.
When Judah and his brothers come to Joseph’s house, he is still there. They fall before him to the ground.
“What deed is this that you have done?” Joseph says to them. “Do you not know that a man like me can indeed practise divination?”

“What shall we say to my lord?” Judah says. “What shall we speak? Or how can we clear ourselves? God has found out the guilt of your servants. Look — we are my lord’s servants, both we and he also in whose hand the cup has been found.”
“Far be it from me that I should do so!” he says. “Only the man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my servant. But as for you, go up in peace to your father.”
Then Judah goes up to him and says, “Oh, my lord, please let your servant speak a word in my lord’s ears, and let not your anger burn against your servant — for you are like Pharaoh himself.
My lord asked his servants, saying, ‘Have you a father, or a brother?’
And we said to my lord, ‘We have a father, an old man, and a young brother, the child of his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother’s children, and his father loves him.’
