“I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, ‘At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you shall know that I am YHWH your God.’”
In the evening quail come up and cover the camp. And in the morning dew lies around the camp.
And when the dew had gone up, there is on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground.
When the people of Israel see it, they say to one another, “What is it?” For they do not know what it is.
“It is the bread that YHWH has given you to eat,” Moses says to them.
“This is what YHWH has commanded: ‘Gather of it, each one of you, as much as he can eat. You shall each take an omer according to the number of the persons that each of you has in his tent.’”
And the people of Israel do so. They gather, some more, some less.
But when they measure it with an omer, whoever gathered much has nothing left over, and whoever gathered little has no lack. Each of them gathers as much as he can eat.
And Moses says to them, “Let no one leave any of it over until the morning.”
But they do not listen to Moses. Some leave part of it until the morning, and it breeds worms and stinks. And Moses is angry with them.
Morning by morning they gather it, each as much as he can eat. But when the sun grows hot, it melts.
On the sixth day they gather twice as much bread, two omers each. And when all the leaders of the congregation come and tell Moses,

he says to them, “This is what YHWH has commanded: ‘Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to YHWH. Bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over lay aside to be kept until the morning.’”
So they lay it aside until the morning, as Moses commanded them. And it does not stink, and there are no worms in it.
“Eat it today,” Moses says, “for today is a Sabbath to YHWH. Today you will not find it in the field.
Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is a Sabbath, there will be none.”
On the seventh day some of the people go out to gather, but they find none.
And YHWH says to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?
See! YHWH has given you the Sabbath. Therefore on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Remain each of you in his place. Let no one go out of his place on the seventh day.”
So the people rest on the seventh day.
Now the house of Israel calls its name manna. It is like coriander seed, white, and the taste of it is like wafers made with honey.

Moses says, “This is what YHWH has commanded: ‘Let an omer of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’”
And Moses says to Aaron, “Take a jar and put an omer of manna in it, and place it before YHWH to be kept throughout your generations.”
As YHWH commanded Moses, so Aaron places it before the testimony to be kept.
The people of Israel eat the manna forty years, until they come to a habitable land. They eat the manna until they come to the border of the land of Canaan.
(An omer is the tenth part of an ephah.)

All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of YHWH, and camped at Rephidim. But there was no water for the people to drink.
Therefore the people quarrel with Moses and say, “Give us water to drink.”
“Why do you quarrel with me?” Moses says to them. “Why do you test YHWH?”
But the people thirst there for water, and the people grumble against Moses and say, “Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?”
So Moses cries to YHWH, “What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me.”
“Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile and go.”
“Look — I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink.”
And Moses does so, in the sight of the elders of Israel.
And he calls the name of the place Massah and Meribah — because of the quarrelling of the people of Israel, and because they tested YHWH by saying, “Is YHWH among us or not?”
Then Amalek comes and fights with Israel at Rephidim.
So Moses says to Joshua, “Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.”
So Joshua does as Moses told him, and fights with Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur go up to the top of the hill.
Whenever Moses holds up his hand, Israel prevails. And whenever he lowers his hand, Amalek prevails.

But Moses’ hands grow heavy, so they take a stone and put it under him, and he sits on it. Aaron and Hur hold up his hands, one on one side and one on the other side. So his hands are steady until the going down of the sun.
And Joshua overwhelms Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.
Then YHWH says to Moses, “Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the hearing of Joshua, that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”
And Moses builds an altar and calls the name of it, YHWH-Nissi,
saying, “A hand upon the throne of YHWH! YHWH will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.”
Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses’ father-in-law, hears of all that God has done for Moses and for Israel his people, how YHWH brought Israel out of Egypt.
Now Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, had taken Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after he had sent her home,
along with her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom (for Moses said, “I have been a sojourner in a foreign land”),
and the name of the other was Eliezer (for he said, “The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh”).
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, comes with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he is encamped at the mountain of God.
And he sends word to Moses, “I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons.”
Moses goes out to meet his father-in-law and bows down and kisses him. And they ask each other of their welfare and go into the tent.
Then Moses tells his father-in-law all that YHWH had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel’s sake, all the hardship that had come upon them in the way, and how YHWH had delivered them.
And Jethro rejoices for all the good that YHWH had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians.
Jethro says, “Blessed be YHWH, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh and has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians.
Now I know that YHWH is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people.”
And Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, brings a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. And Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law before God.
The next day Moses sits to judge the people, and the people stand around Moses from morning till evening.

When Moses’ father-in-law sees all that he is doing for the people, he says, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning till evening?”
“Because the people come to me to inquire of God,” Moses says to his father-in-law.
“When they have a dispute, they come to me and I decide between one person and another, and I make them know the statutes of God and his laws.”
“What you are doing is not good,” Moses’ father-in-law says to him.
“You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone.
Listen now to my voice. I will give you counsel, and God be with you! You shall represent the people before God and bring their cases to God.
You shall warn them about the statutes and the laws, and make them know the way in which they must walk and what they must do.

Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people as chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.

And let them judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, but any small matter they shall decide themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you.
If you do this, God will direct you, you will be able to endure, and all this people also will go to their place in peace.”
So Moses listens to the voice of his father-in-law and does all that he has said.
Moses chooses able men out of all Israel and makes them heads over the people — chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.
And they judge the people at all times. Any hard case they bring to Moses, but any small matter they decide themselves.
Then Moses lets his father-in-law depart, and he goes away to his own country.
On the third new moon after the people of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that very day, they came into the wilderness of Sinai.
They set out from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in the wilderness. And Israel encamped there before the mountain.
And Moses goes up to God. And YHWH calls to him out of the mountain, saying, “Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and tell the people of Israel:
‘You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.
Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine.
And you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.’ These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel.”
So Moses comes and calls the elders of the people and sets before them all these words that YHWH had commanded him.
All the people answer together and say, “All that YHWH has spoken we will do.”
And Moses reports the words of the people to YHWH.
And YHWH says to Moses, “Look — I am coming to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you and may also believe you forever.”
When Moses told YHWH the words of the people,
YHWH says to Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments
and be ready for the third day. For on the third day YHWH will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.
And you shall set limits for the people all around, saying, ‘Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death.
No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot. Whether beast or man, he shall not live.’ When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they shall come up to the mountain.”
So Moses goes down from the mountain to the people and consecrates the people. And they wash their garments.
And he says to the people, “Be ready for the third day. Do not go near a woman.”
On the morning of the third day there are thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp tremble.
Then Moses brings the people out of the camp to meet God, and they take their stand at the foot of the mountain.
Now Mount Sinai is wrapped in smoke because YHWH has come down on it in fire. The smoke of it goes up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembles greatly.
And as the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder.
YHWH comes down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. And YHWH calls Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses goes up.
And YHWH says to Moses, “Go down and warn the people, lest they break through to YHWH to look and many of them perish.
Also let the priests who come near to YHWH consecrate themselves, lest YHWH break out against them.”
“The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai,” Moses says to YHWH, “for you yourself warned us, saying, ‘Set limits around the mountain and consecrate it.’”
And YHWH says to him, “Go down, and come up bringing Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people break through to come up to YHWH, lest he break out against them.”
So Moses goes down to the people and tells them.
And God speaks all these words:
The Prologue
“I am YHWH your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
The First Word
“You shall have no other gods before me.
The Second Word
“You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.
You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I YHWH your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and the fourth generation of those who hate me,
but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
The Third Word
“You shall not take the name of YHWH your God in vain, for YHWH will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.
The Fourth Word
“Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
Six days you shall labour and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to YHWH your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates.
For in six days YHWH made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore YHWH blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.
The Fifth Word
“Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that YHWH your God is giving you.
The Sixth Word
“You shall not murder.
The Seventh Word
“You shall not commit adultery.
The Eighth Word
“You shall not steal.
The Ninth Word
“You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.
The Tenth Word
“You shall not covet your neighbor’s house. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor’s.”
Now when all the people see the thunder and the lightning flashes and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people are afraid and tremble, and they stand far off.
And they say to Moses, “You speak to us, and we will listen. But do not let God speak to us, lest we die.”
“Do not be afraid,” Moses says to the people. “For God has come to test you, so that the fear of him may be before you, so that you may not sin.”
The people stand far off, while Moses draws near to the thick darkness where God is.
And YHWH says to Moses, “Thus you shall say to the people of Israel: ‘You have seen for yourselves that I have talked with you from heaven.
You shall not make gods of silver to be with me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold.

An altar of earth you shall make for me and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you.
If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it.
And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, that your nakedness be not exposed on it.’”
Now these are the rules that you shall set before them.
“When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.
If he comes in single, he shall go out single. If he comes in married, then his wife shall go out with him.
If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master’s, and he shall go out alone.
But if the slave plainly says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children. I will not go out free,’
then his master shall bring him to God, and he shall bring him to the door or the doorpost. And his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever.
“When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do.
If she does not please her master, who has designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her.
If he designates her for his son, he shall deal with her as with a daughter.
If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, or her marital rights.
And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money.
“Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death.
But if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.
But if a man wilfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die.
“Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death.
“Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death.
“Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.
“When men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist and the man does not die but takes to his bed,
then if the man rises again and walks outdoors with his staff, he who struck him shall be clear. Only he shall pay for the loss of his time and shall have him thoroughly healed.
“When a man strikes his slave, male or female, with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, he shall be avenged.
But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money.

“When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm, the one who hit her shall surely be fined, as the woman’s husband shall impose on him, and he shall pay as the judges determine.
But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
“When a man strikes the eye of his slave, male or female, and destroys it, he shall let the slave go free because of his eye.
If he knocks out the tooth of his slave, male or female, he shall let the slave go free because of his tooth.
“When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten, but the owner of the ox shall not be liable.

But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death.
If a ransom is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed on him.
If it gores a man’s son or daughter, he shall be dealt with according to this same rule.
If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.
“When a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit shall make restoration. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead animal shall be his.
“When one man’s ox butts another’s ox and it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and share its price, and the dead beast also they shall share.
Or if it is known that the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall repay ox for ox, and the dead beast shall be his.
When a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for the ox and four sheep for the sheep.
If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there is no bloodguilt for him.
But if the sun has risen on him, there is bloodguilt for him. He must make full restitution. If he has nothing, he is sold for his theft.
If the stolen animal — ox, donkey, or sheep — is found alive in his possession, he shall pay double.
When a man lets his animal loose and it grazes in another man's field or vineyard, he shall make restitution from the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.
When fire breaks out and catches in thorns, so that stacked grain or standing grain or the field itself is consumed, whoever started the fire shall make full restitution.
When a man gives his neighbour money or goods to keep safe, and they are stolen from the neighbour's house — if the thief is found, the thief shall pay double.
If the thief is not found, the owner of the house shall come before God to show whether or not he has laid his hand on his neighbour's property.

In every case of disputed ownership — whether ox, donkey, sheep, clothing, or any lost thing of which someone says, ‘This is mine’ — the case of both parties shall come before God. Whoever God declares guilty shall pay double to his neighbour.
When a man gives his neighbour a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any animal to keep, and it dies or is injured or is driven away, with no one watching —
an oath by YHWH shall be made between them to determine whether or not he has laid his hand on his neighbour’s property. The owner shall accept the oath, and no restitution shall be required.
But if it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to its owner.
If it is torn by a wild animal, he brings the remains as evidence — he need not make restitution for what was torn.
When a man borrows an animal from his neighbour and it is injured or dies while the owner is not with it, the borrower shall make full restitution.
If the owner was with it, no restitution is required. If it was hired out, the loss is covered by the hire fee.
When a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall pay the bride-price and take her as his wife.
If her father refuses outright to give her to him, he shall still pay the bride-price for virgins.
You shall not let a sorceress live.
Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death.
Whoever sacrifices to any god other than YHWH alone shall be put under the ban.
You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him — for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.
You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child.
If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry.
My anger will burn, and I will kill you with the sword. Your wives will become widows and your children fatherless.
If you lend money to any of my people who is poor, you shall not act like a creditor toward him — do not charge him interest.
If you take your neighbour’s cloak in pledge, return it to him before the sun goes down.
It is his only covering — his cloak for his body. In what else will he sleep? And if he cries to me, I will hear him, for I am compassionate.
You shall not revile God, and you shall not curse a ruler of your people.
You shall not hold back from offering the fullness of your harvest and the outflow of your presses. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me.
Do the same with your oxen and your sheep — seven days the young shall remain with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me.
You shall be consecrated to me. Therefore you shall not eat any flesh that has been torn by wild animals in the field — throw it to the dogs.
You shall not spread a false report. Do not join hands with the wicked to be a malicious witness.
You shall not follow a crowd to do evil, nor shall you testify in a lawsuit by siding with a crowd in order to pervert justice.
You shall not show partiality to a poor man in his lawsuit.
When you come across your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him.
When you see the donkey of someone who hates you lying down under its load, you shall resist the urge to leave it — you shall help him with it.
You shall not pervert the justice due to your poor in his lawsuit.
Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and the righteous — for I will not acquit the wicked.
And you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the words of the righteous.
You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.
For six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield.

But in the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, so that the poor among your people may eat. What they leave, the wild animals may eat. Do the same with your vineyard and your olive orchard.
Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest — so that your ox and your donkey may rest, and the son of your female servant and the sojourner may be refreshed.
Pay attention to everything I have told you. Make no mention of the names of other gods — let them not be heard on your lips.
Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me.

You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time in the month of Abib — for in it you came out of Egypt. No one shall appear before me empty-handed.

You shall keep the Feast of Harvest, with the firstfruits of your labour, of what you sow in the field. You shall also keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather in from the field the fruit of your labour.
Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord YHWH.
You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, and the fat of my feast shall not remain until the morning.
The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of YHWH your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.
I am sending an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place I have prepared.
Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice. Do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him.
But if you carefully obey his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.
When my angel goes before you and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I blot them out —
you shall not bow down to their gods or serve them or do as they do. You shall utterly overthrow them and break their pillars in pieces.
You shall serve YHWH your God, and he will bless your bread and your water. I will take sickness away from among you.
None shall miscarry or be barren in your land. I will fulfil the number of your days.
I will send my terror before you and throw into confusion all the people against whom you shall come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.
And I will send hornets before you, which shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite from before you.
I will not drive them out from before you in a single year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you.
Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land.

And I will set your border from the Sea of Reeds to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates — for I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you.
You shall make no covenant with them and their gods.
They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me. For if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you.
And he says to Moses, “Come up to YHWH — you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel — and worship from afar.
Moses alone shall come near to YHWH. The others shall not come near, and the people shall not come up with him.”
Moses comes and tells the people all the words of YHWH and all the rules. All the people answer with a single voice: “Everything YHWH has spoken we will do.”
Moses writes down all the words of YHWH. He rises early in the morning and builds an altar at the foot of the mountain, along with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel.
He sends young men of the people of Israel, and they offer burnt offerings and sacrifice peace offerings of oxen to YHWH.
Moses takes half of the blood and puts it in basins. The other half he throws against the altar.
Then he takes the Book of the Covenant and reads it aloud to the people. They say, “Everything YHWH has spoken we will do, and we will obey.”
Moses takes the blood and throws it on the people. “See,” he says, “the blood of the covenant that YHWH has made with you in accordance with all these words.”
Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel go up.
And they see the God of Israel. Under his feet there is something like a pavement of sapphire stone — like the very sky in its clearness.
He does not lay his hand against the chief men of the people of Israel. They behold God. And they eat and drink.
YHWH says to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain and wait there. I will give you the tablets of stone — the law and the commandment — which I have written for their instruction.”
Moses rises, and his attendant Joshua with him. Moses goes up into the mountain of God.
He says to the elders, “Wait here for us until we come back to you. Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever has a dispute, let him bring it to them.”
Moses goes up onto the mountain, and the cloud covers the mountain.
The glory of YHWH settles on Mount Sinai. The cloud covers it for six days, and on the seventh day he calls to Moses out of the cloud.
To the eyes of the people of Israel, the appearance of the glory of YHWH is like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain.
Moses enters the cloud and goes up on the mountain. And Moses is on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
The Contribution · 25:1–9
YHWH speaks to Moses:
"Speak to the people of Israel, that they bring me a contribution. From every person whose heart moves him, you shall receive the contribution for me.
And this is the contribution you shall receive from them: gold, silver, and bronze;
blue and purple and crimson yarns, and fine linen; goats' hair;
tanned rams' skins; fine leather; acacia wood;
oil for the lamps; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense;
onyx stones, and stones for setting in the ephod and the breastpiece.
And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst.
Exactly as I show you — the pattern of the Tabernacle and the pattern of all its furnishings — so you shall make it.
The Ark · 25:10–22
They shall make an ark of acacia wood — two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, and a cubit and a half high.
You shall overlay it with pure gold, inside and outside, and make a moulding of gold around it.
Cast four rings of gold for it and attach them to its four feet — two rings on one side, two rings on the other.
Make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.
Put the poles through the rings on the sides of the ark, to carry it by them.
The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark — they shall not be removed from it.
And you shall place in the ark the testimony that I will give you.
You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold — two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide.
Make two cherubim of gold — of hammered work — on the two ends of the mercy seat.
One cherub at one end, one cherub at the other end. The cherubim shall be of one piece with the mercy seat at its two ends.
The cherubim shall spread their wings upward, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, facing one another — their faces turned toward the mercy seat.
You shall set the mercy seat on top of the ark, and in the ark you shall place the testimony I will give you.

There I will meet with you. From above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about everything I command you for the people of Israel.
The Table · 25:23–30
You shall make a table of acacia wood — two cubits long, one cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high.
Overlay it with pure gold and make a moulding of gold around it.
Make a rim around it a handsbreadth wide, and a moulding of gold around the rim.
Make four rings of gold for it and fasten the rings at the four corners, at its four legs.
The rings shall sit close to the rim, as holders for the poles to carry the table.
Make the poles of acacia wood, overlay them with gold, and carry the table with them.
Make its plates and dishes, its flagons and bowls for the drink offerings — make them of pure gold.
And you shall set the bread of the Presence on the table before me at all times.
The Lampstand · 25:31–40
You shall make a lampstand of pure gold. The lampstand shall be of hammered work — its base, its shaft, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers all of one piece with it.
Six branches shall extend from its sides — three from one side, three from the other.

Three cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on one branch — and three cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on the other branch. So for all six branches extending from the lampstand.
And on the shaft of the lampstand itself, four cups shaped like almond blossoms, with their calyxes and flowers —
a calyx of one piece with it under each pair of the six branches extending from it.
Their calyxes and their branches shall be of one piece with it — the whole thing a single piece of hammered work, pure gold.
Make seven lamps for it. Set up its lamps so they give light to the space in front of it.
Its snuffers and trays shall be of pure gold.
It shall be made, with all these utensils, from a talent of pure gold.
And see that you make everything after the pattern being shown you on the mountain.
The Linen Curtains · 26:1–6
You shall make the Tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twisted linen — blue and purple and crimson yarns — worked with cherubim by a skilled craftsman.
Each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide — all the curtains the same size.
Five curtains shall be joined to one another, and the other five joined to one another.
Make loops of blue along the edge of the outermost curtain of the first set, and likewise along the edge of the outermost curtain of the second set.
Make fifty loops on the one curtain, and fifty loops on the edge of the curtain in the second set — the loops opposite one another.
Make fifty clasps of gold, and join the curtains to one another with the clasps, so that the Tabernacle is a single whole.
The Goat-Hair Tent · 26:7–14
You shall make curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the Tabernacle — eleven curtains in all.
Each curtain shall be thirty cubits long and four cubits wide — all eleven the same size.
Join five curtains together and six together, then fold the sixth curtain double over the front of the tent.
Make fifty loops on the edge of the outermost curtain in one set, and fifty loops on the edge of the outermost curtain in the other.
Make fifty bronze clasps, put them through the loops, and join the tent into a single whole.
The extra half-curtain that remains shall hang down over the back of the Tabernacle.
The cubit of overhang on either side, in the length of the curtains, shall drape down over the sides of the Tabernacle to cover it.
And make for the tent a covering of tanned rams' skins, and over that a covering of fine leather.
The Frames · 26:15–30
Make upright frames for the Tabernacle of acacia wood.
Each frame shall be ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide.
Each frame shall have two tenons for fitting together. Make all the frames this way.
Make twenty frames for the south side of the Tabernacle.
Make forty silver bases under the twenty frames — two bases under each frame for its two tenons.
For the north side of the Tabernacle, twenty frames
and forty silver bases — two bases under each frame.
For the rear of the Tabernacle, on the west, make six frames.
Make two frames for the corners of the Tabernacle at the rear.
These shall be joined at the bottom and meet at the top in a single ring — both corner frames shall be made this way.
There shall be eight frames in all, with their sixteen silver bases — two under each frame.
Make bars of acacia wood — five for the frames of one side of the Tabernacle,
five for the other side, and five for the rear on the west.
The middle bar shall run through the centre of the frames from end to end.
Overlay the frames with gold, make their rings of gold as holders for the bars, and overlay the bars with gold.
Then erect the Tabernacle according to the plan shown you on the mountain.
The Inner Veil · 26:31–35
Make a veil of blue and purple and crimson yarns and fine twisted linen — worked with cherubim by a skilled craftsman.
Hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold, with hooks of gold, set in four bases of silver.
Hang the veil from the clasps and bring the ark of the testimony inside the veil. The veil shall divide for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy.
Set the mercy seat on the ark of the testimony in the Most Holy Place.
Place the table outside the veil on the north side of the Tabernacle, and the lampstand opposite the table on the south side.
The Entrance Screen · 26:36–37
For the entrance of the tent, make a screen of blue and purple and crimson yarns and fine twisted linen — embroidered work.
Make five pillars of acacia for the screen, overlay them with gold, provide them with hooks of gold, and cast five bronze bases for them.
The Altar of Burnt Offering · 27:1–8
Make the altar of acacia wood — five cubits long, five cubits wide. The altar shall be square, three cubits high.
Make horns for it at its four corners — the horns shall be of one piece with it — and overlay it with bronze.
Make pots for removing its ashes, shovels, basins, forks, and firepans. Make all its utensils of bronze.
Make a grating of bronze mesh for it, and on the mesh make four bronze rings at its four corners.
Set the grating under the ledge of the altar, so the mesh extends halfway down.
Make poles for the altar of acacia wood and overlay them with bronze.
The poles shall be put through the rings, so they sit on the two sides of the altar when it is carried.
Make it hollow, with planks. As it has been shown you on the mountain — so it shall be made.
The Court · 27:9–19
Make the court of the Tabernacle. On the south side, the court shall have hangings of fine twisted linen, one hundred cubits long.
Twenty pillars with twenty bronze bases, and hooks and bands for the pillars of silver.
Likewise on the north side — hangings one hundred cubits long, twenty pillars, twenty bronze bases, with silver hooks and bands.
On the west side, hangings fifty cubits long with ten pillars and ten bases.
The width of the court on the east — the front — shall be fifty cubits.
The hangings for one side of the gate shall be fifteen cubits, with three pillars and three bases.
On the other side, hangings of fifteen cubits, with three pillars and three bases.
For the gate of the court, a screen of twenty cubits — blue and purple and crimson yarns and fine twisted linen, embroidered work — with four pillars and four bases.
All the pillars around the court shall be banded with silver. Their hooks shall be of silver and their bases of bronze.
The court shall be one hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and five cubits high, with hangings of fine twisted linen and bases of bronze.
All the utensils of the Tabernacle for every use, and all its pegs, and all the pegs of the court — all of bronze.
The Perpetual Lamp · 27:20–21
Command the people of Israel to bring you pure beaten olive oil for the light, so that a lamp may burn regularly.

In the tent of meeting, outside the veil that hangs before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening to morning before YHWH. This shall be a permanent statute for the people of Israel throughout all their generations.
The Priestly Garments Commanded · 28:1–5
Bring forward Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, from among the people of Israel — Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar — to serve me as priests.
Make sacred garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and for beauty.
Speak to all the skilled craftsmen I have filled with a spirit of skill, and have them make Aaron's garments to consecrate him for my priesthood.

These are the garments they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash. They shall make these sacred garments for your brother Aaron and his sons, for them to serve me as priests.
They shall use gold and blue and purple and crimson yarns, and fine linen.
The Ephod · 28:6–14
They shall make the ephod of gold, blue and purple and crimson yarns, and fine twisted linen — skillfully worked.
It shall have two shoulder pieces joined to its two edges, so that it holds together.
The woven band on it shall be of one piece with it and made the same way — of gold, blue and purple and crimson yarns, and fine twisted linen.
Take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel —
six names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, in order of their birth.
Engrave the two stones with the names of the sons of Israel as a jeweller engraves a seal, and set them in gold filigree.
Fasten the two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel. Aaron shall bear their names on his two shoulders before YHWH as a remembrance.
Make settings of gold filigree
and two chains of pure gold, twisted like cords, and attach the chains to the settings.
The Breastpiece · 28:15–30
Make the breastpiece of judgment in skilled work — in the manner of the ephod, of gold, blue and purple and crimson yarns, and fine twisted linen.
It shall be square and doubled — a span in length and a span in width.
Set it with four rows of stones. The first row: a ruby, a topaz, and an emerald.
The second row: a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond.
The third row: a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst.
The fourth row: a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. Set them in gold filigree.
The twelve stones shall bear the names of the sons of Israel — one name for each stone, engraved like a seal, for the twelve tribes.
Make for the breastpiece twisted chains of pure gold, like cords.
Make two gold rings for the breastpiece and attach them to its two upper corners.
Fasten the two gold cords to the two rings at the corners of the breastpiece.
Attach the other ends of the cords to the two filigree settings at the front of the ephod's shoulder pieces.
Make two more rings of gold and place them at the two lower corners of the breastpiece, on the inner edge next to the ephod.
Make two more gold rings and attach them to the lower part of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, at the front, close to its seam above the woven band.
Bind the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a cord of blue, so that it rests against the woven band of the ephod and does not come loose from it.
Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart when he goes into the Holy Place — a continual remembrance before YHWH.

Place the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece of judgment. They shall be over Aaron's heart when he goes in before YHWH. So Aaron shall carry the judgment of the people of Israel on his heart before YHWH at all times.
The Robe · 28:31–35
Make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue.
It shall have an opening for the head in the centre, with a woven collar around the opening — like the neck of armour — so that it will not tear.
On its hem make pomegranates of blue and purple and crimson yarns all around, with bells of gold between them —
a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, all the way around the hem of the robe.
Aaron shall wear it when he ministers. Its sound shall be heard when he goes into the Holy Place before YHWH and when he comes out — so that he does not die.
The Golden Plate · 28:36–38
Make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it as on a seal: Holy to YHWH.
Fasten it to the turban with a cord of blue — it shall sit on the front of the turban.

It shall be on Aaron's forehead. Aaron shall bear the guilt arising from the holy things the people of Israel consecrate as their offerings. It shall always be on his forehead, so that they may find acceptance before YHWH.
The Tunic, Turban, and Sash · 28:39–43
Weave the tunic of fine linen in a checked pattern. Make a turban of fine linen and a sash of embroidered work.
For Aaron's sons make tunics, sashes, and headbands — for glory and for beauty.
Dress Aaron your brother and his sons in these garments, anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them to serve me as priests.
Make linen undergarments for them to cover their naked flesh, reaching from waist to thigh.

Aaron and his sons shall wear them when they go into the tent of meeting or approach the altar to serve in the Holy Place — so that they do not bear guilt and die. This shall be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants after him.
The Offerings for Consecration · 29:1–3
This is what you shall do to consecrate them for the priesthood. Take one young bull and two rams without blemish,
and unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil — make them all of fine wheat flour.
Put them in a single basket and bring them along with the bull and the two rams.
The Washing and the Robing · 29:4–9
Bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water.
Take the garments and dress Aaron in the tunic, the robe of the ephod, the ephod itself, and the breastpiece, and fasten the woven band of the ephod around him.
Set the turban on his head and place the holy crown on the turban.
Take the anointing oil and pour it on his head and anoint him.
Then bring his sons forward and put the tunics on them,
and bind the sashes around them and tie the headbands on them. The priesthood shall be theirs as a permanent statute. This is how you shall ordain Aaron and his sons.
The Bull of Purification · 29:10–14
Bring the bull to the front of the tent of meeting. Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the bull's head,
and you shall slaughter the bull before YHWH at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
Take some of the bull's blood and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger, and pour out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar.
Take all the fat that covers the entrails — the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat — and burn them on the altar.
But the flesh of the bull, its hide, and its dung you shall burn outside the camp. It is a purification offering.
The First Ram: Burnt Offering · 29:15–18
Take one of the rams. Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on its head,
and you shall slaughter it, take its blood, and throw it against all sides of the altar.
Cut the ram into pieces. Wash its entrails and legs and set them with the pieces and the head.
Then burn the whole ram on the altar. It is a burnt offering to YHWH — a pleasing aroma, a food offering to YHWH.
The Second Ram: Ordination · 29:19–28
Take the second ram. Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on its head,

and you shall slaughter it. Take some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the right ears of his sons, on the thumbs of their right hands, and on the big toes of their right feet. Then throw the rest of the blood against all sides of the altar.

Take some of the blood from the altar and some of the anointing oil and sprinkle them on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and their garments. He and his garments will be holy — his sons and their garments with him.
From the ram take the fat — the fat tail, the fat covering the entrails, the long lobe of the liver, the two kidneys and their fat, and the right thigh (for this is the ram of ordination) —
along with one loaf of bread, one cake of oil-bread, and one wafer from the basket of unleavened bread that sits before YHWH.
Place all of these on the palms of Aaron and his sons and wave them as a wave offering before YHWH.
Then take them from their hands and burn them on the altar on top of the burnt offering — a pleasing aroma before YHWH, a food offering to YHWH.
Take the breast of the ram of Aaron's ordination and wave it as a wave offering before YHWH. This shall be your portion.
Consecrate the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the priests' contribution — what was waved and what was lifted from the ram of ordination, from Aaron's portion and from his sons' —
as a permanent due for Aaron and his sons from the people of Israel. It is a contribution: the people's contribution to YHWH from their peace offerings.
The Seven Days of Ordination · 29:29–37
The sacred garments of Aaron shall pass to his sons after him. They shall be anointed in them and ordained in them.
The son who succeeds him as high priest — the one who enters the tent of meeting to serve in the Holy Place — shall wear them for seven days.
Take the ram of ordination and cook its flesh in a holy place.
Aaron and his sons shall eat the ram's flesh and the bread in the basket at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
They shall eat what was used to make atonement at their ordination and consecration. No outsider may eat it — it is holy.
If any of the ordination flesh or bread remains until morning, burn it. It is not to be eaten — it is holy.
Do all of this for Aaron and his sons exactly as I have commanded you. Ordain them over seven days.
Each day offer a bull as a purification offering for atonement. Purify the altar by making atonement for it, and anoint it to consecrate it.
Spend seven days making atonement for the altar and consecrating it. The altar will be most holy — whatever touches it will become holy.
The Daily Burnt Offering · 29:38–46
This is what you shall offer on the altar: two year-old lambs, every day, regularly.
Offer one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight.
With the first lamb, a tenth measure of fine flour mixed with a quarter hin of pressed oil, and a quarter hin of wine as a drink offering.
Offer the second lamb at twilight, with the same grain offering and drink offering as in the morning — a pleasing aroma, a food offering to YHWH.
This shall be the regular burnt offering throughout your generations, at the entrance of the tent of meeting before YHWH — where I will meet with you to speak to you there.
There I will meet with the people of Israel, and it will be made holy by my glory.
I will consecrate the tent of meeting and the altar. Aaron and his sons I will consecrate to serve me as priests.
I will dwell among the people of Israel and be their God.
And they shall know that I am YHWH their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt so that I might dwell among them. I am YHWH their God.
The Altar of Incense · 30:1–10
Make an altar for burning incense — make it of acacia wood.
It shall be a cubit long and a cubit wide — square — and two cubits high. Its horns shall be of one piece with it.
Overlay its top and all its sides and its horns with pure gold, and make a moulding of gold around it.
Make two gold rings for it under its moulding on opposite sides, as holders for the poles used to carry it.
Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.
Place it in front of the veil that hangs above the ark of the testimony — in front of the mercy seat that is above the testimony — where I will meet with you.
Aaron shall burn fragrant incense on it every morning when he tends the lamps —
and when Aaron sets the lamps at twilight he shall burn it again. This is the regular incense offering before YHWH throughout your generations.
Do not offer unauthorised incense on it, or a burnt offering, or a grain offering. Do not pour a drink offering on it.

Once a year Aaron shall make atonement on its horns. With the blood of the annual purification offering he shall make atonement for it — once a year, throughout your generations. It is most holy to YHWH.
The Census Tax · 30:11–16
YHWH speaks to Moses:
"When you take a census of the people of Israel, each one shall give a ransom for himself to YHWH when they are counted — so that no plague breaks out among them when they are numbered.
Everyone who is counted shall give a half-shekel, by the sanctuary standard — the shekel being twenty gerahs. Half a shekel is the offering to YHWH.
Everyone counted in the census, twenty years old and over, shall give this offering to YHWH.
The rich shall give no more and the poor shall give no less than the half-shekel when making this offering to YHWH to atone for your lives.
Receive the atonement money from the people of Israel and use it for the service of the tent of meeting. It will be a memorial for the people of Israel before YHWH — an atonement for your lives."
The Bronze Basin · 30:17–21
YHWH speaks to Moses:
"Make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. Place it between the tent of meeting and the altar and put water in it.
Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet from it.
Whenever they enter the tent of meeting or come near the altar to serve — to offer a food offering to YHWH — they shall wash with water so that they do not die.
They shall wash their hands and feet so that they do not die. This is a permanent statute for them — for Aaron and his descendants throughout their generations."
The Anointing Oil · 30:22–33
YHWH speaks to Moses:
"Take the finest spices: five hundred shekels of liquid myrrh, half that amount — two hundred and fifty shekels — of fragrant cinnamon, two hundred and fifty shekels of fragrant cane,
five hundred shekels of cassia — all by the sanctuary standard — and a hin of olive oil.
From these make a sacred anointing oil, blended by a skilled perfumer. It shall be the holy anointing oil.
With it anoint the tent of meeting and the ark of the testimony,
the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense,
the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the basin and its stand.
Consecrate them so they become most holy. Whatever touches them shall become holy.
Anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve me as priests.
Say to the people of Israel: This shall be my holy anointing oil throughout your generations.
It shall not be poured on any ordinary person's body, and you shall make no other oil like it in composition. It is holy, and it shall be treated as holy by you.
Whoever blends anything like it or applies it to an outsider shall be cut off from his people."
The Sacred Incense · 30:34–38
YHWH says to Moses: "Take sweet spices — stacte, onycha, and galbanum — sweet spices with pure frankincense, equal parts of each —
and make an incense, blended by a skilled perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy.
Beat some of it very fine and place part of it before the testimony in the tent of meeting, where I will meet with you. Treat it as most holy.
The incense you make according to this formula you shall not make for yourselves — it is holy to YHWH.
Whoever makes any like it to use as perfume shall be cut off from his people."
Bezalel and Oholiab · 31:1–11
YHWH speaks to Moses:
"See — I have called Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, by name.
I have filled him with the Spirit of God — with skill, with understanding, with knowledge, and with every kind of craftsmanship —
to devise artistic designs, to work in gold and silver and bronze,
in cutting stones for setting and in carving wood, and to work in every craft.
And with him I have appointed Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. I have given skill to every craftsman, so that they can make everything I have commanded you:
the tent of meeting, the ark of the testimony with the mercy seat on it, all the furnishings of the tent,
the table and its utensils, the pure lampstand with all its utensils, the altar of incense,
the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, the basin and its stand,
the woven vestments — the sacred garments for Aaron the priest and the garments of his sons for their priestly service —
the anointing oil, and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. They shall make everything exactly as I have commanded you."
The Sabbath: The Sign of the Covenant · 31:12–17
YHWH says to Moses:
"Tell the people of Israel: Above all, keep my Sabbaths. For this is the sign between me and you throughout your generations — so that you may know that I, YHWH, am the one who makes you holy.
Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy to you. Whoever desecrates it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it shall be cut off from among his people.
Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest, holy to YHWH. Whoever works on the Sabbath day shall be put to death.
The people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations as a covenant for ever.
It is a sign between me and the people of Israel for ever — for in six days YHWH made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested and drew breath."
The Tablets of Stone · 31:18
When YHWH had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, he gave him the two tablets of the testimony — tablets of stone, written by the finger of God.
The Golden Calf · 32:1–6

When the people see that Moses is taking a long time to come down from the mountain, they gather around Aaron. "Get up," they say to him, "make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses — the man who brought us up out of Egypt — we don't know what has happened to him."
Aaron says to them, "Take off the gold rings from the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me."
All the people pull off their gold earrings and bring them to Aaron.
He takes them from their hands, shapes the gold with a tool, and casts it in the form of a calf. And they say, "These are your gods, Israel — who brought you up out of Egypt!"
When Aaron sees this, he builds an altar before it and makes a proclamation: "Tomorrow will be a feast to YHWH."
They rise early the next morning and offer burnt offerings and bring peace offerings. The people sit down to eat and drink, then get up to revel.
YHWH's Anger and Moses' Intercession · 32:7–14
YHWH says to Moses: "Go down — for your people, whom you brought up from Egypt, have corrupted themselves.

They have quickly turned aside from the way I commanded them. They have made a cast calf and worshipped it and sacrificed to it, and said, 'These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt!'"
Then YHWH says to Moses: "I have seen this people — they are a stiff-necked people.
Now let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them and I may consume them. I will make of you a great nation."
But Moses appeals to YHWH his God. "YHWH," he says, "why should your anger burn against your own people — the people you brought out of Egypt with great power and a strong hand?

Why should the Egyptians say, 'He brought them out with evil intentions — to kill them in the mountains and wipe them off the face of the earth'? Turn from your burning anger. Relent from this disaster against your people.

Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel — your servants — to whom you swore by yourself: 'I will make your offspring as many as the stars of the sky, and all this land I promised I will give your offspring as their inheritance for ever.'"
So YHWH relents from the disaster he had spoken of bringing on his people.
Moses Descends · 32:15–20
Moses turns and goes down the mountain, the two tablets of the testimony in his hands — tablets written on both sides, front and back.
The tablets are the work of God, and the writing is the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.
Joshua hears the noise of the people shouting and says to Moses, "There is a sound of war in the camp."
"It is not the sound of victory," Moses says, "nor the sound of defeat — what I hear is singing."
As he nears the camp and sees the calf and the dancing, Moses' anger blazes. He hurls the tablets from his hands and shatters them at the foot of the mountain.
He takes the calf they had made, burns it in fire, grinds it to powder, scatters it on the water, and makes the people of Israel drink it.
Moses Confronts Aaron · 32:21–24
Moses says to Aaron, "What did this people do to you that you brought such a great sin upon them?"
"Do not let my lord's anger burn," Aaron says. "You know this people — they are bent toward evil.
They said to me, 'Make us gods to go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up from Egypt — we don't know what happened to him.'
So I told them, 'Whoever has gold, take it off.' They gave it to me, I threw it into the fire — and out came this calf."
The Levites · 32:25–29
Moses sees that the people have broken loose — Aaron had let them break loose, and they have become a laughingstock to their enemies.
Moses stands at the entrance of the camp and calls out: "Whoever is for YHWH, come to me!" All the Levites gather around him.

He says to them: "This is what YHWH the God of Israel says: Let every man put his sword at his side. Go back and forth through the camp, from gate to gate, and let every man kill his brother, his companion, and his neighbour."
The Levites do as Moses says. About three thousand people fall that day.
Moses says, "You have been set apart for YHWH today — each of you at the cost of his son and his brother — and a blessing has come on you this day."
Moses Intercedes Again · 32:30–35
The next day Moses says to the people, "You have committed a great sin. Now I will go up to YHWH — perhaps I can make atonement for your sin."
Moses returns to YHWH and says: "Ah — this people has committed a great sin. They have made gods of gold for themselves.
But now — if you will forgive their sin... But if not, blot me out of the book you have written."
YHWH says to Moses: "Whoever has sinned against me — I will blot that person out of my book.
But now go, lead the people to the place I told you about. My angel will go before you. But when the day comes for me to visit, I will visit their sin upon them."
And YHWH strikes the people with a plague because of the calf — the one Aaron made.
YHWH Withdraws His Presence · 33:1–6
YHWH says to Moses: "Go, leave this place — you and the people you brought up from Egypt — and go to the land I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: 'To your offspring I will give it.'
I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey. But I will not go up among you — for you are a stiff-necked people — in case I consume you on the way."
When the people hear this terrible word, they mourn. No one puts on any ornaments.

YHWH had said to Moses: "Tell the people of Israel: You are a stiff-necked people. Even a single moment in your midst and I would consume you. Now take off your ornaments, and I will consider what to do with you."
So the people of Israel strip off their ornaments from Mount Horeb onward.
The Tent of Meeting Outside the Camp · 33:7–11
Moses takes a tent and pitches it outside the camp, at a distance. He calls it the tent of meeting. Anyone who seeks YHWH goes out to the tent of meeting outside the camp.
Whenever Moses goes out to the tent, the whole people rises. Each one stands at his tent entrance and watches Moses until he enters the tent.
When Moses enters the tent, the pillar of cloud comes down and stands at its entrance, and YHWH speaks with Moses.
When all the people see the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance of the tent, they all rise and bow down, each at his own tent entrance.
YHWH speaks with Moses face to face, as a man speaks with his friend. Then Moses returns to the camp. But his attendant Joshua son of Nun — a young man — does not leave the tent.
Moses Presses for the Divine Presence · 33:12–17
Moses says to YHWH: "See — you keep telling me, 'Lead this people.' But you haven't told me whom you will send with me. You have said, 'I know you by name, and you have found favour in my sight.'
If I have truly found favour in your sight, show me your ways — let me know you, so that I may continue to find favour. And remember: this nation is your people."
"My presence will go with you," YHWH says, "and I will give you rest."
"If your presence is not going with us," Moses says to him, "do not lead us up from here.

How else will anyone know — I and your people — that we have found favour in your sight? Is it not in your going with us? That is what sets us apart — me and your people — from every other people on the face of the earth."
YHWH says to Moses: "I will do the very thing you have asked — for you have found favour in my sight and I know you by name."
Show Me Your Glory · 33:18–23
Moses says: "Please — show me your glory."

"I will make all my goodness pass before you," YHWH says, "and I will proclaim the name YHWH before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and I will show mercy to whom I will show mercy.
But you cannot see my face — for no one can see me and live."
YHWH says: "There is a place near me. You shall stand on the rock.
When my glory passes by, I will put you in a cleft of the rock and cover you with my hand until I have passed.
Then I will take away my hand, and you will see my back — but my face will not be seen."
The Second Tablets · 34:1–4
YHWH says to Moses: "Cut two tablets of stone like the first ones, and I will write on them the words that were on the first tablets — the ones you shattered.
Be ready in the morning. Come up to Mount Sinai in the morning and present yourself to me there on the summit.
No one is to come with you. No one is to be seen anywhere on the mountain. Not even flocks or herds may graze in front of the mountain."
So Moses cuts two stone tablets like the first. He rises early in the morning and goes up Mount Sinai as YHWH commanded him, taking the two stone tablets in his hands.
The Proclamation of the Name · 34:5–9
YHWH descends in the cloud and stands there with him and proclaims the name YHWH.
YHWH passes before him and calls out:
"YHWH — YHWH —
a God compassionate and gracious,
slow to anger,
abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness,
keeping steadfast love for thousands,
forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin —
yet who will by no means clear the guilty,
visiting the iniquity of the fathers
on the children and the children's children,
to the third and fourth generation."
Moses quickly bows to the ground and worships.

"If I have found favour in your sight, my Lord," he says, "let my Lord go in our midst — even though this is a stiff-necked people. Forgive our iniquity and our sin, and take us as your own inheritance."
The Covenant Renewed · 34:10–27

"Watch," YHWH says. "I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will do wonders — things that have never been done in all the earth or among any nation. All the people you live among will see the work of YHWH, for what I will do with you is awesome.
Keep what I command you today. I will drive out before you the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
Be careful not to make any treaty with the people of the land you are entering, or they will become a snare among you.
Tear down their altars, smash their sacred pillars, and cut down their Asherah poles —
for you shall bow down to no other god, since YHWH — whose name is Jealous — is a jealous God.
Be careful not to make any treaty with the people of the land, for when they prostitute themselves to their gods and sacrifice to them, someone will invite you to eat of the sacrifice,
and you will take their daughters as wives for your sons — and their daughters will prostitute themselves to their gods and draw your sons to do the same.
You shall not make gods of cast metal.
Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. For seven days eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time in the month of Abib — for in the month of Abib you came out of Egypt.
Everything that first opens the womb is mine — every firstborn male of your livestock, whether of ox or sheep.

The firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. And no one shall appear before me empty-handed.
Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest — even during ploughing season and harvest.
Keep the Feast of Weeks — the firstfruits of the wheat harvest — and the Feast of Ingathering at the turning of the year.
Three times a year all your males shall appear before YHWH, the God of Israel.
I will drive out nations before you and widen your borders. No one will covet your land when you go up three times a year to appear before YHWH your God.
Do not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened. Nothing from the Passover feast shall remain until morning.
Bring the best of the firstfruits of your soil to the house of YHWH your God. Do not cook a young goat in its mother's milk."
YHWH says to Moses: "Write down these words — for it is in accordance with these words that I have made a covenant with you and with Israel."
Forty Days and the Second Tablets · 34:28
Moses is there with YHWH forty days and forty nights. He eats no bread and drinks no water. And he writes on the tablets the words of the covenant — the Ten Words.
Moses Descends: His Face Is Radiant · 34:29–35
When Moses comes down from Mount Sinai — the two tablets of the testimony in his hands — he does not know that the skin of his face is radiant from speaking with God.
Aaron and all the people of Israel see Moses — and the skin of his face is shining. They are afraid to come near him.
But Moses calls to them, and Aaron and all the leaders of the assembly come back to him. Moses speaks with them.
Afterward all the people of Israel draw near, and he gives them all the commands YHWH had spoken with him on Mount Sinai.
When Moses finishes speaking with them, he puts a veil over his face.
Whenever Moses goes in before YHWH to speak with him, he removes the veil until he comes out. Then he comes out and tells the people of Israel what he has been commanded.
The people of Israel see that the skin of Moses' face is shining. Then Moses puts the veil back over his face until he goes in again to speak with YHWH.
The Sabbath Repeated · 35:1–3
Moses assembles the whole congregation of the people of Israel and says to them: "These are the things YHWH has commanded you to do.
Six days work shall be done, but the seventh day shall be holy to you — a Sabbath of complete rest for YHWH. Whoever does any work on it shall be put to death.
You shall not light a fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day."
The Offering Called For · 35:4–19
Moses says to the whole congregation of Israel: "This is what YHWH has commanded:
Take a contribution from among you for YHWH. Everyone whose heart is generous — let them bring YHWH's contribution: gold, silver, and bronze;
blue and purple and crimson yarns, and fine linen; goats' hair;
tanned rams' skins and fine leather; acacia wood;
oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense;
onyx stones and gemstones for setting in the ephod and the breastpiece.
Every skilled craftsman among you shall come and make everything YHWH has commanded:
the Tabernacle with its tent and outer covering, its clasps and frames, its bars, pillars, and bases;
the ark with its poles, the mercy seat, and the curtain veil;
the table with its poles and all its utensils, and the bread of the Presence;
the lampstand for the light with its utensils and lamps, and the oil for the light;
the altar of incense with its poles, the anointing oil and fragrant incense, and the entrance screen for the tent;
the altar of burnt offering with its bronze grating, poles, and all its utensils, and the basin and its stand;
the hangings of the court, its pillars and bases, and the screen for the court gate;
the pegs of the Tabernacle and the pegs of the court, and their cords;
the woven vestments for serving in the Holy Place — the sacred garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons for their priestly service."
The People Bring Their Offerings · 35:20–29
The whole congregation of Israel leaves Moses' presence.

And they come — everyone whose heart stirs them, everyone whose spirit moves them — and bring YHWH's contribution for the work of the tent of meeting, for all its service, and for the sacred garments.
They come, men and women alike, all who are willing. They bring brooches, earrings, signet rings, and armlets — every kind of gold object — every person who has made a wave offering of gold to YHWH.
Everyone who has blue or purple or crimson yarn or fine linen or goats' hair or tanned rams' skins or fine leather brings it.
Everyone with a contribution of silver or bronze brings it as YHWH's offering. And everyone with acacia wood suitable for any part of the work brings it.
Every skilled woman spins with her own hands and brings what she has spun — blue and purple and crimson yarn and fine linen.
And all the women whose hearts stir them to use their skill spin the goats' hair.
The leaders bring the onyx stones and other gemstones for setting in the ephod and the breastpiece,
along with the spices and the oil — for the light, for the anointing oil, and for the fragrant incense.
Every man and woman among the people of Israel whose heart moves them freely brings something for all the work YHWH commanded through Moses. It is a freewill offering to YHWH.
Bezalel and Oholiab Commissioned · 35:30–35
Moses says to the people of Israel: "See — YHWH has called Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, by name.
He has filled him with the Spirit of God — with skill, understanding, and knowledge in every kind of craft —
to devise artistic designs, to work in gold and silver and bronze,
in cutting stones for setting and in carving wood, to work in every skilled craft.
And he has given him — and Oholiab son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan — the ability to teach.
He has filled them with skill to do every kind of work — engraving, designing, embroidering in blue and purple and crimson yarn and fine linen, weaving — they are master craftsmen and designers."
The Work Begins — and Too Much Is Given · 36:1–7

Bezalel and Oholiab and every skilled craftsman to whom YHWH has given skill and ability — every one who feels moved to come and do the work — shall carry it out in accordance with everything YHWH has commanded.
Moses calls Bezalel and Oholiab and every skilled craftsman in whose heart YHWH has put ability — everyone whose heart moves them to come and do the work.
They receive from Moses all the contribution the people of Israel had brought for the work of the sanctuary. But the people keep on bringing him freewill offerings every morning.
So all the craftsmen, each leaving the work they are doing on the sanctuary, come
and say to Moses: "The people are bringing far more than is needed for the work YHWH commanded us to do."
Moses gives the order, and a proclamation goes out through the camp: "Let no man or woman bring any more material for the sanctuary offering." So the people are restrained from bringing.
The material they have is more than enough for all the work — and then some.
The Linen Curtains · 36:8–13
All the skilled craftsmen among the workers make the Tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twisted linen — blue and purple and crimson yarns — worked with cherubim by a skilled craftsman.
Each curtain is twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide — all the curtains the same size.
He joins five curtains to one another, and the other five together.
He makes loops of blue along the edge of the outermost curtain of the first set, and the same on the edge of the outermost curtain of the second set.
Fifty loops on one curtain, fifty loops on the edge of the curtain in the second set — the loops opposite one another.
He makes fifty clasps of gold and joins the curtains to one another with the clasps. The Tabernacle becomes a single whole.
The Goat-Hair Tent · 36:14–19
He makes curtains of goats' hair for the tent over the Tabernacle — eleven curtains.
Each curtain is thirty cubits long and four cubits wide — all eleven the same size.
He joins five curtains together and six together.
He makes fifty loops on the edge of the outermost curtain of one set and fifty on the outermost curtain of the other, the loops opposite one another.
He makes fifty bronze clasps to join the tent into a single whole.
He makes a covering for the tent of tanned rams' skins and a covering of fine leather on top.
The Frames and Bars · 36:20–34
He makes the upright frames of acacia wood for the Tabernacle.
Each frame is ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide,
with two tenons for fitting together. He makes all the frames this way.
Twenty frames for the south side of the Tabernacle,
with forty silver bases — two under each frame.
Twenty frames for the north side,
with forty silver bases — two under each frame.
Six frames for the rear of the Tabernacle on the west,
and two corner frames for the rear.
Joined at the bottom and meeting at the top in a single ring — both corner frames made this way.
Eight frames in all, with sixteen silver bases — two under each.
He makes bars of acacia wood — five for the frames on one side,
five for the other side, and five for the rear on the west.
He makes the middle bar to run through the centre of the frames from end to end.
He overlays the frames with gold, makes their rings of gold as holders for the bars, and overlays the bars with gold.
The Veil and the Screen · 36:35–38
He makes the veil of blue and purple and crimson yarns and fine twisted linen — worked with cherubim by a skilled craftsman.
For it he makes four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold, with gold hooks, set in four silver bases.
He makes the entrance screen for the tent of blue and purple and crimson yarns and fine twisted linen — embroidered work.
Its five pillars with their hooks — he overlays their capitals and their bands with gold, with five bronze bases.
The Ark Made · 37:1–9
Bezalel makes the ark of acacia wood — two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide, a cubit and a half high.
He overlays it with pure gold inside and out and makes a moulding of gold around it.
He casts four gold rings for its four feet — two on one side, two on the other.
He makes poles of acacia wood and overlays them with gold,
then puts the poles through the rings on the sides of the ark for carrying it.
He makes the mercy seat of pure gold — two and a half cubits long, a cubit and a half wide.
He makes two cherubim of gold — hammered work — on the two ends of the mercy seat:
one cherub at one end, one at the other. Of one piece with the mercy seat he makes the cherubim at its two ends.
The cherubim spread their wings upward, overshadowing the mercy seat, their faces turned toward one another — toward the mercy seat.
The Table Made · 37:10–16
He makes the table of acacia wood — two cubits long, one cubit wide, a cubit and a half high.
He overlays it with pure gold and makes a moulding of gold around it,
a rim of a handsbreadth around it, and a moulding of gold around the rim.
He casts four gold rings and fastens them to the four corners at its four legs.
Close to the rim are the rings — holders for the poles to carry the table.
He makes the poles of acacia wood and overlays them with gold.
He makes the vessels of pure gold for the table — its plates and dishes, its flagons and bowls for the drink offerings.
The Lampstand Made · 37:17–24
He makes the lampstand of pure gold — of hammered work. Its base, shaft, cups, calyxes, and flowers are all of one piece with it.
