and for the fellowship offering: two bulls, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs in their first year. This is the offering of Gamaliel son of Pedahzur.
On the ninth day, Abidan son of Gideoni—leader of the sons of Benjamin—comes forward.
His offering is one silver dish weighing a hundred and thirty shekels and one silver basin of seventy shekels—both by the sanctuary shekel—filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;
one gold pan of ten shekels, filled with incense;
one young bull, one ram, one male lamb in its first year for a burnt offering;
one male goat for a sin offering;
and for the fellowship offering: two bulls, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs in their first year. This is the offering of Abidan son of Gideoni.
On the tenth day, Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai—leader of the sons of Dan—comes forward.
His offering is one silver dish weighing a hundred and thirty shekels and one silver basin of seventy shekels—both by the sanctuary shekel—filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;
one gold pan of ten shekels, filled with incense;
one young bull, one ram, one male lamb in its first year for a burnt offering;
one male goat for a sin offering;
and for the fellowship offering: two bulls, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs in their first year. This is the offering of Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai.
On the eleventh day, Pagiel son of Ochran—leader of the sons of Asher—comes forward.
His offering is one silver dish weighing a hundred and thirty shekels and one silver basin of seventy shekels—both by the sanctuary shekel—filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;
one gold pan of ten shekels, filled with incense;
one young bull, one ram, one male lamb in its first year for a burnt offering;
one male goat for a sin offering;
and for the fellowship offering: two bulls, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs in their first year. This is the offering of Pagiel son of Ochran.
On the twelfth day, Ahira son of Enan—leader of the sons of Naphtali—comes forward.
His offering is one silver dish weighing a hundred and thirty shekels and one silver basin of seventy shekels—both by the sanctuary shekel—filled with fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering;
one gold pan of ten shekels, filled with incense;
one young bull, one ram, one male lamb in its first year for a burnt offering;
one male goat for a sin offering;
and for the fellowship offering: two bulls, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs in their first year. This is the offering of Ahira son of Enan.
This is the total dedication offering for the altar from the leaders of Israel on the day it is anointed: twelve silver dishes, twelve silver basins, twelve gold pans.
Each silver dish weighs a hundred and thirty shekels and each basin seventy; all the silver of the vessels comes to two thousand four hundred shekels by the sanctuary shekel.
The twelve gold pans filled with incense weigh ten shekels each; all the gold of the pans comes to a hundred and twenty shekels.
The total for the burnt offering: twelve young bulls, twelve rams, twelve male lambs in their first year, along with their grain offerings; twelve male goats for sin offerings.
The total for the fellowship offering: twenty-four bulls, sixty rams, sixty male goats, and sixty male lambs in their first year. This is the dedication offering for the altar after it is anointed.

When Moses goes into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he hears the voice addressing him from between the two cherubim above the mercy seat on the ark of the covenant. And so the LORD speaks to him.
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Speak to Aaron and tell him: when you set up the seven lamps, they are to give light to the space in front of the lampstand."
Aaron does this. He mounts the lamps to face forward, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
The lampstand is made of hammered gold—its shaft and its blossoms all hammered work. Moses makes it exactly according to the pattern the LORD showed him.
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Take the Levites from among the Israelites and cleanse them.
Do this to cleanse them: sprinkle purifying water on them; have them shave their whole body, wash their clothes, and so present themselves.
They are to take a young bull with its grain offering of fine flour mixed with oil; you are to take a second young bull for a sin offering.
Bring the Levites before the tent of meeting and assemble the whole congregation of Israel.
When you bring the Levites before the LORD, the Israelites are to lay their hands on them.
Aaron then presents the Levites before the LORD as a wave offering from the Israelites, so that they may carry out the LORD’s service.
The Levites lay their hands on the heads of the bulls; then one bull is offered as a sin offering to the LORD and the other as a burnt offering, to make atonement for the Levites.
Have the Levites stand before Aaron and his sons and present them as a wave offering to the LORD.
In this way you are to separate the Levites from the rest of the Israelites, and the Levites will be mine.
After you have cleansed them and presented them as a wave offering, they may come to do their work at the tent of meeting.
They are wholly given to me from among the Israelites. I have taken them for myself in place of every firstborn—the one who opens every Israelite womb.
Every firstborn in Israel, whether human or animal, is mine. On the day I struck down every firstborn in Egypt, I set them apart for myself.
And I have taken the Levites in place of every firstborn among the Israelites.

From among all the Israelites, I give the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons, to serve Israel at the tent of meeting and to make atonement for Israel—so that no plague will fall on the Israelites when they draw near the sanctuary."
Moses, Aaron, and the whole congregation of Israel do this with the Levites. The Israelites do to the Levites everything the LORD commanded Moses.
The Levites purify themselves and wash their clothes. Aaron presents them as a wave offering before the LORD and makes atonement for them to cleanse them.
After that the Levites come in to do their work at the tent of meeting under Aaron and his sons. They are dealt with just as the LORD commanded Moses.
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"This applies to the Levites: those who are twenty-five years old and upward are to join the workforce of the tent of meeting.
But at fifty years old they are to retire from the regular work and serve no longer.
They may assist their fellow Levites at the tent of meeting by standing watch over their duties—but they must not do the regular work. This is how you are to handle the Levites and their duties."
The LORD speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai in the first month of the second year after the Israelites came out of Egypt:
"Let the Israelites celebrate the Passover at its appointed time.
Celebrate it at twilight on the fourteenth day of this month, in accordance with all its rules and regulations."
Moses tells the Israelites to celebrate the Passover,
and they do so in the wilderness of Sinai at twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month. The Israelites carry out everything just as the LORD commanded Moses.
But some men are unable to celebrate the Passover that day because they have become unclean through contact with a human corpse. They come before Moses and Aaron that same day
and say to Moses, "We are unclean because of a dead body. Why should we be prevented from presenting the LORD’s offering at its appointed time among the Israelites?"
Moses says to them, "Stand here while I listen to hear what the LORD will command concerning you."
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Tell the Israelites: if any of you or your descendants are unclean from a corpse, or are on a long journey, you may still celebrate the LORD’s Passover.
Celebrate it on the fourteenth day of the second month at twilight, eating the lamb with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Leave none of it until morning and break none of its bones. Keep it according to all the Passover regulations.

But if someone is clean and not on a journey, yet fails to celebrate the Passover—that person must be cut off from their people. Because they did not bring the LORD’s offering at the appointed time, they bear the weight of their own sin.
If a foreigner living among you wants to celebrate the LORD’s Passover, they may do so under the same rules and regulations. The same law applies to everyone—foreigner and native-born alike."
On the day the tabernacle is set up—the tent of the covenant—the cloud covers it. From evening until morning it appears as fire above the tabernacle.
It is always so: the cloud covers it by day, and fire appears at night.
Whenever the cloud lifts from above the tent, the Israelites set out. Wherever the cloud settles, that is where they make camp.
At the LORD’s command they set out, and at the LORD’s command they make camp. As long as the cloud rests over the tabernacle, they stay.
When the cloud remains over the tabernacle for many days, the Israelites keep the LORD’s charge and do not set out.
Sometimes the cloud rests over the tabernacle only a few days: at the LORD’s command they camp, and at the LORD’s command they move.
Sometimes the cloud is there only from evening until morning; when it lifts at dawn, they set out. Day or night, when the cloud lifts, they move.
Whether the cloud rests two days, a month, or longer—however long it lingers over the tabernacle—the Israelites camp and do not move. When it lifts, they set out.
At the LORD’s command they camp, and at the LORD’s command they set out. They keep the LORD’s charge, doing what the LORD commanded through Moses.
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Make two trumpets of hammered silver. You will use them to summon the congregation and to signal the camps to break camp.
When both are sounded, the whole congregation is to gather before you at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
If only one is sounded, the leaders—the heads of Israel’s thousands—are to assemble before you.
When you sound the alarm, the camps on the east side set out.
At the second alarm, the camps on the south set out. The alarm is the signal to move.
But to call the assembly together, sound the trumpets without the alarm.
The sons of Aaron, the priests, are to blow the trumpets. This is a lasting ordinance for you and the generations to come.
When you go to war in your own land against an adversary attacking you, sound the alarm on the trumpets. Then the LORD your God will remember you and you will be rescued from your enemies.

Also on your days of rejoicing—your appointed festivals and new moon celebrations—sound the trumpets over your burnt offerings and fellowship offerings. They serve as a memorial before your God. I am the LORD your God."
On the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, the cloud lifts from above the tabernacle of the covenant.
The Israelites set out from the wilderness of Sinai stage by stage, and the cloud comes to rest in the wilderness of Paran.
This is the first time they set out at the LORD’s command through Moses.
The divisions under the standard of the camp of Judah march out first. Nahshon son of Amminadab is over its division.
Nethanel son of Zuar is over the division of the tribe of Issachar,
and Eliab son of Helon is over the division of the tribe of Zebulun.
The tabernacle is then taken down. The sons of Gershon and Merari, who carry it, set out.
The divisions under the standard of the camp of Reuben march next. Elizur son of Shedeur is over its division.
Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai is over the division of the tribe of Simeon,
and Eliasaph son of Deuel is over the division of the tribe of Gad.
Then the Kohathites set out, carrying the holy things. The tabernacle is set up before they arrive at the next camp.
The divisions under the standard of the camp of Ephraim march next. Elishama son of Ammihud is over its division.
Gamaliel son of Pedahzur is over the division of the tribe of Manasseh,
and Abidan son of Gideoni is over the division of the tribe of Benjamin.
Finally, the divisions under the standard of the camp of Dan—the rear guard for all the divisions—set out last. Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai is over its division.
Pagiel son of Ochran is over the division of the tribe of Asher,
and Ahira son of Enan is over the division of the tribe of Naphtali.
This is the marching order of the Israelites by their divisions as they break camp.

Moses says to Hobab son of Reuel the Midianite, his father-in-law, "We are setting out for the place the LORD promised us. Come with us and we will treat you well—for the LORD has promised good things to Israel."
"No," Hobab answers. "I am going back to my own land and my own people."
Moses says, "Please do not leave us. You know how we are to camp in the wilderness, and you can serve as our eyes.
Come with us, and whatever good the LORD grants us, we will share it with you."
They set out from the mountain of the LORD on a three-day journey. The ark of the covenant goes before them during those three days to seek out a resting place for them.
The cloud of the LORD is over them by day as they set out from the camp.
Whenever the ark sets out, Moses cries out:
"Rise up, LORD!
Let your enemies be scattered,
and those who hate you flee before you!"
And whenever the ark comes to rest, he says:
"Return, LORD,
to the countless thousands of Israel."
The people complain about their hardships in the hearing of the LORD, and his anger burns. Fire from the LORD breaks out and consumes the edge of the camp.
The people cry out to Moses. Moses prays to the LORD, and the fire dies down.
The place is named Taberah—Burning—because the LORD’s fire broke out against them there.
The rabble among them craves other food, and the Israelites weep again and say, "Who will give us meat to eat?
We remember the fish we ate in Egypt—free of charge! The cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, the garlic.
But now our appetite is gone. There is nothing before our eyes but this manna."
The manna is like coriander seed and looks like resin.
The people go out and gather it, then grind it in a handmill or pound it in a mortar, cook it in a pot, and make it into loaves. It tastes like cakes baked in oil.
When the dew falls on the camp at night, the manna falls with it.
Moses hears the people weeping throughout their clans—each at the entrance to his own tent. The LORD’s anger burns hot, and Moses is deeply troubled.
Moses says to the LORD, ";Why have you brought this trouble on your servant? What have I done to displease you, that you put the burden of all these people on me?
Did I conceive all these people? Did I give birth to them, that you should say to me: 'Carry them in your arms, as a nurse carries an infant, all the way to the land you promised their ancestors'?
Where am I to find meat for all these people? They keep weeping to me: 'Give us meat to eat!'
I cannot carry all these people by myself. The burden is far too heavy for me.
If this is how you intend to treat me, then kill me now. If I have found any favor in your eyes, spare me this wretchedness.";
The LORD says to Moses: ";Bring me seventy of Israel’s elders whom you know to be leaders and officials among the people. Have them come to the tent of meeting and stand there with you.

I will come down and speak with you there. I will take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them. They will share the burden of the people with you so that you will not have to carry it alone.

And tell the people: Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, for you will eat meat. You have wept in the LORD’s hearing, saying, 'Who will give us meat?' The LORD has heard you. Now he will give you meat, and you will eat it.
You will not eat it for just one day, or two days, or five, or ten, or twenty days,
but for a whole month—until it comes out of your nostrils and you loathe it—because you have rejected the LORD who is among you and have wept before him, saying, 'Why did we ever leave Egypt?'";
But Moses says, ";The people among whom I stand number six hundred thousand on foot—and you say you will give them enough meat for a whole month!
Even if all the flocks and herds were slaughtered, would that be enough? Even if all the fish of the sea were caught, would that satisfy them?";
The LORD answers Moses, ";Is the LORD’s arm too short? Now you will see whether or not what I say will come true for you.";
Moses goes out and tells the people what the LORD said. He gathers seventy elders and has them stand around the tent.

Then the LORD comes down in the cloud and speaks with Moses. He takes some of the Spirit that is on Moses and puts it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rests on them, they prophesy—and they do not stop.

Two men remain in the camp. One is named Eldad and the other Medad. The Spirit rests on them as well—they are listed among the elders, though they did not go out to the tent. And they prophesy in the camp.
A young man runs and reports to Moses, ";Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!"
Joshua son of Nun, who has been Moses’ aide since youth, speaks up: "Moses, my lord, stop them!"
But Moses says to him, "Are you jealous on my behalf? If only all the LORD’s people were prophets—if only the LORD would put his Spirit on all of them!"
Then Moses and the elders of Israel return to the camp.
Now a wind goes out from the LORD and drives quail in from the sea. It scatters them over the camp and all around it—a day’s journey in every direction—flying about three feet above the ground.
The people spend all that day and night and all the next day gathering quail. No one gathers less than ten homers. They spread them out all around the camp.
But while the meat is still between their teeth, before it is consumed, the anger of the LORD burns against the people and he strikes them with a severe plague.
The place is named Kibroth-hattaavah—Graves of Craving—because there they bury the people who had craved.
From Kibroth-hattaavah the people march on to Hazeroth, where they stay.
Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of his Cushite wife—he has married a Cushite woman.
They say, "Has the LORD spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us as well?" And the LORD hears it.
(Now Moses is a very humble man—more so than anyone else on the face of the earth.)
Suddenly the LORD says to Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, "All three of you—come out to the tent of meeting." They all go out.
The LORD comes down in a pillar of cloud and stands at the entrance to the tent. He calls Aaron and Miriam forward, and both of them step forward.
The LORD says:
"Listen now to my words.
When there is a prophet among you,
I, the LORD, reveal myself in visions;
I speak to them in dreams.
But not so with my servant Moses.
He is faithful in all my house.
With him I speak mouth to mouth—
plainly, and not in riddles.
He sees the very form of the LORD.
Why then were you not afraid
to speak against my servant Moses?"
The anger of the LORD burns against them, and he departs.
When the cloud lifts from above the tent, Miriam is covered with a skin disease—white as snow. Aaron turns to look at her, and there she is: leprous.
Aaron says to Moses, "Please, my lord—do not hold against us the sin we have committed so foolishly.
Do not let her be like a stillborn infant, whose flesh is already half-consumed when it comes out of the womb."
So Moses cries out to the LORD, "Please, God—please heal her!"
The LORD answers Moses, "If her father had spit in her face, would she not bear her shame for seven days? Let her be shut outside the camp for seven days, and after that she may be brought back in."
So Miriam is confined outside the camp for seven days, and the people do not move on until she is brought back.
After that, the people leave Hazeroth and camp in the wilderness of Paran.
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Send men to explore the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites. From each ancestral tribe, send one man—every one a leader among them."
At the LORD’s command, Moses sends them from the wilderness of Paran. All of them are leaders of the Israelites.
These are their names: from the tribe of Reuben, Shammua son of Zaccur;
from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat son of Hori;
from the tribe of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh;
from the tribe of Issachar, Igal son of Joseph;
from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun;
from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti son of Raphu;
from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel son of Sodi;
from the tribe of Manasseh—of the tribe of Joseph—Gaddi son of Susi;
from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel son of Gemalli;
from the tribe of Asher, Sethur son of Michael;
from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi son of Vophsi;
from the tribe of Gad, Geuel son of Machi.
These are the names of the men Moses sends to scout the land. Moses renames Hoshea son of Nun as Joshua.
When Moses sends them to scout the land of Canaan, he says to them, "Go up through the Negev and on into the hill country.
See what the land is like, and whether the people who live there are strong or weak, few or many.
Look at the land itself—whether it is good or poor, and whether the towns are open or fortified.
Assess whether the soil is rich or lean, and whether there are trees in it or not. Be bold, and bring back some of the fruit of the land." It is the season of the first ripe grapes.
They go up and scout the land from the wilderness of Zin all the way to Rehob, near the entrance of Hamath.
They go up through the Negev and come to Hebron, where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai—the descendants of Anak—are living. Hebron had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.
When they reach the Valley of Eshcol, they cut down a single branch bearing one cluster of grapes—so large it takes two men to carry it on a pole. They bring along pomegranates and figs as well.
The place is named the Valley of Eshcol—Cluster Valley—because of the cluster of grapes the Israelites cut down there.
After forty days, they return from scouting the land.
They come back to Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation of Israel at Kadesh in the wilderness of Paran. They make their report to the whole assembly and show them the fruit of the land.
They tell Moses, "We went to the land you sent us to, and it does indeed flow with milk and honey—here is its fruit!
But the people who live there are powerful, and the cities are large and fortified. We also saw the descendants of Anak there.
Amalekites live in the Negev; Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites inhabit the hill country; Canaanites occupy the coast and the banks of the Jordan."
Caleb quiets the people before Moses and says, "Let us go up at once and take the land—we can certainly do it!"
But the men who went with him say, "We cannot attack those people. They are stronger than we are."
And they spread a bad report among the Israelites about the land they had scouted: "The land we explored devours its inhabitants. All the people we saw there are of great stature.
We even saw the Nephilim there—the Anakim come from the Nephilim. We seemed like grasshoppers in our own eyes—and we looked the same way to them."
The whole congregation raises its voice and weeps aloud. The people cry through the night.
All the Israelites grumble against Moses and Aaron. "If only we had died in Egypt!" the whole assembly says. "If only we had died in this wilderness!
Why is the LORD bringing us to this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and children will be taken as plunder. Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt?"
They say to one another, "Let us appoint a leader and head back to Egypt."
Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the whole assembled congregation of Israel.
Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh, two of the men who had scouted the land, tear their clothes
and say to the whole congregation of Israel, "The land we passed through to scout—it is a very good land, an exceedingly good land.
If the LORD delights in us, he will bring us into this land and give it to us—a land flowing with milk and honey.
Only do not rebel against the LORD. And do not fear the people of the land—they are our bread. Their protection is stripped away from them, and the LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them."
But the whole assembly talks about stoning them. Then the glory of the LORD appears at the tent of meeting to all the Israelites.
The LORD says to Moses:
"How long will this people despise me?
How long will they refuse to believe in me,
in spite of all the signs I have done among them?
I will strike them with pestilence and disinherit them,
and make of you a nation greater and mightier than they."
Moses says to the LORD, "But the Egyptians will hear of it—for by your strength you brought this people up from among them.

And they will tell it to the inhabitants of this land. They have already heard that you, LORD, are among this people—that you appear face to face, that your cloud stands over them, and that you go before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
If you kill this people all at once, then the nations who have heard your fame will say:
'The LORD was not able to bring this people into the land he swore to give them, and so he killed them in the wilderness.'
And now, let the Lord's power be displayed, just as you have declared:
"The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in love,
forgiving iniquity and transgression.
Yet he does not leave the guilty unpunished;
he holds the children to account for the sins of their fathers
to the third and fourth generation."
Forgive the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of your love, just as you have pardoned them from Egypt until now."
The LORD answers, "I have pardoned them, as you asked.
But as surely as I live, and as surely as my glory fills the whole earth—
none of the men who saw my glory and the signs I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, and who have tested me these ten times and have not listened to my voice,
will ever see the land I promised on oath to their ancestors. None of those who treated me with contempt will see it.
But my servant Caleb—because he has a different spirit and has followed me wholeheartedly—I will bring into the land he entered, and his descendants will possess it.
Since the Amalekites and Canaanites are living in the valleys, turn back tomorrow and set out toward the wilderness by the way of the Red Sea."
The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron:
"How long will this wicked congregation grumble against me? I have heard the complaints of the Israelites against me.
Tell them: As surely as I live, declares the LORD, I will do to you the very thing I heard you say.
In this wilderness your bodies will fall—every one of you twenty years old or more who was registered in the census and who has grumbled against me.
Not one of you will enter the land I swore with uplifted hand to make your home—except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.
As for your children, whom you said would become plunder—I will bring them in to know the land you rejected.
But as for you—your bodies will fall in this wilderness.
Your children will be shepherds in the wilderness for forty years, bearing the weight of your unfaithfulness, until the last of your bodies has fallen here.
For forty years—one year for each of the forty days you scouted the land—you will bear the consequence of your sins and know what it means to have me against you.
I, the LORD, have spoken. This is what I will do to this entire wicked congregation who has gathered against me. They will meet their end in this wilderness; here they will die."
The ten men Moses had sent to scout the land—those who returned and made the whole congregation grumble against him by bringing a bad report—
those men die of a plague before the LORD.
Of the men who went to scout the land, only Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh survive.
When Moses reports all this to the Israelites, the people mourn deeply.
Early the next morning they go up toward the ridge of the hill country and say, "Here we are. We will go up to the place the LORD promised—for we have sinned."
But Moses says, "Why are you disobeying the LORD’s command? This will not succeed.
Do not go up, for the LORD is not among you. You will be crushed by your enemies.
The Amalekites and Canaanites are there in front of you, and you will fall by the sword. Because you have turned away from the LORD, he will not be with you."
But they presume to go up toward the ridge of the hill country—even though the ark of the covenant and Moses do not leave the camp.
The Amalekites and Canaanites who live in that hill country come down and attack them, and beat them back all the way to Hormah.
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Speak to the Israelites and tell them: when you enter the land I am giving you as a home

and you present a food offering to the LORD—a burnt offering or a sacrifice, whether to fulfill a vow or as a freewill offering or at your appointed festivals—making an aroma pleasing to the LORD, from the herd or the flock,
then the one who presents the offering is to bring a grain offering of a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a quarter of a hin of oil.
With each lamb for the burnt offering or the sacrifice, prepare a quarter of a hin of wine as a drink offering.
With a ram, prepare a grain offering of two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with a third of a hin of oil,
and a third of a hin of wine as a drink offering. Present it as an aroma pleasing to the LORD.
When you prepare a young bull as a burnt offering or sacrifice—to fulfill a vow or as a fellowship offering to the LORD—
bring with the bull a grain offering of three-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with half a hin of oil.
Also bring half a hin of wine as a drink offering. This is a food offering, an aroma pleasing to the LORD.
Each bull, ram, lamb, or goat is to be prepared this way.
Do this for each one, for as many as you prepare.
Every native-born Israelite is to do these things this way when presenting a food offering to the LORD.
For generations to come, whenever a foreigner or anyone living among you presents a food offering as an aroma pleasing to the LORD, they are to do exactly as you do.
The community is to have the same rules for you and for the foreigner residing among you; this is a lasting ordinance for the generations to come. You and the foreigner are alike before the LORD.
The same law and the same regulations apply to both you and the foreigner living among you."
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Speak to the Israelites and tell them: when you enter the land to which I am bringing you
and you eat of the food of the land, you are to present a portion as an offering lifted up to the LORD.
Present a loaf from the first of your ground grain as a contribution; present it as you do the contribution from the threshing floor.
Throughout your generations, give the LORD a contribution from the first of your ground grain."
"Now if you unintentionally fail to keep any of these commands the LORD gave Moses—
any of what the LORD commanded you through Moses, from the day the LORD gave the command and after, throughout your generations—

then if it was done unintentionally, without the community’s awareness, the whole congregation is to offer one young bull for a burnt offering as an aroma pleasing to the LORD, along with its prescribed grain and drink offering, and one male goat for a sin offering.

The priest makes atonement for the whole Israelite community, and they will be forgiven—for it was unintentional, and they have brought their offering, a food offering to the LORD, and their sin offering before the LORD for their unintentional wrong.
The whole Israelite community and the foreigners living among them will be forgiven, since the whole people was involved in the unintentional wrong.
"If just one person sins unintentionally, they must bring a year-old female goat for a sin offering.
The priest makes atonement before the LORD for the one who erred, when they sin unintentionally—making atonement for them so they are forgiven.
The same law applies to everyone who sins unintentionally, whether a native-born Israelite or a foreigner living among you.
But the person who sins defiantly—whether native-born or foreigner—blasphemes the LORD. That person is to be cut off from the people.
Because they have despised the LORD’s word and broken his command, they must certainly be cut off; their guilt remains on them."
While the Israelites are in the wilderness, they find a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day.
Those who find him bring him to Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation.
They hold him in custody, because it has not yet been made clear what should be done with him.
The LORD says to Moses, "The man is certainly to be put to death. The whole congregation is to stone him outside the camp."
So the congregation takes him outside the camp and stones him to death, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Speak to the Israelites and tell them to make tassels on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and to put a blue cord on the tassel at each corner.
These are to be your tassels. When you look at them, you will remember all the LORD’s commands and obey them, and you will not follow after your own hearts and eyes, which lead you astray.
Then you will remember all my commands and be holy to your God.
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt to be your God. I am the LORD your God."
Korah son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, along with Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth—all from the tribe of Reuben—take men
and rise up against Moses. With them are two hundred and fifty Israelites—prominent leaders in the congregation, men of renown.

They come as a group against Moses and Aaron and say, "You have gone too far! The whole congregation is holy—every one of them—and the LORD is among them. Why then do you exalt yourselves above the LORD’s assembly?"
When Moses hears this, he falls on his face.

Then he speaks to Korah and all his followers: "Tomorrow morning the LORD will show who belongs to him and who is holy—he will bring that person near to himself. The man he chooses, he will bring near.
Do this: take censers, Korah and all your followers.
Tomorrow, put fire in them and place incense before the LORD. The man the LORD chooses will be the one who is holy. You Levites have gone too far!"
Moses says to Korah, "Listen, you Levites!

Is it not enough for you that the God of Israel has set you apart from the rest of the Israelite community, bringing you near to himself to do the work of the LORD’s tabernacle and to stand before the community to serve them?
He has brought you and all your fellow Levites near—and now you are reaching for the priesthood as well?
It is against the LORD that you and all your followers have gathered together. Who is Aaron that you should grumble against him?"
Then Moses summons Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab. But they say, "We will not come!
Is it not enough that you have brought us up from a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness? Now you also want to lord it over us?
Moreover, you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey or given us fields and vineyards. Do you want to gouge out the eyes of these men? We will not come!"
Moses becomes very angry and says to the LORD, "Do not accept their offering. I have not taken so much as a single donkey from them, and I have not wronged any of them."
Moses says to Korah, "You and all your followers are to appear before the LORD tomorrow—you and they and Aaron.
Each man is to take his censer and put incense in it—two hundred and fifty censers in all—and present it before the LORD. You and Aaron are also to present your censers."
So each of them takes his censer, puts fire in it, lays incense on it, and stands at the entrance to the tent of meeting with Moses and Aaron.
When Korah has assembled the whole congregation against them at the entrance to the tent, the glory of the LORD appears to all of them.
The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron:
"Separate yourselves from this congregation—
I will put an end to them in a moment."
Moses and Aaron fall on their faces and cry, "O God, God of the spirits of all living creatures—will you be angry with the whole congregation when only one man sins?"
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Tell the congregation: move away from the dwellings of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram."
Moses gets up and goes to Dathan and Abiram, with the elders of Israel following him.
He warns the congregation, "Move away from the tents of these wicked men! Do not touch anything belonging to them, or you will be swept away because of all their sins."
So they move away from the area around Korah, Dathan, and Abiram’s tents. Dathan and Abiram come out and stand at the entrances of their tents with their wives, sons, and small children.
Moses says, "By this you will know that the LORD sent me to do all these things, and that this was not my own doing.
If these men die the common death—if their fate is no different from that of all people—then the LORD has not sent me.

But if the LORD does something unprecedented—if the ground opens its mouth and swallows them with everything that belongs to them, so they go down alive into Sheol—then you will know that these men have treated the LORD with contempt."
The moment Moses finishes speaking, the ground under them splits open.
The earth opens its mouth and swallows them, along with their households—all of Korah’s people and all their possessions.
They go down alive into Sheol, with everything they own. The earth closes over them, and they vanish from the assembly.
At their cries, all the Israelites around them scatter and run, saying, "The earth will swallow us too!"
And fire comes out from the LORD and consumes the two hundred and fifty men who were presenting the incense.
The LORD says to Moses:
"Tell Eleazar son of Aaron the priest to take the censers out of the smoldering ruins and scatter the coals away, because those censers are holy—

the censers of the men who sinned at the cost of their lives. Have them hammered into sheets to overlay the altar, for they were presented before the LORD and have become holy. Let them be a sign to the Israelites."
Eleazar the priest collects the bronze censers that those who were burned had presented, and has them hammered into plates to overlay the altar,

as the LORD directed him through Moses. This is to remind the Israelites that no one except a descendant of Aaron should approach to burn incense before the LORD—or else he would become like Korah and his followers.
The next day the whole Israelite congregation grumbles against Moses and Aaron: "You have killed the LORD’s people!"
As the congregation assembles against Moses and Aaron, they turn toward the tent of meeting—and the cloud has covered it. The glory of the LORD appears.
Moses and Aaron come to the front of the tent of meeting,
and the LORD says to Moses,
"Get away from this congregation so I can end them in an instant."

Then they fall on their faces. Moses says to Aaron, "Take your censer, put fire from the altar in it, add incense, go quickly to the congregation, and make atonement for them. Wrath has gone out from the LORD—the plague has started."
Aaron does as Moses says and runs into the middle of the assembly. The plague has already begun among the people. He offers the incense and makes atonement for them.
He stands between the dead and the living, and the plague is stopped.
But fourteen thousand seven hundred have died from the plague, in addition to those who died in the Korah affair.
Then Aaron returns to Moses at the entrance to the tent of meeting. The plague is over.
The LORD speaks to Moses:
"Speak to the Israelites and collect a staff from each ancestral house—one staff for each leader, twelve staffs in all. Write each man’s name on his staff.
Write Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi, for there is to be one staff for the head of each ancestral house.
Place them in the tent of meeting in front of the ark of the covenant, where I meet with you.
The staff of the man I choose will sprout. In this way I will put an end to the constant grumbling of the Israelites against you."
Moses speaks to the Israelites, and each of their leaders gives him a staff—one for each leader, twelve staffs in all. Aaron’s staff is among them.
Moses places the staffs before the LORD in the tent of the covenant.
The next day Moses enters the tent of the covenant—and Aaron’s staff, the staff of the house of Levi, has sprouted. It has put out buds, produced blossoms, and borne ripe almonds.
Moses brings out all the staffs from before the LORD to all the Israelites. They look, and each man takes his own staff.
The LORD says to Moses, "Put Aaron’s staff back in front of the ark of the covenant, to be kept as a sign for the rebellious. This will put an end to their grumbling against me, so they do not die."
Moses does what the LORD commands him.
The Israelites say to Moses, "We are dying! We are lost—we are all lost!
Everyone who comes anywhere near the tabernacle of the LORD dies. Are we all to perish?"

The LORD says to Aaron, "You, your sons, and your father’s family are to bear responsibility for offenses against the sanctuary; you and your sons alone are to bear responsibility for offenses against the priesthood.
Bring your fellow Levites from your ancestral tribe to join you and assist you when you and your sons minister before the tent of the covenant.
They are to be responsible to you and are to perform all the duties of the tent. But they must not come near the furnishings of the sanctuary or the altar—otherwise both they and you will die.
They are to join you and be responsible for the care of the tent of meeting—all its service. No one else may come near where you are.
You are to be responsible for the care of the sanctuary and the altar, so that my wrath will not fall on the Israelites again.
I myself have selected your fellow Levites from among the Israelites as a gift to you, dedicated to the LORD to do the work at the tent of meeting.

But only you and your sons may serve as priests in connection with everything at the altar and inside the curtain. I give you the service of the priesthood as a gift. Anyone else who comes near the sanctuary is to be put to death."
The LORD says to Aaron, "I give you the care of the contributions brought to me. All the holy offerings the Israelites present to me I give to you and your sons as your portion—your perpetual share.
From the most holy offerings kept from the fire, this is what belongs to you: every grain offering, sin offering, and guilt offering they present to me is most holy, for you and your sons.
Eat it as something most holy; every male may eat it. It is holy to you.

This also is yours: whatever the Israelites set aside as a wave offering. I give this to you and your sons and daughters as your perpetual share. Everyone in your household who is ceremonially clean may eat it.
I give you all the finest olive oil, all the finest new wine, and all the finest grain—the firstfruits they give to the LORD.
All the land’s firstfruits they bring to the LORD will be yours. Everyone in your household who is ceremonially clean may eat it.
Everything in Israel that is devoted to the LORD is yours.
The first offspring of every womb brought to the LORD—whether human or animal—is yours. But you must redeem every firstborn son and every firstborn of unclean animals.
When they are a month old, you must redeem them at the set redemption price of five shekels of silver, by the sanctuary shekel—which is twenty gerahs.
But you must not redeem the firstborn of a cow, a sheep, or a goat; they are holy. Splash their blood against the altar and burn their fat as a food offering, an aroma pleasing to the LORD.
Their meat is to be yours, just as the breast of the wave offering and the right thigh are yours.

Whatever the Israelites set aside as holy contributions to the LORD, I give to you, your sons, and your daughters as your perpetual share. It is an everlasting covenant of salt before the LORD for both you and your offspring."
The LORD says to Aaron:
"You will have no inheritance in their land,
nor any portion among them.
I am your portion and your inheritance
among the Israelites."
"I give to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as their inheritance in return for the work they do while serving at the tent of meeting.
From now on the Israelites must not go near the tent of meeting, or they will bear the consequence of their sin and will die.

It is the Levites who are to do the work at the tent of meeting and bear the responsibility for any offenses against it. This is a lasting ordinance for the generations to come. They will receive no inheritance among the Israelites.

Instead, I give to the Levites as their inheritance the tithes that the Israelites present as an offering to the LORD. That is why I said concerning them: They will have no inheritance among the Israelites."
The LORD says to Moses:
"Speak to the Levites and tell them: when you receive from the Israelites the tithe I give you as your inheritance, you must present a tenth of that tithe as the LORD’s offering.
Your offering will be credited to you as if it were grain from the threshing floor or juice from the winepress.
In this way you also will present an offering to the LORD from all the tithes you receive from the Israelites. From these tithes you must give the LORD’s portion to Aaron the priest.
You must present as the LORD’s portion the best and holiest part of everything given to you.
Say to the Levites: when you present the best part, it will be credited to you as the product of the threshing floor or the winepress.
You and your households may eat the rest of it anywhere, for it is your wage for your work at the tent of meeting.
By presenting the best part of it you will not be guilty in this matter; you will not profane the holy offerings of the Israelites, and you will not die."
The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron:
"This is a requirement of the law that the LORD has commanded: tell the Israelites to bring you a red heifer without defect—one that has no blemish and has never been put under a yoke.
Give it to Eleazar the priest; it is to be brought outside the camp and slaughtered in his presence.
Eleazar the priest is to take some of its blood on his finger and sprinkle it seven times toward the front of the tent of meeting.
While Eleazar watches, the heifer is to be burned—its hide, flesh, blood, and intestines.
The priest is to take some cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet yarn and throw them onto the burning heifer.
After that, the priest must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water. He may then come into the camp, but he will be ceremonially unclean until evening.
The man who burns it must also wash his clothes and bathe with water, and he too will be unclean until evening.

A man who is ceremonially clean is to gather up the ashes of the heifer and put them in a clean place outside the camp. They are to be kept by the Israelite community for use in the water of purification—it is for cleansing from sin.

The man who gathers the ashes of the heifer must also wash his clothes, and he will be unclean until evening. This is a lasting ordinance both for the Israelites and for the foreigner residing among them."
"Whoever touches a human corpse will be ceremonially unclean for seven days.

They must purify themselves with the water on the third day and on the seventh day; then they will be clean. But if they do not purify themselves on the third and seventh days, they will not be clean.

Anyone who touches a corpse, the body of a human being who has died, and fails to purify themselves defiles the LORD’s tabernacle. That person must be cut off from Israel. Since the water of purification has not been sprinkled on them, they are unclean; their uncleanness remains.
"This is the law when a person dies inside a tent: everyone who enters the tent and everyone already in it will be unclean for seven days.
Every open container without a lid fastened on it will be unclean.
Anyone in the open country who touches someone who has been killed with a sword or who has died naturally, or who touches a human bone or a grave, will be unclean for seven days."
"For the unclean person, put some of the ashes from the burned purification offering into a vessel and pour fresh water over them.

Then a man who is ceremonially clean is to take some hyssop, dip it in the water, and sprinkle the tent and all the furnishings and the people who were there, and whoever touched a human bone, or someone who was killed or who died naturally, or a grave.

The clean person is to sprinkle those who are unclean on the third and seventh days, and on the seventh day he is to purify them. Those who are purified must then wash their clothes and bathe with water, and that evening they will be clean.

But if those who are unclean do not purify themselves, they must be cut off from the community, because they have defiled the sanctuary of the LORD. The water of purification has not been sprinkled on them; they are unclean.
This is a lasting ordinance for them. The man who sprinkles the water of purification must also wash his clothes, and anyone who touches the water will be unclean until evening.
Anything that an unclean person touches becomes unclean, and anyone who touches it becomes unclean until evening."
The whole Israelite congregation arrives in the wilderness of Zin in the first month, and the people settle at Kadesh. Miriam dies there and is buried there.
There is no water for the congregation, and they assemble against Moses and Aaron.
The people quarrel with Moses. "If only we had died when our brothers fell dead before the LORD!" they say.
"Why have you brought the LORD’s community into this wilderness for us and our livestock to die here?
Why did you bring us up out of Egypt to this terrible place? It has no grain or figs, no vines or pomegranates. And there is no water to drink!"
Moses and Aaron move away from the assembly to the entrance to the tent of meeting and fall on their faces. The glory of the LORD appears to them.
The LORD speaks to Moses:

"Take the staff, and you and your brother Aaron gather the assembly together. Speak to that rock before their eyes and it will pour out its water. You will bring water out of the rock for the community so they and their livestock can drink."
So Moses takes the staff from before the LORD, just as he commanded him.
He and Aaron gather the assembly in front of the rock, and Moses says to them, "Listen, you rebels—must we bring water out of this rock for you?"
Then Moses raises his arm and strikes the rock twice with his staff. Water gushes out, and the community and their livestock drink.
But the LORD says to Moses and Aaron, "Because you did not trust in me enough to honor me as holy in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this community into the land I give them."
These are the waters of Meribah—where the Israelites quarreled with the LORD and where he showed himself holy among them.
Moses sends messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom: "This is what your brother Israel says: You know all the hardship that has come on us.
Our ancestors went down into Egypt, and we lived there many years. The Egyptians mistreated us and our ancestors,
but when we cried out to the LORD, he heard our cry and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. Now we are here at Kadesh, a town on the edge of your territory.

Please let us pass through your country. We will not go through any field or vineyard, or drink water from any well. We will travel along the King’s Highway and not turn to the right or to the left until we have passed through your territory."
But Edom answers, "You may not pass through here. If you try, we will march out and attack you with the sword."
The Israelites say, "We will go along the main road, and if we or our livestock drink any of your water, we will pay for it. We only want to pass through on foot—nothing else."
Again Edom answers, "You may not pass through." Then Edom comes out against them with a large and powerful army.
Since Edom refuses to let them pass through their territory, Israel turns away from them.
The whole Israelite community sets out from Kadesh and comes to Mount Hor.
At Mount Hor, near the border of Edom, the LORD says to Moses and Aaron,
"Aaron will be gathered to his people. He will not enter the land I give the Israelites, because both of you rebelled against my command at the waters of Meribah.
Get Aaron and his son Eleazar and take them up Mount Hor.
Remove Aaron’s garments and put them on his son Eleazar, for Aaron will be gathered to his people; he will die there."
Moses does what the LORD commands. They go up Mount Hor in the sight of the whole community.
Moses removes Aaron’s garments and puts them on his son Eleazar. And Aaron dies there on top of the mountain. Then Moses and Eleazar come down from the mountain.
When the whole community learns that Aaron has died, all the house of Israel mourns for him thirty days.
When the Canaanite king of Arad, who lives in the Negev, hears that Israel is coming along the road to Atharim, he attacks Israel and captures some of them.
Israel makes a vow to the LORD: "If you will deliver these people into our hands, we will totally destroy their cities."
The LORD listens to Israel’s plea and gives the Canaanites over to them. They completely destroy them and their towns. So the place is named Hormah—Destruction.
They travel from Mount Hor along the route to the Red Sea, to go around Edom. But the people grow impatient along the way;
they speak against God and against Moses: "Why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no bread! There is no water! And we detest this miserable food!"
Then the LORD sends venomous snakes among them; they bite the people, and many Israelites die.
The people come to Moses and say, "We sinned when we spoke against the LORD and against you. Pray that the LORD will take the snakes away from us." So Moses prays for the people.
The LORD says to Moses, "Make a snake and put it up on a pole; anyone who is bitten can look at it and live."
So Moses makes a bronze snake and puts it up on a pole. Then when anyone is bitten by a snake and looks at the bronze snake, they live.
The Israelites move on and camp at Oboth.
Then they set out from Oboth and camp in Iye-abarim, in the wilderness on the eastern border of Moab.
From there they move on and camp in the Zered Valley.
They set out from there and camp alongside the Arnon, which is in the wilderness extending into Amorite territory. The Arnon is the border of Moab, between Moab and the Amorites.
That is why the Book of the Wars of the LORD says:
"Waheb in Suphah and the valleys of Arnon,
and the slopes of the valleys
that reach to the dwelling of Ar
and lean against the border of Moab."
From there they continue on to Beer, the well where the LORD said to Moses, "Gather the people together and I will give them water."
Then Israel sings this song:
"Spring up, O well! Sing about it—
about the well that the princes dug,
that the nobles of the people sank,
the nobles with their scepters and staffs!"
From the wilderness they go on to Mattanah, then to Nahaliel, then to Bamoth,
and from Bamoth to the valley in the territory of Moab where the top of Pisgah overlooks the wasteland.
Israel sends messengers to say to Sihon king of the Amorites:
"Let us pass through your country. We will stay on the King’s Highway until we have passed through your territory."
But Sihon will not let Israel pass through his territory. He musters his entire army and marches out into the wilderness against Israel. When he reaches Jahaz, he fights Israel.
Israel cuts him down with the sword and takes over his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok, but only as far as the Ammonite border, because the Ammonites’ border is fortified.
Israel captures all the Amorite cities and settles in them, including Heshbon and all its surrounding settlements.
Heshbon was the city of Sihon king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab and taken from him all his land as far as the Arnon.
That is why the poets say:
"Come to Heshbon and let it be rebuilt!
Let the city of Sihon be restored!
Fire went out from Heshbon,
a blaze from the city of Sihon.
It consumed Ar of Moab,
the lords of the heights of Arnon.
Woe to you, Moab!
You are destroyed, O people of Chemosh!
He has made his sons fugitives
and his daughters captives
of Sihon king of the Amorites.
We have demolished them as far as Nophah,
which reaches to Medeba."
So Israel settles in the land of the Amorites.
After Moses sends men to spy out Jazer, they capture its surrounding settlements and drive out the Amorites who are there.
Then they turn and go up along the road toward Bashan, and Og king of Bashan and his whole army march out to meet them in battle at Edrei.

The LORD says to Moses, "Do not be afraid of him, for I have delivered him into your hands, along with his whole army and his land. Do to him what you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon."
So they strike him down, together with his sons and his whole army, leaving no survivors. And they take possession of his land.
The Israelites travel on and camp on the plains of Moab beside the Jordan across from Jericho.
Now Balak son of Zippor sees everything Israel has done to the Amorites,
and Moab is terrified because there are so many people. Indeed, Moab is filled with dread because of the Israelites.
The Moabites say to the elders of Midian, "This horde is going to lick up everything around us, as an ox licks up the grass of the field." So Balak son of Zippor, who is king of Moab at that time,

sends messengers to summon Balaam son of Beor, who is at Pethor, near the Euphrates River, in his native land. Balak says: "A people has come out of Egypt; they cover the face of the land and have settled next to me.

Now come and put a curse on these people, because they are too powerful for me. Perhaps then I will be able to defeat them and drive them out of the land. For I know that whoever you bless is blessed, and whoever you curse is cursed."
The elders of Moab and Midian leave, taking with them the fee for divination. When they come to Balaam, they deliver Balak’s message.
"Spend the night here," Balaam says to them, "and I will report back to you whatever the LORD tells me." So the Moabite officials stay with him.
God comes to Balaam and asks, "Who are these men with you?"
Balaam says to God, "Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent me this message:
'A people that has come out of Egypt covers the face of the land. Now come and put a curse on them for me. Perhaps then I will be able to fight them and drive them away.'"
But God says to Balaam, "Do not go with them. You must not put a curse on that people, because they are blessed."
The next morning Balaam gets up and says to Balak’s officials, "Go back to your own country, for the LORD has refused to let me go with you."
So the Moabite officials return to Balak and say, "Balaam refused to come with us."
Then Balak sends other officials, more numerous and more distinguished than the first.
They come to Balaam and say: "This is what Balak son of Zippor says: Do not let anything keep you from coming to me,
because I will reward you handsomely and do whatever you say. Come and put a curse on these people for me."
But Balaam answers them, "Even if Balak gave me all the silver and gold in his palace, I could not do anything great or small to go beyond the command of the LORD my God.
Now spend the night here so I can find out what else the LORD will tell me."
That night God comes to Balaam and says, "Since these men have come to summon you, go with them. But do only what I tell you."
Balaam gets up in the morning, saddles his donkey, and goes with the Moabite officials.
But God’s anger burns because he goes, and the angel of the LORD stands in the road to oppose him. Balaam is riding on his donkey, and his two servants are with him.
When the donkey sees the angel of the LORD standing in the road with a drawn sword in his hand, she turns off the road into a field. Balaam beats her to get her back on the road.
Then the angel of the LORD stands in a narrow path through the vineyards, with walls on both sides.
When the donkey sees the angel of the LORD, she presses close to the wall, crushing Balaam’s foot against it. So he beats her again.
Then the angel of the LORD moves on ahead and stands in a narrow place where there is no room to turn, either to the right or to the left.
When the donkey sees the angel of the LORD, she lies down under Balaam, and he is angry and beats her with his staff.
Then the LORD opens the donkey’s mouth, and she says to Balaam, "What have I done to you to make you beat me these three times?"
Balaam answers the donkey, "You have made a fool of me! If only I had a sword in my hand, I would kill you right now."
The donkey says to Balaam, "Am I not your own donkey, which you have always ridden, to this day? Have I been in the habit of doing this to you?" "No," he says.
Then the LORD opens Balaam’s eyes, and he sees the angel of the LORD standing in the road with his sword drawn. So he bows low and falls face down.
The angel of the LORD asks him, "Why have you beaten your donkey these three times? I have come here to oppose you because your path is reckless before me.
The donkey saw me and turned away from me these three times. If she had not turned away, I would certainly have killed you by now, but I would have spared her."
Balaam says to the angel of the LORD, "I have sinned. I did not realize you were standing in the road to oppose me. Now if you are displeased, I will go back."
The angel of the LORD says to Balaam, "Go with the men, but speak only what I tell you." So Balaam goes on with Balak’s officials.
When Balak hears that Balaam is coming, he goes out to meet him at the Moabite town on the Arnon border, at the edge of his territory.
Balak says to Balaam, "Did I not send you an urgent summons? Why didn’t you come to me? Am I really not able to reward you?"
"Well, I have come to you now," Balaam replies. "But I can’t say whatever I please. I must speak only what God puts in my mouth."
Then Balaam goes with Balak to Kiriath-huzoth.
Balak sacrifices cattle and sheep, and gives some to Balaam and the officials who are with him.
The next morning Balak takes Balaam up to Bamoth-baal, and from there he can see the outskirts of the Israelite camp.
Balaam says to Balak, "Build me seven altars here, and prepare seven bulls and seven rams for me."
Balak does what Balaam says, and the two of them offer a bull and a ram on each altar.

Then Balaam says to Balak, "Stay here beside your burnt offering while I go aside. Perhaps the LORD will come to meet me. Whatever he reveals to me I will tell you." Then he goes off to a barren height.
God meets with Balaam, and Balaam says to him, "I have prepared seven altars and offered a bull and a ram on each."
The LORD puts a word in Balaam’s mouth and says, "Go back to Balak and give him this word."
So he returns to him and finds him standing beside his burnt offering with all the Moabite officials.
Then Balaam utters his oracle:
"From Aram, Balak has brought me—
the king of Moab from the mountains of the east.
'Come, curse Jacob for me!
Come, denounce Israel!'
How can I curse whom God has not cursed?
How can I denounce whom the LORD has not denounced?
From the rocky peaks I see them;
from the heights I look down on them—
a people who dwell apart,
who do not count themselves among the nations.
Who can count the dust of Jacob,
or number even a fourth of Israel?
Let me die the death of the upright!
May my end be like theirs!"
Balak says to Balaam, "What have you done to me? I brought you to curse my enemies, but you have done nothing but bless them!"
Balaam answers, "Must I not speak what the LORD puts in my mouth?"
Then Balak says to him, "Come with me to another place where you can see them—you will see only a part of them, not all of them—and curse them for me from there."
So he takes him to the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah, and there he builds seven altars and offers a bull and a ram on each altar.
Balaam says to Balak, "Stay here beside your burnt offering while I meet with him over there."
The LORD meets with Balaam and puts a word in his mouth. Then he says, "Go back to Balak and say this to him."
So Balaam returns to him and finds him standing beside his burnt offering with the Moabite officials. Balak asks him, "What did the LORD say?"
Then Balaam utters his oracle:
"Rise up, Balak, and hear!
Listen to me, son of Zippor.
God is not a human, that he should lie—
not a son of man, that he should change his mind.
Does he speak and then not act?
Does he promise and not fulfill?
I have received a command to bless;
he has blessed, and I cannot reverse it.
He has not seen trouble in Jacob;
he has observed no misfortune in Israel.
The LORD their God is with them;
the shout of a king is among them.
God brought them out of Egypt;
he is for them like the horns of a wild ox.
There is no divination against Jacob,
no sorcery against Israel.
Now it is said of Jacob and Israel:
'See what God has done!'
The people rise like a lioness;
like a lion they lift themselves up.
They do not rest until they devour their prey
and drink the blood of those they have struck down."
Then Balak says to Balaam, "Neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!"
Balaam answers, "Did I not tell you: I must do whatever the LORD says?"
Then Balak says to Balaam, "Come, let me take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God to let you curse them for me from there."
And Balak takes Balaam to the top of Peor, overlooking the wasteland.
Balaam says, "Build me seven altars here, and prepare seven bulls and seven rams for me."
Balak does what Balaam asks and offers a bull and a ram on each altar.
Now when Balaam sees that it pleases the LORD to bless Israel, he does not go off as before in search of omens, but turns his face toward the wilderness.
When Balaam looks out and sees Israel camped tribe by tribe, the Spirit of God comes on him
and he utters his oracle:
"The oracle of Balaam son of Beor—
the oracle of the man whose eye is clear;
the oracle of one who hears the words of God,
who sees a vision from the Almighty,
who falls prostrate, yet with eyes wide open:
How beautiful are your tents, O Jacob,
your dwelling places, O Israel!
Like valleys they spread out,
like gardens beside a river—
like aloes the LORD has planted,
like cedars beside the waters.
Water will flow from their buckets;
their seed will have abundant water.
Their king will be greater than Agag;
their kingdom will be exalted.
God brought them out of Egypt;
his strength is like that of a wild ox.
He devours hostile nations,
crushing their bones,
piercing them through with his arrows.
Like a lion they crouch and lie down—
like a lioness: who dares to rouse them?
May those who bless you be blessed!
May those who curse you be cursed!"
Then Balak’s anger burns against Balaam. He strikes his hands together and says, "I summoned you to curse my enemies, but you have blessed them these three times.
Now leave! Go home! I said I would reward you handsomely, but the LORD has kept you from any reward."
Balaam answers Balak, "Did I not tell the messengers you sent to me:
'Even if Balak gave me all the silver and gold in his palace, I could not do anything of my own accord, good or bad, to go beyond the command of the LORD—and I must say only what the LORD says'"?
"Now I am going back to my people. But let me warn you what this people will do to your people in the days to come."
Then Balaam utters his oracle:
"The oracle of Balaam son of Beor—
the oracle of the man whose eye is clear;
the oracle of one who hears the words of God,
who has knowledge from the Most High,
who sees a vision from the Almighty,
who falls prostrate, yet with eyes wide open:
I see him—but not now;
I behold him—but not near.
A star will come out of Jacob;
a scepter will rise out of Israel.
He will crush the foreheads of Moab,
the skulls of all the sons of Sheth.
Edom will be a possession,
Seir a possession of its enemies,
while Israel grows strong.
A ruler will come from Jacob
and destroy the survivors of the city."
Then Balaam sees Amalek and utters his oracle: "Amalek was first among the nations, but their end is utter destruction."
Then he sees the Kenites and utters his oracle: "Your dwelling place is secure, your nest is set in the rock;
yet you Kenites will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive."
Then he utters his oracle: "Alas! Who can live when God does this?
Ships will come from the shores of Kittim; they will subdue Asshur and Eber, but they too will come to ruin."
Then Balaam gets up and returns home, and Balak goes his own way.
While Israel is staying in Shittim, the men begin to engage sexually with Moabite women,
who invite them to the sacrifices of their gods. The people eat and bow down before those gods.
So Israel joins in worshipping Baal of Peor. The LORD’s anger burns against them.
The LORD says to Moses, "Take all the leaders of the people and execute them in broad daylight before the LORD, so that the LORD’s fierce anger may turn away from Israel."
So Moses says to the judges of Israel, "Each of you must put to death those of your people who have joined in worshipping Baal of Peor."
Then an Israelite man brings into the camp a Midianite woman, right before the eyes of Moses and the whole assembly while they are weeping at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
When Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, sees this, he leaves the assembly, takes a spear in his hand,
and follows the Israelite man into the tent. He drives the spear through both of them—through the Israelite and into the woman’s belly. Then the plague against the Israelites stops.
The number who die in the plague is twenty-four thousand.
The LORD says to Moses,
"Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned my anger away from the Israelites. Since he was as zealous for my honor among them as I am, I did not put an end to them in my zeal.
Therefore tell him I am making my covenant of peace with him:
“This covenant will be for him and his descendants after him—
a covenant of an everlasting priesthood,
because he was zealous for his God
and made atonement for the Israelites.”
The name of the Israelite who was killed—the one killed with the Midianite woman—was Zimri son of Salu, the leader of a Simeonite family.
And the name of the Midianite woman who was killed was Cozbi daughter of Zur, a tribal chief of a Midianite family.
The LORD says to Moses,
"Treat the Midianites as enemies and strike them down,
because they treated you as enemies when they deceived you at Peor and because of Cozbi, the daughter of the Midianite leader, the woman who was killed when the plague came as a result of Peor."
After the plague, the LORD says to Moses and Eleazar son of Aaron the priest,
"Take a census of the whole Israelite community by families—all those twenty years old or more who are able to serve in Israel’s army."
So Moses and Eleazar the priest speak with them in the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho
and count those who are twenty years old and upward, just as the LORD commanded Moses and the Israelites who came out of Egypt.
Reuben, the firstborn of Israel. The Reubenite clans: the Hanochite clan from Hanoch, the Palluite clan from Pallu,
the Hezronite clan from Hezron, the Carmite clan from Carmi.
These are the Reubenite clans. Those listed number 43,730.
The son of Pallu is Eliab.
The sons of Eliab are Nemuel, Dathan, and Abiram—the same Dathan and Abiram chosen by the community who rebelled against Moses and Aaron as part of Korah’s faction when they defied the LORD.
The ground opens its mouth and swallows them together with Korah, whose followers die when the fire consumes the 250 men. They become a warning sign.
But the sons of Korah do not die.
The Simeonite clans: the Nemuelite clan from Nemuel, the Jaminite clan from Jamin, the Jakinite clan from Jakin,
the Zerahite clan from Zerah, the Shaulite clan from Shaul.
These are the Simeonite clans. Those listed number 22,200.
The Gadite clans: the Zephonite clan from Zephon, the Haggite clan from Haggi, the Shunite clan from Shuni,
the Oznite clan from Ozni, the Erite clan from Eri,
the Arodite clan from Arodi, the Arelite clan from Areli.
These are the Gadite clans. Those listed number 40,500.
Er and Onan, sons of Judah, die in the land of Canaan.
The Judahite clans: the Shelanite clan from Shelah, the Perezite clan from Perez, the Zerahite clan from Zerah.
The descendants of Perez: the Hezronite clan from Hezron and the Hamulite clan from Hamul.
These are the Judahite clans. Those listed number 76,500.
The Issacharite clans: the Tolaite clan from Tola, the Puaite clan from Puah,
the Jashubite clan from Jashub, the Shimronite clan from Shimron.
These are the Issacharite clans. Those listed number 64,300.
The Zebulunite clans: the Seredite clan from Sered, the Elonite clan from Elon, the Jahleelite clan from Jahleel.
These are the Zebulunite clans. Those listed number 64,400.
The sons of Joseph by their clans: Manasseh and Ephraim.
The Manassites: from Makir, the Makirite clan. Makir is the father of Gilead; from Gilead, the Gileadite clan.
The descendants of Gilead: the Iezerite clan from Iezer, the Helekite clan from Helek,
the Asrielite clan from Asriel, the Shechemite clan from Shechem,
the Shemidaite clan from Shemida, and the Hepherite clan from Hepher.
Zelophehad son of Hepher has no sons, only daughters. Their names are Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.
These are the Manassite clans. Those listed number 52,700.
The Ephraimite clans: the Shuthelahite clan from Shuthelah, the Bekerite clan from Beker, the Tahanite clan from Tahan.
The descendants of Shuthelah: the Eranite clan from Eran.
These are the Ephraimite clans. Those listed number 32,500.
The Benjaminite clans: the Belaite clan from Bela, the Ashbelite clan from Ashbel, the Ahiramite clan from Ahiram,
the Shuphamite clan from Shupham, the Huphamite clan from Hupham.
The sons of Bela are Ard and Naaman: the Ardite clan from Ard and the Naamite clan from Naaman.
These are the Benjaminite clans. Those listed number 45,600.
The Danite clans: the Shuhamite clan from Shuham.
These are the Danite clans. Those listed number 64,400.
The Asherite clans: the Imnite clan from Imnah, the Ishvite clan from Ishvi, the Beriite clan from Beriah.
The descendants of Beriah: the Heberite clan from Heber and the Malkielite clan from Malkiel.
Asher has a daughter named Serah.
These are the Asherite clans. Those listed number 53,400.
The Naphtalite clans: the Jahzeelite clan from Jahzeel, the Gunite clan from Guni,
the Jezerite clan from Jezer, the Shillemite clan from Shillem.
These are the Naphtalite clans. Those listed number 45,400.
The total of all the Israelites comes to 601,730.
The LORD says to Moses,
"Divide the land among these tribes as an inheritance, according to the number of names.
To a larger group give a larger inheritance, and to a smaller group a smaller one. Each tribe is to receive its inheritance according to the number of those registered.
Be sure the land is divided by lot. Each tribe will receive its inheritance according to the names of its ancestral tribe.
Each inheritance is to be divided by lot among the larger and smaller tribes."
These are the Levites counted by their clans: the Gershonite clan from Gershon, the Kohathite clan from Kohath, the Merarite clan from Merari.
These also are Levite clans: the Libnite clan, the Hebronite clan, the Mahlite clan, the Mushite clan, and the Korahite clan. Kohath is the ancestor of Amram.
The name of Amram’s wife is Jochebed, a descendant of Levi, born to the Levites in Egypt. To Amram she bears Aaron, Moses, and their sister Miriam.
Aaron is the father of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
But Nadab and Abihu die when they make an offering of unauthorized fire before the LORD.
The total Levites counted is 23,000—all males a month old or more. They are not counted along with the other Israelites because they receive no inheritance among them.
These are the ones counted by Moses and Eleazar the priest when they count the Israelites on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho.
Not one of them is among those counted by Moses and Aaron the priest when they count the Israelites in the wilderness of Sinai.
For the LORD has told them, "They will surely die in the wilderness." Not one of them is left except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.
The daughters of Zelophehad son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Makir, the son of Manasseh, come forward—Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah are their names.
They stand before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the leaders, and the whole congregation at the entrance to the tent of meeting and say,
"Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among Korah’s followers, who banded together against the LORD. He died for his own sin without leaving any sons.
Why should our father’s name disappear from his clan because he had no son? Give us property among our father’s brothers."
Moses brings their case before the LORD.
And the LORD says to him,
"What the daughters of Zelophehad say is right. You shall give them property as an inheritance among their father’s brothers and transfer their father’s inheritance to them.
"Say to the Israelites: if a man dies and leaves no son, transfer his inheritance to his daughter.
If he has no daughter, give his inheritance to his brothers.
If he has no brothers, give his inheritance to his father’s brothers.

If his father had no brothers, give his inheritance to the nearest relative in his clan, and he will take possession of it. This is to be a legal requirement for the Israelites, as the LORD commanded Moses."
The LORD says to Moses:
"Go up into the Abarim range and see the land I have given the Israelites.
After you have seen it,
you too will be gathered to your people,
as your brother Aaron was gathered—
for when the community rebelled at the waters in the wilderness of Zin,
both of you disobeyed my command to honor me as holy before their eyes."
Moses says to the LORD:
"May the LORD—the God of the spirits of all flesh—
appoint a man over this congregation
who will go out before them and come in,
who will lead them out and bring them in,
so the LORD’s people will not be like sheep without a shepherd."
The LORD says to Moses, "Take Joshua son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.
Have him stand before Eleazar the priest and the entire congregation and commission him in their sight.
Give him some of your authority so the whole Israelite community will obey him.

He is to stand before Eleazar the priest, who will obtain decisions for him by inquiring of the Urim before the LORD. At his command the whole community of Israel—including all who go out and come in—will set out and come back."
Moses does as the LORD commands him. He takes Joshua and has him stand before Eleazar the priest and the whole assembly.
Moses lays his hands on Joshua and commissions him, just as the LORD instructed through Moses.
The LORD says to Moses:
"Give this command to the Israelites: be careful to present to me at the appointed time the food offering, as an aroma pleasing to me.
Tell them: this is the food offering you are to present to the LORD—two lambs a year old without defect, as a regular burnt offering each day.
