But if you cannot tell me, then you will give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.” They say to him: “Put your riddle. Let us hear it.”
He says to them:
“Out of the eater came something to eat,
out of the strong came something sweet.”
For three days they cannot solve the riddle.
On the fourth day they say to Samson’s wife: “Coax your husband to tell us the riddle, or we will burn you and your father’s house with fire. Did you invite us here to make us poor?”

Samson’s wife weeps over him and says: “You only hate me — you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told it to me.” He says to her: “Look — I have not told it to my father or my mother. Why would I tell it to you?”
She weeps over him the seven days of their feast. On the seventh day, because she presses him hard, he tells her. And she tells the riddle to her people.
The men of the city say to him on the seventh day, before the sun goes down:
“What is sweeter than honey?
What is stronger than a lion?”
He says to them: “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have figured out my riddle.”

The Spirit of YHWH rushes upon him, and he goes down to Ashkelon and strikes down thirty men of them, takes their belongings, and gives the changes of clothes to those who told the riddle. His anger burns, and he goes up to his father’s house.
And Samson’s wife is given to his companion — the one who had been his best man.
After some time, at the days of the wheat harvest, Samson visits his wife with a young goat. He says: “I will go in to my wife in the chamber.” But her father will not let him go in.
Her father says: “I truly thought that you completely hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister better than she? Take her instead.”
Samson says to them: “This time I am blameless toward the Philistines, when I do them harm.”
Samson goes and catches three hundred foxes. He takes torches, turns the foxes tail to tail, and puts a torch between each pair of tails.
He sets the torches on fire and lets the foxes loose in the standing grain of the Philistines. He burns up the shocks and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and the olive groves.

The Philistines say: “Who has done this?” They are told: “Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite — because he took his wife and gave her to his companion.” So the Philistines go up and burn her and her father with fire.
Samson says to them: “If this is how you act, then I will not stop until I have taken vengeance on you.”
He strikes them hip and thigh — a great blow. Then he goes down and stays in the cleft of the rock of Etam.
The Philistines go up and camp in Judah. They spread out at Lehi.
The men of Judah say: “Why have you come up against us?” They say: “We have come up to bind Samson — to do to him as he has done to us.”

Three thousand men of Judah go down to the cleft of the rock of Etam and say to Samson: “Don’t you know that the Philistines are ruling over us? What is this you have done to us?” He says to them: “As they did to me, so I have done to them.”
They say to him: “We have come down to bind you, to hand you over to the Philistines.” Samson says to them: “Swear to me that you yourselves will not attack me.”
They say to him: “No — we will only bind you tightly and hand you over to them. We will not kill you.” So they bind him with two new ropes and bring him up from the rock.
When he comes to Lehi, the Philistines shout to meet him. The Spirit of YHWH rushes upon him. The ropes on his arms become like flax burned with fire, and his bonds melt off his hands.
He finds a fresh jawbone of a donkey, reaches out his hand and takes it, and strikes down with it a thousand men.
Samson says:
“With the jawbone of a donkey —
heap upon heaps.
With the jawbone of a donkey
I have struck down a thousand men.”
When he finishes speaking, he throws the jawbone from his hand. That place is named Ramath-lehi.
He is very thirsty, and he calls to YHWH and says: “You have given this great deliverance through the hand of your servant — and now I will die of thirst and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?”
So God splits open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water comes out from it. He drinks; his spirit returns, and he revives. So its name is called En-hakkore, which is at Lehi to this day.
He judges Israel twenty years in the days of the Philistines.
Samson goes to Gaza. There he sees a prostitute, and he goes in to her.

The Gazites are told: “Samson has come here.” They surround the place and lie in wait for him all night at the gate of the city. They are still all night, saying: “Wait until the morning light — then we will kill him.”

Samson lies there till midnight. At midnight he gets up, takes hold of the doors of the city gate and the two posts, pulls them up — bar and all — puts them on his shoulders, and carries them up to the top of the hill that is opposite Hebron.
Some time after this, he falls in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek. Her name is Delilah.

The lords of the Philistines come up to her and say to her: “Coax him, and find out what makes his strength so great, and how we might overpower him, so that we may bind him and humble him. Each one of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”
So Delilah says to Samson: “Tell me, please, what makes your strength so great, and with what could you be bound to be humbled.”
Samson says to her: “If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I will become weak and be like any other man.”
The lords of the Philistines bring up to her seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, and she binds him with them.

Now men are lying in wait in an inner room. She says to him: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” But he snaps the bowstrings as a strand of tow snaps when it touches fire. The secret of his strength is not known.
Delilah says to Samson: “Look — you have mocked me and told me lies. Now please tell me — with what could you be bound?”
He says to her: “If they bind me tightly with new ropes that have never been used for work, then I will become weak and be like any other man.”
So Delilah takes new ropes and binds him with them, and says to him: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” — with men lying in wait in the inner room. But he snaps them off his arms like a thread.
Delilah says to Samson: “Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me with what you could be bound.” He says to her: “If you weave the seven locks of my head into the web of the loom.”
So she fastens it with the pin and says to him: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He wakes from his sleep, and pulls away the pin of the loom and the web.
She says to him: “How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not with me? Three times now you have mocked me, and you have not told me what makes your strength so great.”
Because she presses him with her words day after day and urges him, his soul grows short to death.

He tells her all his heart and says to her: “A razor has never come on my head — for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me; I will become weak and be like any other man.”

When Delilah sees that he has told her all his heart, she sends and summons the lords of the Philistines, saying: “Come up this once, for he has told me all his heart.” So the lords of the Philistines come up to her, bringing the silver in their hand.
She makes him sleep on her knees, and she calls a man and has him shave off the seven locks of his head. She begins to humble him. His strength leaves him.
She says: “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He wakes from his sleep and says: “I will go out as at other times and shake myself free.” But he does not know that YHWH has left him.
The Philistines seize him and gouge out his eyes. They bring him down to Gaza and bind him with bronze fetters, and he grinds at the mill in the prison.
But the hair of his head begins to grow again after it was shaved.
The lords of the Philistines gather to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god, and to celebrate. They say:
“Our god has given Samson our enemy
into our hand.”
When the people see him, they praise their god, for they say:
“Our god has given into our hand
our enemy,
the ravager of our land,
who multiplied our slain.”
And when their hearts are merry, they say: “Call Samson — let him entertain us.” So they call Samson from the prison, and he entertains them. They make him stand between the pillars.
Samson says to the young man holding his hand: “Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean on them.”
The house is full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines are there, and on the roof are about three thousand men and women watching as Samson entertains.
Samson calls to YHWH and says:
“Lord YHWH, remember me, I beg you.
Strengthen me only this once, O God,
that I may take from the Philistines
one stroke of vengeance for my two eyes.”
Samson takes hold of the two middle pillars on which the house stands, and he braces himself against them — one with his right hand, one with his left.

Samson says: “Let me die with the Philistines.” He pushes with all his strength, and the house falls on the lords and on all the people in it. So the dead he killed in his death are more than those he killed in his life.
His brothers and all his father’s house come down and take him up. They bring him up and bury him between Zorah and Eshtaol, in the tomb of Manoah his father. He judged Israel twenty years.
There is a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name is Micah.

He says to his mother: “The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you — about which you spoke a curse, and which you even spoke in my hearing — look, the silver is with me. I took it.” His mother says: “Blessed be my son by YHWH.”

He returns the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother. His mother says: “I solemnly consecrate the silver to YHWH from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a cast image. Now then, I will return it to you.”
So he returns the silver to his mother. His mother takes two hundred pieces of silver and gives them to the silversmith, who makes from it a carved image and a cast image. They are in Micah’s house.
This man Micah has a shrine. He makes an ephod and household gods, and consecrates one of his sons, who becomes his priest.
In those days there is no king in Israel. Each man does what is right in his own eyes.
There is a young man from Bethlehem of Judah, from the clan of Judah. He is a Levite, and he is sojourning there.
The man departs from the city, from Bethlehem of Judah, to sojourn wherever he can find a place. He comes to the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah’s house, as he travels.
Micah says to him: “Where are you from?” He says to him: “I am a Levite from Bethlehem of Judah, and I am going to sojourn wherever I can find a place.”
Micah says to him: “Stay with me, and be a father and a priest to me. I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, a set of clothes, and your food.” So the Levite goes in.
The Levite is content to stay with the man, and the young man becomes to him like one of his sons.
Micah consecrates the Levite, and the young man becomes his priest. He is in Micah’s house.
Micah says: “Now I know that YHWH will do me good — because I have a Levite as priest.”

In those days there is no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the Danites is seeking an inheritance to settle in — for to that day no inheritance has fallen to them among the tribes of Israel.

The Danites send from their clan five men from their whole number, men of valor, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and explore it. They say to them: “Go, explore the land.” They come to the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah’s house, and spend the night there.
While they are at Micah’s house, they recognize the voice of the young Levite. They turn aside there and say to him: “Who brought you here? What are you doing here? What is there for you here?”
He says to them: “Thus and thus has Micah done for me. He has hired me, and I have become his priest.”
They say to him: “Please inquire of God, that we may know whether the journey we are taking will be successful.”
The priest says to them: “Go in peace. The way you are going is before YHWH.”

The five men go on and come to Laish. They see the people there — how they live in safety, in the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and trusting, with no one in the land lacking anything as ruler. They are far from the Sidonians and have no dealings with anyone.
The men come back to their kinsmen at Zorah and Eshtaol, and their brothers say to them: “What do you report?”
They say: “Get up — let us go up against them. We have seen the land, and look, it is very good. Will you keep quiet? Do not be slow to go, to enter and take possession of the land.
When you go, you will come to a trusting people. The land is broad — for God has given it into your hand — a place where there is no lack of anything that is on the earth.”
So six hundred men of the clan of the Danites, armed with weapons of war, set out from there — from Zorah and Eshtaol.
They go up and camp at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That is why the place is called Mahaneh-dan — Dan’s Camp — to this day. It is west of Kiriath-jearim.
From there they pass through the hill country of Ephraim, and they come to Micah’s house.

Then the five men who had gone to spy out the land of Laish say to their kinsmen: “Did you know that in these houses there is an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a cast image? Now consider what you should do.”
So they turn aside there and come to the house of the young Levite — to Micah’s house — and they greet him.
The six hundred Danites stand at the entrance of the gate, armed with their weapons of war.

The five men who had gone to spy out the land go up and enter there. They take the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the cast image, while the priest stands at the entrance of the gate with the six hundred armed men.
When these men enter Micah’s house and take the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the cast image, the priest says to them: “What are you doing?”

They say to him: “Be quiet. Put your hand on your mouth. Come with us, and be a father and a priest to us. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and a clan in Israel?”
The priest’s heart is glad. He takes the ephod, the household gods, and the carved image, and goes in the midst of the people.
They turn and depart, putting the children, the livestock, and the goods before them.
They have gone some distance from Micah’s house when the men in the houses near Micah’s are called out, and they overtake the Danites.
They shout to the Danites, who turn around and say to Micah: “What is the matter with you, that you have called out your men?”
He says: “You have taken my gods — the ones I made — and you have taken the priest, and you have gone away. What is left to me? How can you say to me, ‘What is the matter with you?’”
The Danites say to him: “Do not let your voice be heard among us, or men of bitter spirit will fall upon you, and you will lose your life and the lives of your household.”
The Danites go on their way. When Micah sees that they are too strong for him, he turns and goes back to his house.

They take what Micah had made, along with the priest who was his, and they come upon Laish — a people quiet and trusting — and they strike them down with the edge of the sword and burn down the city with fire.
There is no one to rescue, because it is far from Sidon and they have no dealings with anyone. It is in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. They rebuild the city and live in it.
They name the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor, who was born to Israel. But the city’s original name was Laish.
The Danites set up the carved image for themselves. And Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses — he and his sons — are priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day the land goes into captivity.
They set up for themselves Micah’s carved image, the one he had made, all the days that the house of God was at Shiloh.
In those days, when there is no king in Israel, there is a certain Levite sojourning in the remote part of the hill country of Ephraim. He takes for himself a concubine from Bethlehem of Judah.
But his concubine is unfaithful to him and goes away from him to her father’s house at Bethlehem of Judah. She is there four months.

Her husband gets up and goes after her, to speak tenderly to her and bring her back. He has his servant and a pair of donkeys with him. She brings him into her father’s house, and when the girl’s father sees him, he is glad to meet him.
His father-in-law, the girl’s father, detains him. He stays with him three days. They eat and drink and lodge there.
On the fourth day they rise early in the morning, and he gets up to go. The girl’s father says to his son-in-law: “Sustain your heart with a piece of bread, and after that you can go.”
So the two of them sit down together and eat and drink. The girl’s father says to the man: “Please be willing to spend the night, and let your heart be merry.”
When the man gets up to go, his father-in-law urges him, so he stays the night there again.
He rises early on the morning of the fifth day to go. The girl’s father says: “Please sustain your heart and linger until the day declines.” So the two of them eat.

When the man gets up to go — he and his concubine and his servant — his father-in-law, the girl’s father, says to him: “Look — the day is drawing to evening. Spend the night, please. Look — the day is declining. Lodge here and let your heart be merry. Tomorrow you can rise early for your way and go to your tent.”
But the man is not willing to spend the night. He gets up, departs, and comes to a point opposite Jebus — which is Jerusalem — with his pair of saddled donkeys, his concubine, and his servant.
When they are near Jebus, the day is very far gone, and the servant says to his master: “Come, please, let us turn aside to this Jebusite city and spend the night in it.”
But his master says to him: “We will not turn aside into a foreign city, where none of the Israelites live. We will pass on to Gibeah.”
He says to his servant: “Come, let us approach one of these places. We will spend the night in Gibeah or in Ramah.”
So they pass on and travel, and the sun goes down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They turn aside there to go in and spend the night in Gibeah. The man goes in and sits down in the open square of the city, but no one takes them into his house to spend the night.
Then look — an old man comes in from his work in the field at evening. The man is from the hill country of Ephraim, and he is sojourning in Gibeah. But the men of the place are Benjaminites.
He lifts up his eyes and sees the wayfarer in the open square of the city. The old man says: “Where are you going, and where do you come from?”

He says to him: “We are passing from Bethlehem of Judah to the remote part of the hill country of Ephraim. I am from there. I went to Bethlehem of Judah, and now I am going home. There is no one taking me into his house.
We have straw and fodder for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me, for your servant, and for the young man with your servants. There is no lack of anything.”
The old man says: “Peace be to you. Let me take care of all your needs. Only do not spend the night in the square.”
He brings him into his house and feeds the donkeys. They wash their feet, eat, and drink.

As they are making their hearts merry, look — the men of the city, worthless men, surround the house. They beat on the door and say to the old man, the master of the house: “Bring out the man who came into your house, that we may know him.”
The man, the master of the house, goes out to them and says to them: “No, my brothers, please do not act so wickedly. Since this man has come into my house, do not do this outrage.
Here is my virgin daughter, and his concubine. Let me bring them out now. Humble them and do to them what is good in your eyes. But to this man do not do this outrageous thing.”
But the men will not listen to him. So the man seizes his concubine and brings her out to them. They know her, and abuse her all night until morning. They send her away as the dawn comes up.
As morning approaches, the woman comes and falls down at the door of the man’s house — where her master is — and lies there until daylight.
Her master gets up in the morning, opens the doors of the house, and goes out to go on his way. Look — the woman, his concubine, has fallen at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.
He says to her: “Get up. Let us go.” But there is no answer. So he puts her on the donkey, and the man gets up and goes to his place.
When he comes into his house, he takes a knife, takes hold of his concubine, and cuts her — limb by limb — into twelve pieces. He sends her throughout all the territory of Israel.
Everyone who sees it says: “Nothing like this has ever been done or seen, from the day the Israelites came up out of the land of Egypt to this day. Consider it. Take counsel. Speak up.”
So all the Israelites go out, and the assembly is gathered together as one man, from Dan to Beersheba, with the land of Gilead, to YHWH at Mizpah.
The chiefs of all the people — all the tribes of Israel — take their stand in the assembly of the people of God: four hundred thousand foot soldiers who draw the sword.
The Benjaminites hear that the Israelites have gone up to Mizpah. The Israelites say: “Speak — how did this evil thing happen?”
The Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answers and says: “I came to Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin, with my concubine, to spend the night.
The lords of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house at night because of me. They meant to kill me, and they violated my concubine, and she died.
I took my concubine, cut her in pieces, and sent her through all the territory of Israel’s inheritance — for they have done a vile and outrageous thing in Israel.
Look — all of you Israelites, give your word and counsel here.”
All the people rise as one man, saying: “None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will turn aside to his house.
Now this is the thing we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot.

We will take ten men from a hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, a hundred from a thousand, and a thousand from ten thousand, to gather provisions for the people, so that when they come to Gibeah of Benjamin they will repay it for all the outrage it has done in Israel.”
So all the men of Israel are gathered against the city as one man, united.
The tribes of Israel send men through the whole tribe of Benjamin, saying: “What is this evil that has happened among you?

Now then, hand over the worthless men who are in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and purge the evil from Israel.” But the Benjaminites will not listen to the voice of their brothers, the Israelites.
The Benjaminites gather from the cities to Gibeah, to go out to battle against the Israelites.
The Benjaminites mustered from the cities on that day are twenty-six thousand swordsmen, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who are mustered as seven hundred picked men.
From all this army there are seven hundred picked men who are left-handed. Each of them can sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
The men of Israel — apart from Benjamin — are mustered as four hundred thousand swordsmen. All these are men of war.
The Israelites rise and go up to Bethel and inquire of God. They say: “Who shall go up first for us to battle against the Benjaminites?” YHWH says: “Judah first.”
The Israelites rise in the morning and camp against Gibeah.
The men of Israel go out to fight against Benjamin, and the men of Israel array themselves in battle order against them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites come out from Gibeah and strike down on that day twenty-two thousand men of Israel — to the ground.
But the people, the men of Israel, take courage. They array themselves again for battle in the place where they had arrayed themselves the first day.
The Israelites go up and weep before YHWH until evening. They inquire of YHWH: “Shall I again draw near for battle against the Benjaminites my brother?” YHWH says: “Go up against him.”
The Israelites approach the Benjaminites on the second day.
Benjamin comes out against them from Gibeah on the second day, and again strikes down eighteen thousand men of the Israelites — all of them swordsmen.

Then all the Israelites — all the people — go up and come to Bethel. They weep and sit there before YHWH. They fast that day until evening, and they offer burnt offerings and peace offerings before YHWH.
The Israelites inquire of YHWH. (In those days the ark of the covenant of God is there.

Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, is standing before it in those days.) They say: “Shall I go out yet again to battle against the Benjaminites my brother, or shall I cease?” YHWH says: “Go up — for tomorrow I will give him into your hand.”
So Israel sets ambushes around Gibeah.
The Israelites go up against the Benjaminites on the third day, and they array themselves against Gibeah as before.

The Benjaminites come out to meet the people, and they are drawn away from the city. They begin to strike down some of the people, slain as before — on the highways, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah — about thirty men of Israel in the open country.
The Benjaminites say: “They are defeated before us as at the first.” But the Israelites have said: “Let us flee, and draw them away from the city to the highways.”
So all the men of Israel rise from their place and array themselves for battle at Baal-tamar, while the Israelite ambush rushes out from its place west of Geba.
Ten thousand picked men out of all Israel come opposite Gibeah, and the battle is fierce. But they do not know that disaster is near them.
YHWH strikes Benjamin before Israel, and on that day the Israelites destroy twenty-five thousand one hundred Benjaminites — all of them swordsmen.
The Benjaminites see that they are defeated. The men of Israel give way to Benjamin, because they trust the ambush they had set against Gibeah.
The ambush rushes out and spreads against Gibeah. The ambush advances and strikes the whole city with the edge of the sword.
The agreed signal between the men of Israel and the ambush is to make a great cloud of smoke rise from the city.
When the men of Israel turn in the battle, Benjamin begins to strike down the men of Israel — about thirty men — for they say: “Surely they are defeated before us as in the first battle.”
But when the signal — the column of smoke — begins to rise from the city, the Benjaminites look behind them, and look — the whole city is going up to the sky in flames.
Then the men of Israel turn back, and the men of Benjamin are dismayed, for they see that disaster has come upon them.
They turn before the men of Israel toward the wilderness, but the battle overtakes them. Those who come out of the cities cut them down in their midst.
They surround the Benjaminites, pursue them, and tread them down without rest as far as opposite Gibeah on the east.
Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fall — all of them men of valor.

They turn and flee toward the wilderness, to the rock of Rimmon. Five thousand of them are cut down on the highways, and they are pursued hard as far as Gidom, and two thousand of them are struck down.
So all who fell of Benjamin that day are twenty-five thousand swordsmen — all of them men of valor.
But six hundred men turn and flee toward the wilderness, to the rock of Rimmon, and they stay at the rock of Rimmon four months.
The men of Israel turn back against the Benjaminites and strike them down with the edge of the sword — the whole city, the cattle, all they find. And every city they come upon they set on fire.
The men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah: “None of us will give his daughter to a Benjaminite as wife.”
The people come to Bethel and sit there before God until evening. They lift up their voices and weep with bitter weeping.
They say: “Why, YHWH God of Israel, has this happened in Israel — that one tribe should be missing from Israel today?”
The next day the people rise early and build an altar there. They offer burnt offerings and peace offerings.

The Israelites say: “Who from all the tribes of Israel did not come up to the assembly to YHWH?” — for they had sworn a great oath about anyone who did not come up to YHWH at Mizpah: “He must surely be put to death.”
The Israelites grieve over their brother Benjamin. They say: “Today one tribe has been cut off from Israel.
What shall we do about wives for those who are left, since we have sworn by YHWH not to give them our daughters as wives?”
They say: “Which one of the tribes of Israel did not come up to YHWH at Mizpah?” It happens that no one had come into the camp from Jabesh-gilead to the assembly.
When the people are mustered, look — no one is there from the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead.
So the assembly sends there twelve thousand of the valiant men, commanding them: “Go, strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword — the women and the little ones.
This is the thing you are to do: every male and every woman who has known a man you must put under the ban.”
They find among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young virgins who had not known a man by lying with a male, and they bring them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
The whole assembly sends and speaks to the Benjaminites who are at the rock of Rimmon, and proclaims peace to them.
So Benjamin returns at that time, and they give them the women whom they had kept alive from the women of Jabesh-gilead — but they are not enough for them.
The people are sorry for Benjamin, because YHWH had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.
The elders of the assembly say: “What shall we do for wives for those who are left? — for the women of Benjamin have been destroyed.”
They say: “There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe is not blotted out from Israel.
But we cannot give them our daughters as wives.” — for the Israelites had sworn: “Cursed is anyone who gives a wife to Benjamin.”
So they say: “Look — there is the yearly feast of YHWH at Shiloh.” (Shiloh is north of Bethel, on the east of the road that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.)
They command the Benjaminites: “Go and lie in wait in the vineyards.

Watch — and when the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out from the vineyards. Each of you, seize a wife for himself from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.

If their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them: ‘Be gracious to them on our account, because we did not take wives for each of them in the war, and you did not give them to them — otherwise you would now be guilty.’”
The Benjaminites do so. They take wives, equal to their number, from the women who danced, whom they carried off. Then they go back to their inheritance, rebuild the cities, and live in them.
At that time the Israelites depart from there — each to his tribe and his clan — and they go out from there, each to his own inheritance.
In those days there is no king in Israel. Each man does what is right in his own eyes.
Famine, Loss, and the Road Home · 1:1–7
In the days when the judges judged, there is a famine in the land. A man from Bethlehem of Judah goes to sojourn in the country of Moab — he and his wife and his two sons.

The man's name is Elimelech, his wife's name is Naomi, and the names of his two sons are Mahlon and Chilion. They are Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They go to the country of Moab and remain there.
But Elimelech, Naomi's husband, dies — and she is left with her two sons.
These take Moabite wives. The name of the one is Orpah and the name of the other Ruth. They live there about ten years.
Then both Mahlon and Chilion die — so the woman is left without her two sons and her husband.
Then she sets out with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she has heard in the fields of Moab that YHWH has visited his people and given them food.
So she sets out from the place where she had been living, with her two daughters-in-law. They begin to go back to the land of Judah.
Naomi Urges Them to Return · 1:8–14
But Naomi says to her two daughters-in-law: "Go, return each of you to your mother's house. May YHWH deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me.
May YHWH grant that you each find rest in the house of your husband!" Then she kisses them — and they lift up their voices and weep.
They say to her: "No — we will return with you to your people."
But Naomi says: "Turn back, my daughters. Why will you go with me? Do I still have sons in my womb who could become your husbands?
Turn back, my daughters, go. I am too old to have a husband. Even if I thought there was hope for me — even if I had a husband tonight and bore sons —
would you wait for them to grow up? Would you refrain from marrying? No, my daughters. It is much more bitter for me than for you, for the hand of YHWH has gone out against me."
They lift up their voices and weep again. Then Orpah kisses her mother-in-law and turns back — but Ruth holds fast to her.
Ruth's Declaration · 1:15–18
"Look," says Naomi, "your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods. Return after your sister-in-law."
But Ruth says:
"Do not urge me to leave you
or to return from following you —
for where you go I will go,
and where you lodge I will lodge.
Your people shall be my people,
and your God my God.
Where you die I will die —
and there I will be buried.
May YHWH do so to me and more also
if anything but death parts me from you."
When Naomi sees that Ruth is determined to go with her, she says nothing more to her.
Arrival in Bethlehem · 1:19–22
So the two of them go on until they come to Bethlehem. When they come to Bethlehem, the whole town stirs because of them. The women say: "Is this Naomi?"
She says to them: "Do not call me Naomi — call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.
I went away full, and YHWH has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when YHWH has testified against me and the Almighty has brought calamity upon me?"
So Naomi returns — and Ruth the Moabite her daughter-in-law with her, who returned from the country of Moab. They come to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
Ruth Goes to Glean · 2:1–3
Now Naomi had a relative of her husband's — a worthy man from the clan of Elimelech, whose name is Boaz.
And Ruth the Moabite says to Naomi: "Let me go to the field and glean among the ears of grain after him in whose sight I may find favour." Naomi says to her: "Go, my daughter."
So she sets out and goes and gleans in the field after the reapers. And it happens that she comes to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who is of the clan of Elimelech.
Boaz Notices Ruth · 2:4–17
And look — Boaz comes from Bethlehem. He says to the reapers: "YHWH be with you!" And they answer: "YHWH bless you!"
Then Boaz says to his young man who is in charge of the reapers: "Whose young woman is this?"
The young man in charge of the reapers answers: "She is the young Moabite woman who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab.
She said, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the reapers.' So she came, and she has continued from early morning until now — except for a short rest."
Then Boaz says to Ruth: "Now, listen, my daughter — do not go to glean in another field or leave this one, but stay close to my young women.
Let your eyes be on the field they are reaping, and go after them. Have I not charged the young men not to touch you? When you are thirsty, go to the vessels and drink what the young men have drawn."
Then she falls on her face, bowing to the ground: "Why have I found favour in your eyes, that you should take notice of me — since I am a foreigner?"

But Boaz answers her: "All that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband has been fully told to me — how you left your father and mother and your native land and came to a people that you did not know before.
May YHWH repay you for what you have done — and may a full reward be given to you by YHWH the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge!"
Then she says: "I have found favour in your eyes, my lord — for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not one of your servants."

At mealtime Boaz says to her: "Come here and eat some bread, and dip your morsel in the wine." So she sits beside the reapers, and he passes to her roasted grain. She eats until she is satisfied, and she has some left over.
When she gets up to glean, Boaz instructs his young men: "Let her glean even among the sheaves — and do not reproach her.
And also pull out some from the bundles for her and leave it for her to glean — and do not rebuke her."
So she gleans in the field until evening. When she beats out what she has gleaned, it is about an ephah of barley.
Ruth Returns to Naomi · 2:18–23
She carries it into the town and her mother-in-law sees what she has gleaned. She also brings out and gives her what food she had left over after being satisfied.

Her mother-in-law says to her: "Where did you glean today? Where have you worked? Blessed be the man who took notice of you." So she tells her mother-in-law with whom she had worked: "The man's name with whom I worked today is Boaz."

And Naomi says to her daughter-in-law: "May he be blessed by YHWH, whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead!" Naomi also says to her: "The man is a close relative of ours — he is one of our redeemers."
And Ruth the Moabite says: "Besides, he said to me, 'You shall keep close by my young men until they have finished all my harvest.'"
And Naomi says to Ruth her daughter-in-law: "It is good, my daughter, that you go out with his young women — lest in another field you be assaulted."
So she keeps close to the young women of Boaz, gleaning until the end of the barley and wheat harvests. And she lives with her mother-in-law.
Naomi's Plan · 3:1–5
Then Naomi her mother-in-law says to her: "My daughter, should I not seek rest for you — so that it may go well with you?
Is not Boaz our relative, with whose young women you were? See — he is winnowing barley tonight at the threshing floor.
Wash therefore and anoint yourself, put on your cloak, and go down to the threshing floor. Do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking.
But when he lies down, observe the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down — and he will tell you what to do."
Ruth says to her: "All that you say I will do."
At the Threshing Floor · 3:6–13
So she goes down to the threshing floor and does everything her mother-in-law had told her.
When Boaz has eaten and drunk and his heart is merry, he goes to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then she comes softly and uncovers his feet and lies down.
At midnight the man is startled and turns over — and look, a woman is lying at his feet!
He says: "Who are you?" She answers: "I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wings over your servant — for you are a redeemer."
And he says: "May you be blessed by YHWH, my daughter — for this last kindness is greater than the first. You have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich.
And now, my daughter, do not be afraid. I will do for you all that you ask — for all my fellow townspeople know that you are a worthy woman.
And now it is true that I am a redeemer. But there is a redeemer nearer than I.
Remain tonight, and in the morning — if he will redeem you, good. Let him do it. But if he does not wish to redeem you, then as YHWH lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until morning."
Ruth Returns to Naomi · 3:14–18
So she lies at his feet until morning — then rises before one could recognise another. For he said: "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor."
And he says: "Bring the garment you are wearing and hold it out." So she holds it out, and he measures out six measures of barley and puts it on her. Then she goes into the city.
When she comes to her mother-in-law, Naomi says: "How did it go, my daughter?" Then she tells her everything that the man had done for her,
saying: "These six measures of barley he gave to me — for he said, 'You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law.'"
Naomi says: "Wait, my daughter, until you learn how the matter turns out — for the man will not rest until he has settled it today."
The Gate · 4:1–12
Now Boaz goes up to the gate and sits down there. And look — the redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken comes by. Boaz says: "Turn aside, friend — sit down here." So he turns aside and sits down.
And Boaz takes ten men of the elders of the city and says: "Sit down here." So they sit down.
Then he says to the redeemer: "Naomi, who has come back from the country of Moab, is selling the parcel of land that belonged to our relative Elimelech.

So I thought I would tell you of it and say: 'Buy it in the presence of those sitting here and in the presence of the elders of my people.' If you will redeem it, redeem it. But if you will not, tell me — so that I may know. For there is no one besides you to redeem it, and I am after you." He says: "I will redeem it."
Then Boaz says: "The day you buy the field from the hand of Naomi, you also acquire Ruth the Moabite, the widow of the dead man, in order to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance."
The redeemer says: "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I damage my own inheritance. Take my right of redemption yourself — for I cannot redeem it."

Now in earlier times in Israel, this was the custom for redeeming and exchanging: to confirm a transaction, one party drew off his sandal and gave it to the other. This was the manner of attesting in Israel.
So the redeemer says to Boaz: "Buy it for yourself." And he draws off his sandal.
Then Boaz says to the elders and all the people: "You are witnesses this day that I have bought from the hand of Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech and all that belonged to Chilion and to Mahlon.

Also Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Mahlon, I have acquired to be my wife, to perpetuate the name of the dead in his inheritance — so that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers and from the gate of his native place. You are witnesses this day."
Then all the people who were at the gate and the elders say:
"We are witnesses.
May YHWH make the woman who is coming into your house
like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel.
May you act worthily in Ephrathah
and be renowned in Bethlehem.
May your house be like the house of Perez,
whom Tamar bore to Judah —
because of the offspring that YHWH will give you
by this young woman."
A Son Is Born · 4:13–17
So Boaz takes Ruth, and she becomes his wife. And he goes in to her — and YHWH gives her conception — and she bears a son.
Then the women say to Naomi:
"Blessed be YHWH, who has not left you this day without a redeemer!
May his name be renowned in Israel!
He shall be to you a restorer of life
and a nourisher of your old age —
for your daughter-in-law who loves you,
who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him!"
Then Naomi takes the child and lays him on her lap and becomes his nurse.
And the women of the neighborhood give him a name, saying: "A son has been born to Naomi." They name him Obed. He is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
The Genealogy · 4:18–22
Now these are the generations of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron,
Hezron fathered Ram, Ram fathered Amminadab,
Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon,
Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed,
Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David.
There is a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from the hill country of Ephraim — his name Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
He has two wives. One is named Hannah; the other is named Peninnah. Peninnah has children, but Hannah has no children.
Year after year this man goes up from his city to worship and sacrifice to YHWH of hosts at Shiloh, where Hophni and Phinehas, the two sons of Eli, serve as priests of YHWH.
On the day when Elkanah sacrifices, he gives portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But to Hannah he gives a double portion, because he loves her — yet YHWH has closed her womb.
Her rival provokes her bitterly, to make her miserable, because YHWH has closed her womb.
So year after year, whenever she goes up to the house of YHWH, Peninnah provokes her. Hannah weeps and will not eat.
Elkanah her husband says to her, “Hannah, why are you weeping? Why will you not eat? Why is your heart so troubled? Am I not more to you than ten sons?”
After they eat and drink at Shiloh, Hannah rises. Eli the priest is sitting on his seat beside the doorpost of the temple of YHWH.
She is bitter in soul and prays to YHWH, weeping without restraint.

She makes a vow and says, “O YHWH of hosts — if you will truly see the affliction of your servant, if you will remember me and not forget your servant, but will give your servant a son, then I will give him to YHWH all the days of his life, and no razor shall ever come upon his head.”
As she keeps praying before YHWH, Eli watches her mouth.
Hannah is speaking in her heart. Only her lips move, and her voice is not heard. Eli takes her for a drunk.
He says to her, “How long will you make yourself drunk? Put away your wine!”
“No, my lord,” Hannah answers. “I am a woman deeply troubled. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink. I have been pouring out my soul before YHWH.
Do not take your servant for a worthless woman. It is out of the depths of my anguish and grief that I have been speaking all this time.”
Eli answers her, “Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant what you have asked of him.”
She says, “May your servant find favor in your eyes.” The woman goes her way, eats, and her face is troubled no more.
They rise early in the morning and worship before YHWH, then return to their house at Ramah. Elkanah is with Hannah his wife, and YHWH remembers her.
In due course Hannah conceives and bears a son, and she calls his name Samuel, saying, “Because I asked him of YHWH.”
The man Elkanah and all his household go up to offer to YHWH the yearly sacrifice and to fulfill his vow.
But Hannah does not go up, for she says to her husband, “As soon as the child is weaned I will bring him, so that he may appear before YHWH and remain there always.”
Elkanah her husband says to her, “Do what seems best to you; wait until you have weaned him. Only may YHWH confirm his word.” So the woman stays and nurses her son until she weans him.
When she has weaned him, she takes him up with her — a three-year-old bull, one ephah of flour, and a skin of wine — and brings him to the house of YHWH at Shiloh. The child is young.
They slaughter the bull and bring the child before Eli.
She says, “Oh, my lord — as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you, praying to YHWH.
For this child I prayed, and YHWH has given me what I asked of him.
So I have given him back to YHWH. As long as he lives, he is given to YHWH.” And she worships YHWH there.
Hannah prays and says:
My heart exults in YHWH;
my horn is lifted high in YHWH.
My mouth opens wide against my enemies,
for I rejoice in your salvation.
There is no Holy One like YHWH —
there is none beside you;
there is no Rock like our God.
Talk no more with such proud boasting;
let no arrogance come from your mouth —
for YHWH is a God of knowledge,
and by him all actions are weighed.
The bows of the mighty are broken,
but those who stumbled are girded with strength.
Those who were full now hire themselves out for bread,
but those who were hungry are hungry no more.
The barren has borne seven,
but she who had many children is forlorn.
YHWH kills and brings to life;
he brings down to Sheol and raises up.
YHWH makes poor and makes rich;
he brings low and he exalts.
He raises the poor from the dust,
he lifts the needy from the ash heap,
to seat them with princes
and give them a throne of honor.
For the pillars of the earth are YHWH’s,
and on them he has set the world.
He guards the feet of his faithful ones,
but the wicked are cut off in darkness —
for not by strength shall any man prevail.
Those who oppose YHWH are shattered;
from heaven he thunders against them.
YHWH will judge the ends of the earth;
he will give strength to his king
and exalt the horn of his anointed.
Elkanah goes home to Ramah, but the boy Samuel ministers before YHWH in the presence of Eli the priest.
Now the sons of Eli are worthless men. They do not know YHWH.
The custom of the priests with the people is this: when any man offers sacrifice, the priest’s servant comes while the meat is still boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand,

and he thrusts it into the basin, or the kettle, or the pot, or the cauldron — and whatever the fork brings up, the priest takes for himself. This is what they do to all the Israelites who come to sacrifice at Shiloh.

Moreover, before the fat has even been burned, the priest’s servant comes and says to the man offering sacrifice, “Give meat for the priest to roast. He will not take boiled meat from you — only raw.”
And if the man says, “Let the fat be burned first, then take as much as you want,” the servant answers, “No — hand it over now, or I will take it by force.”
The sin of these young men is very great before YHWH, for they have treated the offering of YHWH with contempt.
Samuel is ministering before YHWH — a boy clothed in a linen ephod.
His mother makes him a little robe and brings it to him each year when she goes up with her husband for the yearly sacrifice.
Eli blesses Elkanah and his wife and says, “May YHWH give you children by this woman in place of the one she dedicated to YHWH.” Then they return home.
YHWH visits Hannah; she conceives and bears three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grows before YHWH.
Now Eli is very old. He hears all that his sons are doing to all Israel, and how they lie with the women who serve at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
He says to them, “Why do you do such things? I hear of your evil dealings from all the people here.
No, my sons — it is no good report that I hear spreading among the people of YHWH.

If one man sins against another, God can mediate for him, but if a man sins against YHWH, who will intercede for him?” But they will not listen to their father’s voice, for YHWH has resolved to put them to death.
The boy Samuel, meanwhile, goes on growing, increasing in favor both with YHWH and with people.
A man of God comes to Eli and says to him, “Thus says YHWH: Did I not reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt, as slaves to the house of Pharaoh?

I chose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest — to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear the ephod before me — and I gave to your father’s house all the fire-offerings of the people of Israel.
Why then do you look with greedy eye at my sacrifices and my offerings that I commanded? Why do you honor your sons above me, fattening yourselves on the best of every offering of my people Israel?

Therefore YHWH the God of Israel declares: ‘I promised that your house and your father’s house would walk before me forever.’ But now YHWH declares: ‘Far be it from me! Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be brought to nothing.
The days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father’s house, so that there will be no elder in your house.
You will look upon the distress of my dwelling, amid all the good that I do for Israel, and there will never be an elder in your house again.
The one I do not cut off from my altar will be left to consume your eyes and break your heart, and all the offspring of your house shall die by the sword.
And this shall be the sign for you: both your sons Hophni and Phinehas shall die on the same day.
And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest who will do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. I will build him a sure house, and he will walk before my anointed always.

And everyone who is left in your house shall come to implore him for a piece of silver or a loaf of bread, and shall say, ‘Please appoint me to one of the priestly offices, so that I may eat a morsel of bread.’”
The boy Samuel is ministering before YHWH under the guidance of Eli. The word of YHWH is rare in those days; visions do not break through often.
At that time Eli, whose eyesight has begun to grow dim so that he can barely see, is lying down in his own place.
The lamp of God has not yet gone out, and Samuel is lying down in the temple of YHWH, where the ark of God is.
Then YHWH calls to Samuel, and Samuel says, “Here I am!”
He runs to Eli and says, “Here I am, for you called me.” But Eli says, “I did not call. Go back and lie down.” So he goes and lies down.
YHWH calls again: “Samuel!” And Samuel rises and goes to Eli and says, “Here I am, for you called me.” But Eli says, “I did not call, my son. Go back and lie down.”
Now Samuel does not yet know YHWH, and the word of YHWH has not yet been revealed to him.
YHWH calls Samuel a third time. He rises and goes to Eli and says, “Here I am, for you called me.” Then Eli understands that YHWH is calling the boy.
Eli says to Samuel, “Go, lie down. If he calls you, you shall say: ‘Speak, YHWH — your servant is listening.’” So Samuel goes and lies down in his place.
YHWH comes and stands there and calls as at the other times: “Samuel! Samuel!” And Samuel says, “Speak — your servant is listening.”
Then YHWH says to Samuel, “Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears it ring.
On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end.
I have told him that I am about to judge his house forever, because of the sin he knew about — his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them.
Therefore I swear to the house of Eli: the iniquity of Eli’s house shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering.”
Samuel lies down until morning, then opens the doors of the house of YHWH. He is afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
But Eli calls Samuel and says, “Samuel, my son.” And Samuel says, “Here I am.”
Eli says, “What did he say to you? Do not hide it from me. May God do so to you, and more, if you conceal from me a single word of all that he told you.”
So Samuel tells him everything and holds nothing back. Eli says, “It is YHWH. Let him do what seems good to him.”
Samuel grows, and YHWH is with him, letting none of his words fall to the ground.
All Israel from Dan to Beersheba comes to know that Samuel has been established as a trustworthy prophet of YHWH.
YHWH continues to appear at Shiloh, revealing himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of YHWH.
The word of Samuel comes to all Israel. Now Israel goes out to meet the Philistines in battle and camps at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camp at Aphek.
The Philistines draw up their lines against Israel. The battle spreads, Israel is struck down before the Philistines, and they kill about four thousand men on the field.

When the troops come back to the camp, the elders of Israel say, “Why has YHWH defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of YHWH here from Shiloh, so that he may come among us and save us from the hand of our enemies.”

So the people send to Shiloh and bring from there the ark of the covenant of YHWH of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. The two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, are there with the ark of the covenant of God.
When the ark of the covenant of YHWH enters the camp, all Israel breaks into a great shout, so that the earth resounds.
When the Philistines hear the noise of the shout, they ask, “What is this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?” Then they learn that the ark of YHWH has come to the camp.
The Philistines are afraid, for they say, “God has come into the camp!” And they say, “Woe to us — nothing like this has ever happened before.
Woe to us! Who can deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every kind of plague in the wilderness.
Summon your courage and be men, O Philistines, lest you become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been to you. Be men and fight!”
So the Philistines fight, and Israel is defeated. Every man flees to his own home. The slaughter is very great — thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fall.
The ark of God is captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, die.
A man of Benjamin runs from the battle line and comes to Shiloh the same day, his clothes torn and dirt on his head.
When he arrives, Eli is sitting on his seat beside the road, watching, for his heart trembles for the ark of God. The man enters the city with his news, and the whole city cries out.
When Eli hears the sound of the outcry he says, “What is this uproar?” The man hurries and comes and tells Eli.
Now Eli is ninety-eight years old and his eyes are set so that he cannot see.
The man says to Eli, “I have come from the battle — I fled from the battle line today.” Eli says, “How did it go, my son?”

The messenger answers, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured.”
When he mentions the ark of God, Eli falls backward off his seat by the side of the gate. His neck breaks and he dies, for the man is old and heavy. He has judged Israel forty years.

Now Eli’s daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, is pregnant and close to the time of her delivery. When she hears the news that the ark of God has been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband are dead, she goes into labor and gives birth — for her birth pains come upon her suddenly.
As she is dying, the women tending her say, “Do not be afraid — you have borne a son!” But she gives no answer and pays no attention.
She names the child Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel!” — because the ark of God has been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
She says, “The glory has departed from Israel — for the ark of God has been taken.”
When the Philistines capture the ark of God, they bring it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
Then the Philistines take the ark of God and bring it into the house of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon.
When the people of Ashdod rise early the next day, Dagon has fallen face down on the ground before the ark of YHWH. They take Dagon and put him back in his place.

But when they rise early the following morning, Dagon has again fallen face down on the ground before the ark of YHWH — and this time the head of Dagon and both his hands are lying severed on the threshold. Only the stump of Dagon is left.
This is why the priests of Dagon and all who enter the house of Dagon do not step on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.
The hand of YHWH is heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he terrifies them and strikes them with tumors — Ashdod and all its territory.
When the men of Ashdod see what is happening, they say, “The ark of the God of Israel must not stay with us, for his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god.”

So they send and gather all the lords of the Philistines to them and say, “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” The men of Gath answer, “Let the ark of the God of Israel be moved to Gath.” So they move the ark of the God of Israel to Gath.
But after they bring it to Gath, the hand of YHWH is against that city as well, causing a very great panic. He strikes the men of the city, both young and old, so that tumors break out on them.
So they send the ark of God on to Ekron. But when the ark of God comes to Ekron, the people of Ekron cry out, “They have brought the ark of the God of Israel around to us to kill us and our people!”

They send and gather all the lords of the Philistines and say, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel — let it go back to its own place, so it does not kill us and our people.” For deadly panic fills the whole city; the hand of God is very heavy there.
Those who do not die are struck with tumors, and the cry of the city goes up to heaven.
The ark of YHWH has been in Philistine territory for seven months.
The Philistines summon the priests and the diviners and say, “What shall we do with the ark of YHWH? Tell us how to send it back to its place.”

They say, “If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty. You must by all means return a guilt offering to him. Then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand has not turned away from you.”

They ask, “What guilt offering shall we return to him?” The priests answer, “Five golden tumors and five golden mice, matching the number of the lords of the Philistines — for the same plague has been on all of you and on your lords.
Make figures of your tumors and figures of your mice that ravage the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand from upon you and your gods and your land.
Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? When he dealt harshly with them, did they not send Israel away and they departed?
Now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which no yoke has ever come. Hitch the cows to the cart but bring their calves home, away from them.
Take the ark of YHWH and place it on the cart. Put in a chest beside it the golden objects you are returning to him as a guilt offering. Then send it off and let it go its way.

Watch: if it goes up the road to its own territory, to Beth-shemesh, then it is YHWH who has done us this great harm. But if not, then we will know it was not his hand that struck us — it happened to us by chance.”
The men do this: they take two milk cows, hitch them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home.
They set the ark of YHWH on the cart, along with the chest containing the golden mice and the figures of their tumors.

The cows go straight along the road toward Beth-shemesh, keeping to the one highway, lowing as they go, turning neither to the right nor to the left. The lords of the Philistines follow them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.
Now the people of Beth-shemesh are reaping their wheat harvest in the valley. They look up and see the ark and rejoice at the sight.
The cart comes into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stops there beside a great stone. The men of Beth-shemesh split up the wood of the cart and offer the cows as a burnt offering to YHWH.

The Levites take down the ark of YHWH and the chest beside it, in which are the golden objects, and set them on the great stone. The men of Beth-shemesh offer burnt offerings and sacrifice sacrifices to YHWH that day.
When the five lords of the Philistines see this, they return to Ekron the same day.
These are the golden tumors that the Philistines return as a guilt offering to YHWH: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron.

The golden mice correspond to the number of all the Philistine cities belonging to the five lords, both fortified cities and open villages. The great stone on which they set down the ark of YHWH stands as a witness in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh to this day.

But YHWH strikes down some of the men of Beth-shemesh because they have looked into the ark of YHWH. He strikes down seventy of them, and the people mourn because YHWH has struck the people with a great blow.
Then the men of Beth-shemesh say, “Who is able to stand before YHWH, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up from here?”
So they send messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying, “The Philistines have returned the ark of YHWH. Come down and take it up to yourselves.”
The men of Kiriath-jearim come and take up the ark of YHWH and bring it into the house of Abinadab on the hill. They consecrate his son Eleazar to have charge of the ark of YHWH.
From the day the ark is lodged at Kiriath-jearim a long time passes — twenty years — and all the house of Israel laments and longs after YHWH.

Samuel says to all the house of Israel, “If you are returning to YHWH with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you. Direct your hearts to YHWH and serve him only, and he will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.”
So the Israelites put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth and serve YHWH only.
Then Samuel says, “Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to YHWH for you.”
They gather at Mizpah, draw water and pour it out before YHWH, and fast that day. “We have sinned against YHWH,” they say. And Samuel judges the people of Israel at Mizpah.
When the Philistines hear that Israel has gathered at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines march up against Israel. When the Israelites hear it, they are afraid of the Philistines.
The Israelites say to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to YHWH our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines.”
Samuel takes a nursing lamb and offers it as a whole burnt offering to YHWH. He cries out to YHWH for Israel, and YHWH answers him.

As Samuel is offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines draw near to attack Israel — but YHWH thunders with a great sound against the Philistines that day, throws them into confusion, and they are routed before Israel.
The men of Israel go out from Mizpah and pursue the Philistines, striking them down as far as below Beth-car.
Then Samuel takes a stone and sets it up between Mizpah and Shen. He calls it Ebenezer — Stone of Help — and says, “Till now YHWH has helped us.”
The Philistines are subdued and do not come again into the territory of Israel. The hand of YHWH is against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.

The cities the Philistines had taken from Israel are restored, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel delivers their surrounding territory from Philistine hands. There is also peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judges Israel all the days of his life.
Year after year he makes a circuit through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel at each of these places.
Then he returns to Ramah, for his house is there, and there too he judges Israel. And he builds an altar to YHWH there.
When Samuel is old, he makes his sons judges over Israel.
His firstborn son is named Joel and his second son Abijah. They judge in Beersheba.
Yet his sons do not walk in his ways. They turn aside after dishonest gain, take bribes, and pervert justice.
So all the elders of Israel gather together and come to Samuel at Ramah.
They say to him, “You are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us — like all the nations.”
The thing is evil in Samuel’s eyes when they say, “Give us a king to judge us.” Samuel prays to YHWH.
YHWH says to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you — they have rejected me from being king over them.
They are doing to you exactly as they have done to me from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day, forsaking me and serving other gods.
So listen to their voice. But you must solemnly warn them and show them what the king who will reign over them will do.”
Samuel speaks all the words of YHWH to the people who are asking him for a king.
He says, “This is what the king who reigns over you will do: he will take your sons and assign them to his chariots and his cavalry, and they will run before his chariots.
He will appoint them as commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and to plow his ground and reap his harvest, and to make his weapons and the equipment for his chariots.
He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks and bakers.
He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his officials.
He will take a tenth of your grain and your vineyards and give it to his officers and servants.
He will take your male and female servants and the best of your young men and your donkeys and put them to his work.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves.
On that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you chose for yourselves, but YHWH will not answer you in that day.”
But the people refuse to listen to Samuel’s voice. They say, “No! There must be a king over us,
so that we too may be like all the nations — our king will judge us and go out before us and fight our battles.”
When Samuel has heard all the people’s words, he speaks them in the ears of YHWH.
YHWH says to Samuel, “Listen to their voice and make them a king.” Samuel then says to the men of Israel, “Go, every man to his city.”
There is a man of Benjamin named Kish — son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah — a Benjaminite of standing.
He has a son named Saul, a young man more handsome than any other in Israel. From his shoulders upward he is taller than anyone among the people.
Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul’s father, have strayed. Kish says to his son Saul, “Take one of the young men with you and go — search for the donkeys.”
They pass through the hill country of Ephraim and through the land of Shalishah, but find nothing. They pass through the land of Shaalim — nothing. They pass through the land of Benjamin — nothing.
When they come to the land of Zuph, Saul says to his young man, “Come, let us go back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us.”
But the young man says, “Look — there is a man of God in this city. He is held in honor, and everything he says comes true. Perhaps he can tell us about the journey we are on.”
Saul says, “But if we go, what do we bring the man? The bread in our bags is gone, and we have no gift to bring the man of God. What do we have?”
The young man answers, “I have a quarter-shekel of silver here. I’ll give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way.”
(Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he would say: “Come, let us go to the seer” — for the one now called a prophet was formerly called a seer.)
Saul says to the young man, “Good. Let’s go.” So they head toward the city where the man of God is.
As they climb the hill to the city, they meet some young women coming out to draw water and ask them, “Is the seer here?”
They answer, “He is — just ahead of you. Hurry. He came to the city today because there is a sacrifice for the people at the high place.

As soon as you enter the city you will find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he arrives, for he must bless the sacrifice. Only then will the invited guests eat. Go up now — you’ll find him right away.”
So they go up to the city. As they are entering, Samuel is coming out toward them on his way up to the high place.
Now YHWH has revealed something to Samuel the day before Saul comes:

“Tomorrow at this hour I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin. Anoint him as prince over my people Israel. He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines — for I have seen my people’s suffering, and their cry has reached me.”
When Samuel sees Saul, YHWH says to him, “This is the man I told you about. He is the one who will govern my people.”
Saul approaches Samuel at the gate and says, “Where is the house of the seer?”
Samuel answers, “I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place — today you will eat with me, and in the morning I will send you on your way and tell you everything that is on your mind.

As for the donkeys that went missing three days ago — do not worry about them; they have been found. And for whom is everything desirable in Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father’s house?”
Saul answers, “Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of Israel’s tribes? And is not my clan the most insignificant of all the clans of Benjamin? Why do you speak to me like this?”
SAUL HonorED AT THE FEAST · 9:22–27
Samuel takes Saul and his young man and brings them into the hall, giving them a place at the head of the thirty or so invited guests.
Samuel says to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you — the one I told you to set aside.”

The cook lifts up the leg and sets it before Saul. Samuel says, “Here is what was kept for you. Set it before you and eat, for it has been reserved for you for this appointed hour.” So Saul eats with Samuel that day.
After they come down from the high place into the city, Samuel speaks with Saul on the roof.
They rise early, and at the break of dawn Samuel calls up to Saul on the roof: “Get up, so I can send you on your way.” Saul rises, and the two of them — Samuel and Saul — go out together.

As they are going down to the edge of the city, Samuel says to Saul, “Tell the young man to go on ahead.” He does so. Then Samuel says, “Stop here a moment, and I will make known to you the word of God.”

Samuel takes a flask of oil and pours it on Saul’s head. He kisses him and says, “Has not YHWH anointed you to be prince over his people Israel? You shall reign over the people of YHWH and save them from the hand of their enemies round about. And this shall be the sign that YHWH has anointed you prince over his inheritance.

“When you leave me today, you will meet two men by Rachel’s tomb in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah. They will say to you: ‘The donkeys you went to search for have been found. Your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and is anxious about you, asking, What shall I do about my son?’

From there go on to the oak of Tabor, where three men on their way up to God at Bethel will meet you — one carrying three young goats, one carrying three loaves of bread, and one carrying a skin of wine.
They will greet you and offer you two loaves of bread, which you shall take from their hand.

After that you will come to Gibeath-elohim, where there is a Philistine garrison. As you enter the town you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre before them, and they will be prophesying.
Then the Spirit of YHWH will rush upon you and you will prophesy with them, and you will be turned into a different man.
When these signs meet you, do whatever your hand finds to do — for God is with you.
Go down before me to Gilgal. I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”
When Saul turns to leave Samuel, God gives him a new heart. And all these signs come to pass that day.
When they reach Gibeah, a company of prophets meets him, the Spirit of God rushes upon him, and he prophesies among them.
When everyone who knew him before sees him prophesying with the prophets, the people say to one another, “What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
A man from that place answers, “And who is their father?” So it becomes a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
When he finishes prophesying, he goes to the high place.
Saul’s uncle says to him and his young man, “Where did you go?” He answers, “To look for the donkeys. When we couldn’t find them, we went to Samuel.”
His uncle says, “Tell me — what did Samuel say to you?”
Saul says to his uncle, “He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found.” But the matter of the kingship, which Samuel had spoken of, he tells him nothing.
Samuel summons the people to YHWH at Mizpah

and says to the Israelites, “Thus says YHWH, the God of Israel: I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.

But today you have rejected your God — the one who saves you from all your disasters and your distress — and you have said to him: ‘Set a king over us.’ Now then, present yourselves before YHWH by your tribes and by your thousands.”
Samuel brings all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin is taken by lot.
He brings the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites is taken by lot. Then Saul son of Kish is taken by lot. But when they search for him, he cannot be found.
They inquire of YHWH again: “Is there a man still to come?” YHWH says, “There he is — he has hidden himself among the baggage.”
They run and fetch him from there. When he stands among the people, he is taller than any of them from his shoulders upward.
Samuel says to all the people, “Do you see the one YHWH has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” And all the people shout, “Long live the king!”
Samuel then declares to the people the rights and duties of kingship. He writes them in a scroll and lays it up before YHWH. Then he sends all the people home, each to his own place.
Saul also goes home to Gibeah, and with him go men of valor whose hearts God has touched.
But some worthless men say, “How can this man save us?” They despise him and bring him no gift. But Saul holds his peace.
Nahash the Ammonite goes up and besieges Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh say to Nahash, “Make a treaty with us and we will be your subjects.”
Nahash the Ammonite says to them, “On this condition I will make a treaty with you: that I gouge out every man’s right eye, and so bring disgrace on all Israel.”
The elders of Jabesh say to him, “Give us seven days to send messengers throughout all Israel. If there is no one to save us, we will surrender to you.”
When the messengers come to Gibeah of Saul and speak these words in the hearing of the people, all the people weep aloud.
Now Saul is coming in from the field behind his oxen, and he says, “What is wrong with the people? Why are they weeping?” They tell him the news from Jabesh.
When he hears it, the Spirit of God rushes upon Saul and his anger blazes hot.

He takes a yoke of oxen, cuts them to pieces, and sends the pieces throughout all Israel by the hand of messengers, saying, “Whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel — this is what will be done to his oxen.” The terror of YHWH falls on the people, and they come out as one man.
He musters them at Bezek: three hundred thousand from Israel and thirty thousand from Judah.

They say to the messengers who came, “Tell the men of Jabesh-gilead: Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you will have deliverance.” When the messengers go and report this to the men of Jabesh, they are overjoyed.
So the men of Jabesh say to Nahash, “Tomorrow we will surrender to you, and you may do to us whatever you think right.”

The next morning Saul puts the people in three divisions. They break into the Ammonite camp in the morning watch and strike them down until the heat of the day. Those who survive are so scattered that no two of them are left together.
Then the people say to Samuel, “Who said ‘Shall Saul reign over us?’ Hand those men over and we will put them to death.”
But Saul says, “Not a man shall be put to death today — for today YHWH has worked deliverance in Israel.”
Samuel says to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingship.”
So all the people go to Gilgal and make Saul king there before YHWH. They sacrifice peace offerings before YHWH, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoice greatly.
