Samuel says to all Israel, “I have listened to your voice in everything you said to me and have set a king over you.
And now the king walks before you. I am old and gray, and my sons are here among you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day.

Here I am. Testify against me before YHWH and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated? Whom have I oppressed? From whose hand have I taken a bribe to look the other way? Tell me, and I will make it right.”
They say, “You have not cheated us or oppressed us or taken anything from any man’s hand.”
He says to them, “YHWH is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have found nothing in my hand.” And they say, “He is witness.”
Samuel says to the people, “YHWH is witness — the one who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your ancestors up out of Egypt.
Now stand still so that I may contend with you before YHWH concerning all the saving acts YHWH has done for you and your ancestors.
When Jacob entered Egypt, your ancestors cried out to YHWH, and YHWH sent Moses and Aaron, who brought them out of Egypt and settled them in this place.

But they forgot YHWH their God, and he gave them into the hand of Sisera, the commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab — and these oppressed them.
Then they cried out to YHWH and said: ‘We have sinned — we have forsaken YHWH and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. But now deliver us from the hand of our enemies and we will serve you.’
So YHWH sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you from the hand of your enemies on every side. You lived in safety.
But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was coming against you, you said to me: ‘No — a king shall reign over us,’ even though YHWH your God was your king.
Now here is the king you chose, the one you asked for. YHWH has set a king over you.
If you will fear YHWH and serve him and listen to his voice and not rebel against his commands — if both you and the king who reigns over you follow YHWH your God — all will be well.
But if you will not listen to the voice of YHWH and you rebel against his commands, the hand of YHWH will be against you as it was against your ancestors.
Now stand still and see this great thing YHWH is about to do before your eyes.
Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call on YHWH to send thunder and rain. Then you will know and see how great the evil is that you have done in YHWH’s sight in asking for a king.”
Samuel calls on YHWH, and YHWH sends thunder and rain that day. All the people stand in great fear of YHWH and of Samuel.
All the people say to Samuel, “Pray to YHWH your God for your servants, so that we do not die — for we have added this evil to all our other sins: we have asked for a king.”
Samuel says to the people, “Do not be afraid. You have done all this evil — but do not turn away from following YHWH. Serve him with all your heart.
Do not turn aside after empty things that cannot help or deliver, for they are empty.
YHWH will not abandon his people, for the sake of his great name — because it has pleased YHWH to make you his people.
As for me, far be it from me that I should sin against YHWH by ceasing to pray for you. I will go on instructing you in the good and right way.
Only fear YHWH and serve him faithfully with all your heart. Consider the great things he has done for you.
But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away.”
Saul is [---] years old when he becomes king, and he reigns over Israel two years. ⟨The number for his age at accession has not survived in the Hebrew text.⟩

He chooses three thousand men from Israel: two thousand remain with Saul at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand are with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the army he sends home, every man to his tent.
Jonathan strikes the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines get word of it. Saul has the trumpet sounded throughout the whole land, calling out, “Let the Hebrews hear!”
All Israel hears that Saul has struck the Philistine garrison and that Israel has become a stench to the Philistines. The people are summoned to join Saul at Gilgal.
The Philistines muster to fight Israel — thirty thousand chariots, six thousand cavalry, and foot soldiers as numerous as sand on the seashore. They come up and camp at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.
When the men of Israel see that they are in dire straits, the people hide in caves, in holes, among rocks, in tombs, and in cisterns.
Some Hebrews even cross the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. But Saul remains at Gilgal, and all the people who are still with him tremble.
He waits seven days — the time Samuel appointed. But Samuel does not come to Gilgal, and the people begin scattering from him.
Saul says, “Bring the burnt offering and the peace offerings to me.” And he offers the burnt offering himself.
As soon as he finishes, Samuel arrives. Saul goes out to meet him and greet him.
Samuel says, “What have you done?” Saul says, “When I saw the people scattering from me, and that you hadn’t come in the appointed days, and that the Philistines were mustering at Michmash,
I thought: now the Philistines will come down on me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of YHWH. So I forced myself and offered the burnt offering.”
Samuel says to Saul, “You have acted foolishly. You have not kept the commandment of YHWH your God. Had you kept it, YHWH would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.
But now your kingdom will not stand. YHWH has sought out a man after his own heart and appointed him prince over his people — because you have not kept what YHWH commanded you.”
Samuel rises and goes up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul musters the people remaining with him — about six hundred men.
Saul and his son Jonathan and the people with them are staying at Geba of Benjamin while the Philistines camp at Michmash.
Raiders go out from the Philistine camp in three columns: one column turns toward Ophrah in the land of Shual,
another turns toward Beth-horon, and a third turns toward the borderland overlooking the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.
There is not a single blacksmith in all the land of Israel — for the Philistines have said, “Lest the Hebrews make swords or spears.”
So all the Israelites have to go down to the Philistines to sharpen a plowshare, a mattock, an axe, or a sickle.
The charge is two-thirds of a shekel for plowshares and mattocks, and a third of a shekel for sharpening axes and setting goads.
So on the day of battle, not a sword or a spear is to be found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan — only Saul and Jonathan have them.
And the Philistine garrison goes out to the pass of Michmash.
One day Jonathan son of Saul says to the young man carrying his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the Philistine garrison on the other side.” But he does not tell his father.
Saul is staying at the edge of Gibeah under the pomegranate tree at Migron, with about six hundred men around him.
Among them is Ahijah son of Ahitub, brother of Ichabod, son of Phinehas son of Eli, the priest of YHWH at Shiloh, wearing the ephod. The people do not know that Jonathan has gone.
On each side of the rocky pass that Jonathan means to cross to reach the Philistine garrison, there is a sheer crag. One is called Bozez, the other Seneh.
The one crag rises on the north, facing Michmash; the other is on the south, facing Geba.
Jonathan says to his armor-bearer, “Come, let us cross over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. Perhaps YHWH will act for us — for nothing holds YHWH back from saving, whether by many or by few.”
His armor-bearer says, “Do all that is in your heart. Go — I am with you, heart and soul.”
Jonathan says, “Then this is what we will do: we will cross over to the men and let them see us.
If they say, ‘Stay back until we reach you,’ we will stand still and not go up to them.
But if they say, ‘Come up to us,’ we will climb up — for that will be the sign that YHWH has given them into our hand.”
So the two of them reveal themselves to the Philistine garrison. The Philistines say, “Look — Hebrews crawling out of the holes they’ve been hiding in!”

The men of the garrison call out to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come up to us and we’ll show you something!” Jonathan says to his armor-bearer, “Climb up after me — YHWH has given them into Israel’s hand.”
Jonathan scrambles up on hands and feet, with his armor-bearer right behind him. The Philistines fall before Jonathan and his armor-bearer cuts them down as he follows.
In that first strike, Jonathan and his armor-bearer kill about twenty men within an area of roughly half an acre.
Terror breaks out in the camp, in the open field, among all the people. The garrison and the raiding parties tremble, the ground shakes, and the panic becomes overwhelming.
Saul’s lookouts at Gibeah of Benjamin see the Philistine army melting away in all directions.
Saul says to the people with him, “Muster and see who is missing.” When they check, Jonathan and his armor-bearer are not there.
Saul says to Ahijah, “Bring the ark of God.” For the ark of God was with Israel at that time.
But while Saul is still speaking to the priest, the uproar in the Philistine camp keeps growing. Saul says to the priest, “Withdraw your hand — leave it.”
Saul and all his men rally and rush into the battle, and every man’s sword is turned against his fellow Philistine — an immense confusion.
The Hebrews who had previously gone over to the Philistines and been serving in their camp — even they turn and join the Israelites with Saul and Jonathan.
Likewise, when all the men of Israel who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim hear that the Philistines are fleeing, they too pour out of hiding and press hard after them in the battle.
So YHWH delivers Israel that day. The battle carries on past Beth-aven.

The men of Israel are in a desperate state that day, for Saul has bound the people under an oath: “Cursed be the man who eats any food before evening — before I have avenged myself on my enemies.” So no one touches food.
The whole army comes to a forest where honey is lying on the ground.
When the people enter the forest, the honey is dripping — but no one raises a hand to his mouth, for the people dread the oath.
But Jonathan has not heard his father put the people under this oath. He reaches out the tip of his staff, dips it in the honeycomb, raises his hand to his mouth, and his eyes light up.
One of the soldiers says, “Your father put the army under a strict oath — ‘Cursed be the man who eats food today.’ That is why the men are faint.”
Jonathan says, “My father has brought trouble on the land. Look how my eyes have come alive from tasting just a little of this honey.
How much better if the men had eaten freely today from the spoil of their enemies! Would the defeat of the Philistines not have been far greater?”
They strike the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. The army is utterly exhausted.
They fall on the plunder and seize sheep, cattle, and calves, slaughtering them on the bare ground. The people eat the meat with the blood still in it.
Someone tells Saul, “The people are sinning against YHWH by eating meat with the blood.” He says, “You have acted treacherously. Roll a large stone here to me at once.”

Saul says, “Go out among the people and tell every man to bring his ox or his sheep to me here and slaughter it properly. Do not sin against YHWH by eating with the blood.” So every soldier brings his animal that night and slaughters it there.
Saul builds an altar to YHWH there — the first altar he has ever built to YHWH.

Saul says, “Let us go down after the Philistines tonight and plunder them till dawn — leave not a man of them alive.” They say, “Do whatever seems good to you.” But the priest says, “Let us draw near to God first.”
So Saul inquires of God: “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into Israel’s hand?” But YHWH does not answer him that day.
Saul says, “Come near, all you leaders of the people — find out what sin has been committed today.
As YHWH lives who saves Israel, even if it is in my son Jonathan, he shall surely die.” But not a man among all the people answers him.
He says to all Israel, “You stand on one side, and Jonathan my son and I will stand on the other.” The people say, “Do what seems good to you.”

Saul says to YHWH, the God of Israel, “Why have you not answered your servant today? O YHWH, God of Israel, if this guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, give Urim. But if it is in your people Israel, give Thummim.” Jonathan and Saul are indicated, and the people are cleared.
Saul says, “Cast the lot between me and Jonathan my son.” Jonathan is indicated.
Saul says to Jonathan, “Tell me what you have done.” Jonathan tells him, “I only tasted a little honey with the tip of my staff. And now I am to die.”
Saul says, “May God do the same to me and more — Jonathan, you will surely die.”

But the people say to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die — Jonathan, who has won this great victory for Israel? Never! As YHWH lives, not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground — for he worked this day with God.” So the people ransom Jonathan, and he does not die.
Then Saul withdraws from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines return to their own territory.
After Saul takes the kingship over Israel, he fights against all his enemies on every side — Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turns he inflicts defeat.
He acts with great valor, striking down the Amalekites and rescuing Israel from those who plundered them.
Saul’s sons are Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. His two daughters: the elder is named Merab and the younger Michal.
Saul’s wife is Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of his army is Abner son of Ner, who is Saul’s uncle.
Kish is the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner is the son of Abiel.
There is bitter fighting against the Philistines all of Saul’s days. Whenever Saul sees a strong and courageous man, he takes him into his service.
Samuel says to Saul, “YHWH sent me to anoint you king over his people Israel. Now listen to the voice of YHWH.
Thus says YHWH of hosts: I have reckoned what Amalek did to Israel — how they opposed them on the road when they came up out of Egypt.
Now go, strike Amalek and put everything under the ban — do not spare them. Kill man and woman, infant and nursing child, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.”
Saul summons the army and musters them at Telaim: two hundred thousand foot soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah.
Saul approaches the city of Amalek and sets an ambush in the valley.

He says to the Kenites, “Go — leave the Amalekites, come down from among them, or I will destroy you with them. For you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt.” So the Kenites withdraw from among the Amalekites.
Saul defeats the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which is east of Egypt.
He takes Agag king of the Amalekites alive and puts the rest of the people under the ban with the edge of the sword.

But Saul and the army spare Agag, and the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and the lambs — everything that is good. They are unwilling to destroy these. Only what is worthless and inferior they put under the ban.
The word of YHWH comes to Samuel:
“I regret that I made Saul king, for he has turned back from following me and has not carried out my words.” Samuel is furious, and he cries out to YHWH all night.
Samuel rises early to meet Saul in the morning. He is told, “Saul went to Carmel, where he set up a monument to himself, then turned and went down to Gilgal.”
When Samuel reaches Saul, Saul says, “Blessed are you by YHWH! I have carried out the command of YHWH.”
Samuel says, “Then what is this bleating of sheep I hear, and this lowing of cattle?”
Saul says, “They were brought from the Amalekites. The army spared the best sheep and cattle in order to sacrifice to YHWH your God. The rest we have put under the ban.”
Samuel says to Saul, “Stop. Let me tell you what YHWH said to me last night.” “Speak,” he says.
Samuel says, “When you were small in your own eyes, were you not head of the tribes of Israel? YHWH anointed you king over Israel.
And YHWH sent you on a mission and said: ‘Go, put the sinners, the Amalekites, under the ban — make war on them until you have wiped them out.’
Why did you not obey the voice of YHWH? Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in YHWH’s eyes?”
Saul says to Samuel, “But I have obeyed the voice of YHWH — I went on the mission YHWH sent me on. I brought back Agag king of Amalek and put the Amalekites under the ban.
It was the army that took from the spoil — the best of what was put under the ban, sheep and cattle — to sacrifice to YHWH your God at Gilgal.”
Samuel says:
Does YHWH delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices
as much as in obeying the voice of YHWH?
Behold — to obey is better than sacrifice,
to listen than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is as the sin of divination,
and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry.
Because you have rejected the word of YHWH,
he has rejected you from being king.
Saul says to Samuel, “I have sinned — I transgressed the command of YHWH and your words. I feared the people and listened to their voice.
Now please forgive my sin and return with me, so that I may bow before YHWH.”
Samuel says to Saul, “I will not return with you. You rejected the word of YHWH, and YHWH has rejected you from being king over Israel.”
As Samuel turns to leave, Saul grabs the hem of his robe — and it tears.
Samuel says to him, “YHWH has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and given it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you.
And the Glory of Israel does not lie and does not relent — for he is not a mortal, that he should relent.”
Saul says, “I have sinned. But please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel — come back with me so that I may worship YHWH your God.”
So Samuel turns back after Saul, and Saul worships YHWH.
Samuel says, “Bring Agag king of the Amalekites to me.” Agag comes to him cheerfully, saying, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.”
Samuel says, “As your sword made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women.” And Samuel cuts Agag down before YHWH at Gilgal.
Then Samuel goes to Ramah, and Saul goes up to his house at Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel does not see Saul again until the day of his death — though Samuel grieves for Saul. And YHWH regrets that he made Saul king over Israel.

YHWH says to Samuel, “How long will you grieve for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have chosen a king for myself among his sons.”
Samuel says, “How can I go? If Saul hears, he will kill me.” YHWH says, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to YHWH.’
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what to do. You shall anoint for me the one I point out to you.”
Samuel does what YHWH says and comes to Bethlehem. The elders of the town come out to meet him, trembling, and ask, “Do you come in peace?”
“In peace,” he says. “I have come to sacrifice to YHWH. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” He consecrates Jesse and his sons and invites them.
When they arrive, Samuel sees Eliab and thinks, “Surely YHWH’s anointed is standing before him.”

But YHWH says to Samuel, “Do not look on his appearance or the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For YHWH does not see as man sees — man looks on the outward appearance, but YHWH looks on the heart.”
Then Jesse calls Abinadab and makes him pass before Samuel. Samuel says, “Neither has YHWH chosen this one.”
Then Jesse makes Shammah pass by, and Samuel says, “Neither has YHWH chosen this one.”
Jesse makes seven of his sons pass before Samuel, and Samuel says to Jesse, “YHWH has not chosen any of these.”
Samuel says to Jesse, “Are all your sons here?” Jesse says, “There is still the youngest — he is out keeping the sheep.” Samuel says, “Send for him. We will not sit down until he comes.”
Jesse sends and brings him in. He is ruddy, with bright eyes and a handsome face. YHWH says, “Rise and anoint him — this is the one.”
Samuel takes the horn of oil and anoints David in the midst of his brothers. And the Spirit of YHWH rushes upon David from that day forward. Then Samuel rises and goes to Ramah.
Now the Spirit of YHWH has departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from YHWH torments him.
Saul’s servants say to him, “A harmful spirit from God is tormenting you, my lord.
Command your servants to search for a man skilled at playing the lyre. When the harmful spirit from God comes upon you, he will play, and you will be well.”
Saul says to his servants, “Find me a man who plays well and bring him to me.”
One of the young men speaks up: “I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite — skillful in playing, a man of valor, a warrior, shrewd in speech, a handsome man. And YHWH is with him.”
So Saul sends messengers to Jesse: “Send me your son David, the one who keeps the sheep.”
Jesse loads a donkey with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sends them with his son David to Saul.
David comes to Saul and enters his service. Saul loves him deeply and David becomes his armor-bearer.
Saul sends word to Jesse: “Let David remain in my service — he has found favor in my eyes.”
Whenever the harmful spirit from God comes upon Saul, David takes the lyre and plays. Saul is refreshed and feels better, and the harmful spirit leaves him.
The Philistines gather their armies for battle. They muster at Socoh in Judah and camp between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel also gather and camp in the Valley of Elah, drawing up in battle line against the Philistines.
The Philistines stand on the mountain on one side and Israel on the mountain on the other side, with the valley between them.
A champion comes out from the Philistine camp — his name is Goliath of Gath. His height is six cubits and a span.
He has a bronze helmet on his head and wears a coat of scale armor weighing five thousand shekels of bronze.
He has bronze greaves on his legs and a bronze javelin slung between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear is like a weaver’s beam, and the head of his spear weighs six hundred shekels of iron. His shield-bearer walks before him.

He stands and shouts to the ranks of Israel: “Why have you come out and drawn up for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves and let him come down to me.
If he can fight me and kill me, we will be your servants. But if I overcome him and kill him, you will be our servants and serve us.”
The Philistine says, “I defy the ranks of Israel this day! Give me a man — let us fight each other.”
When Saul and all Israel hear these words, they are shattered with fear.
Now David is the son of an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah named Jesse, who has eight sons. In the days of Saul, Jesse is old and well advanced in years.
His three eldest sons have followed Saul to the war: Eliab the firstborn, then Abinadab, then Shammah.
David is the youngest. While the three eldest are with Saul,
David goes back and forth from Saul to feed his father’s sheep at Bethlehem.
For forty days the Philistine steps forward, morning and evening, and takes his stand.
One day Jesse says to his son David, “Take this ephah of roasted grain and these ten loaves for your brothers — hurry to the camp.
Take these ten cheeses to the commander of their unit. See how your brothers are and bring back some token from them.”
Saul, the brothers, and all the men of Israel are in the Valley of Elah, fighting the Philistines.

David rises early, leaves the sheep with a shepherd, loads up the provisions, and sets out as Jesse has commanded. He arrives at the camp just as the army is going out to the battle line with a war cry.
Israel and the Philistines are drawing up their battle lines, army against army.
David hands over the provisions to the keeper of the stores, runs to the front, and greets his brothers.
While he is talking with them, Goliath the Philistine champion from Gath steps out from the Philistine lines and shouts his challenge again. David hears him.
When all the men of Israel see the man, they turn and flee from him in terror.

The Israelites say, “Did you see that man who came up? He has come to defy Israel. The king will lavish riches on the man who kills him, give him his daughter, and exempt his father’s house from taxes in Israel.”

David says to the men standing near him, “What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel? Who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?”
The soldiers tell him the same as before: such-and-such will be done for the man who kills him.

When Eliab his eldest brother hears David speaking to the men, he flares with anger and says, “Why have you come down here? Who is looking after those few sheep back in the wilderness? I know you — your arrogance and the evil of your heart. You came down here just to see the battle.”
David says, “What have I done now? It was only a question.”
He turns away and asks someone else, and the people give him the same answer.
What David says is overheard and reported to Saul, who sends for him.
David says to Saul, “Let no man’s heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight this Philistine.”
Saul says to David, “You cannot go against this Philistine and fight him — you are only a boy, and he has been a warrior since his youth.”
David says to Saul, “Your servant used to keep his father’s sheep. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock,
I went after it, struck it, and took the lamb from its mouth. When it rose against me, I seized it by the jaw and struck it down and killed it.
Your servant has killed both lions and bears — this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God.”
David says, “YHWH who delivered me from the paw of the lion and the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine.” Saul says to David, “Go — and may YHWH be with you.”
Saul dresses David in his own armor — a bronze helmet on his head and a coat of mail.
David straps on the sword over the armor and tries to walk. He cannot — he has never worn these things. David says to Saul, “I cannot move in these — I’m not used to them.” And he takes them off.
He takes his staff in his hand, chooses five smooth stones from the wadi, and puts them in his shepherd’s pouch. With his sling in hand, he walks toward the Philistine.
The Philistine comes on, moving closer to David, his shield-bearer going ahead of him.
When the Philistine looks and sees David, he despises him — for he is only a boy, ruddy and handsome.
The Philistine says to David, “Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?” And he curses David by his gods.
“Come here,” the Philistine says, “and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and the beasts of the field.”
David says to the Philistine, “You come to me with sword and spear and javelin — but I come to you in the name of YHWH of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

This day YHWH will give you into my hand. I will strike you down and cut off your head. I will give the bodies of the Philistine army to the birds and the wild animals this day — so that all the earth will know there is a God in Israel,
and so that all this assembly will know that YHWH does not save by sword or spear. The battle belongs to YHWH, and he will give you into our hands.”
When the Philistine rises and moves to meet him, David runs quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.
David reaches into his pouch, takes out a stone, slings it, and strikes the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sinks into his forehead and he falls face down on the ground.
So David prevails over the Philistine with a sling and a stone. He strikes the Philistine and kills him — without a sword in his hand.
David runs and stands over him, draws the Philistine’s own sword from its sheath, and kills him with it, cutting off his head. When the Philistines see that their champion is dead, they turn and run.

Then the men of Israel and Judah surge forward with a shout and pursue the Philistines as far as Gath and to the gates of Ekron. The Philistine dead fall all along the road from Shaaraim to Gath and Ekron.
The Israelites return from the pursuit and plunder the Philistine camp.
David takes the head of the Philistine and brings it to Jerusalem, and puts Goliath’s armor in his own tent.
When Saul had watched David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, commander of the army, “Abner, whose son is that young man?” Abner says, “As your soul lives, O king, I do not know.”
The king says, “Find out whose son he is.”
When David returns from killing the Philistine, Abner brings him before Saul — the head of the Philistine still in his hand.
Saul says to him, “Whose son are you, young man?” David answers, “I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem.”
When David finishes speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan is bound to the soul of David — and Jonathan loves him as his own soul.
Saul takes David from that day and will not let him return to his father’s house.
Jonathan makes a covenant with David, because he loves him as his own soul.
Jonathan strips off the robe he is wearing and gives it to David, along with his armor, his sword, his bow, and his belt.
David goes out on every campaign Saul sends him on and succeeds so well that Saul puts him in command of the fighting men. This is pleasing to all the people and to Saul’s servants as well.

When the army returns from striking down the Philistines, women come out from all the towns of Israel to meet King Saul — singing and dancing, with tambourines, shouts of joy, and musical instruments.
The women sing back and forth as they celebrate:
“Saul has struck down his thousands,
and David his ten thousands.”
Saul is furious. The song is evil in his eyes. He says, “They have credited David with ten thousands but me with only thousands. What is left for him but the kingdom itself?”
From that day on, Saul eyes David.
The next day a harmful spirit from God rushes upon Saul, and he raves in his house while David is playing the lyre as he does daily. Saul’s spear is in his hand.
Saul hurls the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David slips away from him — twice.
Saul is afraid of David, because YHWH is with David but has departed from Saul.
So Saul removes him from his presence and makes him commander of a thousand. David goes out and comes in at the head of the troops.
In everything David undertakes he succeeds, for YHWH is with him.
When Saul sees how consistently he succeeds, he stands in dread of him.
But all Israel and Judah love David, for he goes out and comes in before them.

Saul says to David, “Here is my elder daughter Merab — I will give her to you as a wife. Only serve me with valor and fight YHWH’s battles.” For Saul thinks, “Let the Philistines’ hand be against him — not mine.”
David says to Saul, “Who am I, and what is my family — my father’s clan in Israel — that I should become the king’s son-in-law?”
But when the time comes for Merab, Saul’s daughter, to be given to David, she is given instead to Adriel the Meholathite as a wife.
Now Michal, Saul’s other daughter, loves David. When Saul is told about it, he is pleased.
Saul thinks, “I will give her to him — she will become a snare for him, and the Philistines’ hand will be against him.” So Saul says to David a second time, “Today you shall be my son-in-law.”
Saul instructs his servants, “Speak to David privately and say: ‘The king delights in you, and all his servants love you. Now is the time to become the king’s son-in-law.’”
Saul’s servants repeat this to David. He says, “Do you think it a small thing to become the king’s son-in-law? I am a poor man of no importance.”
His servants report back to Saul: “This is what David said.”
Saul says, “Say this to David: ‘The king wants no bride-price except a hundred Philistine foreskins — to take revenge on the king’s enemies.’” Saul intends to have David fall by Philistine hands.
When the servants tell David, the terms seem good to him. Before the time runs out,
David sets out with his men and kills two hundred Philistines. He brings back their foreskins in full count, and Saul gives him his daughter Michal as his wife.
Then Saul sees and knows that YHWH is with David and that Michal his daughter loves David.
Saul is even more afraid of David — and Saul is David’s enemy from that day forward.
The Philistine commanders keep attacking, and every time they do, David wins more success than all of Saul’s other officers. His name becomes very famous.
Saul speaks to his son Jonathan and to all his servants about killing David. But Jonathan delights greatly in David.
Jonathan tells David, “My father Saul is looking for a way to kill you. Be on your guard tomorrow morning. Find a secret place and hide.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will speak to him about you. Whatever I find out I will tell you.”
Jonathan speaks well of David to Saul his father and says to him, “Let the king not sin against his servant David — he has done nothing against you, and his deeds have been nothing but good for you.

He put his life in his hands when he struck down the Philistine, and YHWH won a great victory for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Why would you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause?”
Saul listens to Jonathan’s voice and swears, “As YHWH lives, he will not be put to death.”
Jonathan calls David and reports everything to him. He brings David back to Saul, and David is in his presence as before.
War breaks out again. David goes out and fights the Philistines and strikes them with a great blow, so that they flee before him.
But a harmful spirit from YHWH comes upon Saul again as he sits in his house, spear in hand, while David is playing the lyre.
Saul tries to pin David to the wall with the spear, but David slips away and the spear drives into the wall. David flees and escapes that night.
Saul sends men to watch David’s house and kill him in the morning. But Michal his wife tells him, “If you don’t get away tonight, tomorrow you are a dead man.”
So Michal lets David down through the window, and he flees and escapes.
Michal takes a household idol, lays it in the bed, puts a mat of goat’s hair at its head, and covers it with a garment.
When Saul sends messengers to seize David, she says, “He is sick.”
Saul sends the messengers back again: “Bring him to me in the bed so I can kill him.”
But when the messengers enter the room, they find the idol in the bed with the mat of goat’s hair at its head.
Saul says to Michal, “Why did you deceive me like this and let my enemy go?” Michal answers, “He told me, ‘Let me go or I will kill you.’”
David flees and escapes, comes to Samuel at Ramah, and tells him everything Saul has done to him. Then David and Samuel go and stay at Naioth.
Word reaches Saul: “David is at Naioth in Ramah.”

Saul sends messengers to seize David. But when they see a group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing over them as their head, the Spirit of God comes upon Saul’s messengers and they too begin to prophesy.
Saul is told, and he sends another group of messengers. They also prophesy. He sends a third group — and they also prophesy.
Then Saul goes to Ramah himself. He comes to the great cistern at Secu and asks, “Where are Samuel and David?” They say, “At Naioth in Ramah.”
He goes there — and the Spirit of God comes upon him too. He walks along prophesying until he arrives at Naioth in Ramah.
He strips off his robes and prophesies before Samuel, and lies down naked all that day and all that night. That is why people say, “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
David flees from Naioth in Ramah and comes to Jonathan. “What have I done?” he says. “What is my offense? What sin have I committed against your father, that he is trying to kill me?”
Jonathan says, “That is unthinkable — you will not die. My father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. Why would he hide this from me? It cannot be.”

But David swears again: “Your father knows very well that I have found favor with you, and he says to himself, ‘Jonathan must not know this, or he will be grieved.’ But as YHWH lives, and as you yourself live, there is barely a step between me and death.”
Jonathan says to David, “Whatever you say, I will do for you.”
David says, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and I am expected to sit at the king’s table. Let me go and hide in the field until the evening of the third day.
If your father notices I am missing, say: ‘David asked me urgently for leave to run to Bethlehem — there is a yearly family sacrifice there for his whole clan.’
If he says, ‘Good,’ then your servant is safe. But if he flares with anger, you will know the harm is decided.
Deal with your servant in loyal love — you brought your servant into a covenant before YHWH with you. And if there is any guilt in me, kill me yourself rather than bring me before your father.”
Jonathan says, “Never! If I knew my father had decided to harm you, would I not tell you?”
David says, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?”
Jonathan says, “Come, let us go out to the field.” And they go out into the field together.
Jonathan says to David, “YHWH, God of Israel, be witness! I will sound out my father by this time tomorrow or the day after. If he is well disposed toward you, I will send word and let you know.
But if my father means to harm you, may YHWH do so to me and more if I do not warn you and send you away safely. May YHWH be with you as he was with my father.
And while I still live — show me the loyal love of YHWH, so that I do not die.
And never cut off your loyal love from my house — not even when YHWH has cut off every one of David’s enemies from the face of the earth.”
So Jonathan makes a covenant with the house of David, and YHWH holds David’s enemies to account.
Jonathan makes David swear again by his love for him — for he loves him as he loves his own soul.
Jonathan says to him, “Tomorrow is the new moon. You will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
On the third day go quickly to the place where you hid when this whole matter began, and stay near the stone there.
I will shoot three arrows to one side of it, as if aiming at a target.
Then I will send the boy: ‘Go find the arrows.’ If I call out, ‘The arrows are on this side of you — get them,’ then come, for all is well and there is no danger — as YHWH lives.
But if I say to the boy, ‘The arrows are beyond you,’ then go — for YHWH has sent you away.
As for the word we have spoken — YHWH stands between you and me, forever.”
So David hides in the field. At the new moon the king sits down to eat.
The king takes his usual seat by the wall. Jonathan sits opposite, and Abner beside Saul. David’s place is empty.
Saul says nothing that day, thinking, “Something has happened to him — he must be unclean, certainly unclean.”
But on the second day, the day after the new moon, David’s place is empty again. Saul says to Jonathan his son, “Why hasn’t the son of Jesse come to the meal — either yesterday or today?”
Jonathan answers Saul, “David asked me urgently for leave to go to Bethlehem.

He said: ‘Please let me go — our clan has a sacrifice in the city and my brother summoned me. If I have found favor in your eyes, let me slip away to see my brothers.’ That is why he has not come to the king’s table.”
Saul’s anger blazes against Jonathan. He says, “You son of a perverse and rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame and the shame of your mother?
For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be secure. Now send for him and bring him to me — for he is as good as dead.”
Jonathan answers his father Saul, “Why should he die? What has he done?”
Saul hurls his spear at Jonathan to strike him. So Jonathan knows for certain that his father has decided to kill David.
Jonathan rises from the table in blazing anger and eats nothing on the second day of the month. He is grieved for David because his father has disgraced him.
In the morning Jonathan goes out to the field for the appointed meeting with David, and a young boy goes with him.
He says to the boy, “Run and find the arrows I shoot.” The boy runs, and Jonathan shoots an arrow beyond him.
When the boy reaches the spot where the arrow has fallen, Jonathan calls out after him, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?”
He calls out again, “Quickly — hurry up, don’t stop!” The boy gathers the arrows and comes back to his master.
The boy understands nothing. Only Jonathan and David know the meaning.
Jonathan hands his weapons to the boy and says, “Go, take these back to the city.”
When the boy has gone, David rises from beside the stone, falls with his face to the ground, and bows three times. Then they kiss each other and weep together — David weeping the most.

Jonathan says to David, “Go in peace. We have sworn to each other in the name of YHWH — YHWH shall be between me and you, and between my children and your children, forever.” Then David rises and leaves, and Jonathan goes back into the city.
David comes to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech comes out to meet him trembling and asks, “Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?”
David says to Ahimelech the priest, “The king sent me on a mission and told me: ‘Let no one know anything about the errand I am sending you on.’ I have arranged to meet my men at a certain place.
Now what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread — or whatever you can find.”
The priest answers David, “I have no ordinary bread. There is only holy bread — provided the young men have kept themselves from women.”
David says to the priest, “Women have certainly been kept from us, as always on campaigns. Even on an ordinary march the men’s gear is holy — how much more so today.”
So the priest gives him the holy bread, for the only bread there was the Bread of the Presence — just removed from before YHWH to be replaced with fresh loaves on the day it is taken away.
Now one of Saul’s servants is there that day, detained before YHWH — a man named Doeg the Edomite, chief of Saul’s herdsmen.
David says to Ahimelech, “Do you have a spear or sword here? I didn’t bring my own weapons with me — the king’s business was urgent.”

The priest says, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine — the one you struck down in the Valley of Elah — is here, wrapped in cloth behind the ephod. If you want it, take it. There is nothing else here.” David says, “There is none like it. Give it to me.”
That same day David rises and flees from Saul. He comes to Achish king of Gath.
But the servants of Achish say to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land? Is this not the one they sing about in their dances:
‘Saul has struck down his thousands,
and David his ten thousands?’”
David takes these words to heart and is very much afraid of Achish king of Gath.
So he disguises his sanity before them — acting deranged in their hands, scratching marks on the doors of the gate and letting his saliva run down his beard.
Achish says to his servants, “Look at the man — he is clearly mad. Why have you brought him to me?
Do I have a shortage of madmen, that you bring this one to rave in my presence? Is this fellow to enter my house?”
David leaves there and escapes to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and all his father’s household hear of it, they come down to him there.
And everyone in distress, everyone in debt, everyone bitter in soul — they all rally to him, and he becomes their captain. There are about four hundred men with him.
From there David goes to Mizpeh of Moab and says to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother stay with you until I know what God will do for me.”
So he leaves them with the king of Moab, and they stay with him all the time David is in the stronghold.
Then the prophet Gad says to David, “Do not stay in the stronghold — go, and head into the land of Judah.” So David goes and enters the forest of Hereth.
Saul hears that David has been found and that men are with him. He is sitting at Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the height, spear in hand, with all his servants standing around him.
Saul says to his servants, “Listen, men of Benjamin. Will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards? Will he make you all commanders of thousands and hundreds?

Is that why all of you have conspired against me? Not one of you tells me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. Not one of you shows me any concern, or tells me that my own son has stirred up my servant to lie in wait against me, as he is doing today.”
Then Doeg the Edomite, who is standing with Saul’s servants, speaks up: “I saw the son of Jesse come to Nob, to Ahimelech son of Ahitub.
Ahimelech inquired of YHWH for him, gave him provisions, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.”
The king sends for Ahimelech the priest, son of Ahitub, and all his father’s house — the priests who are at Nob. They all come before the king.
Saul says, “Listen, son of Ahitub.” He answers, “Here I am, my lord.”

Saul says, “Why have you conspired against me — you and the son of Jesse — by giving him bread and a sword and inquiring of God for him, so that he rises against me to ambush me, as he is doing today?”
Ahimelech answers the king, “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David — the king’s son-in-law, captain of your bodyguard, honored in your own house?
Was today the first time I inquired of God for him? Never! Let the king charge neither his servant nor anyone in my father’s house with anything — your servant knew nothing at all about any of this.”
The king says, “You will surely die, Ahimelech — you and your whole father’s house.”

The king says to the guards standing around him, “Turn and kill the priests of YHWH — for they are hand in hand with David. They knew he was fleeing and said nothing to me.” But the king’s servants will not raise their hands to strike the priests of YHWH.
The king says to Doeg, “You — turn and strike the priests.” Doeg the Edomite turns and strikes. That day he kills eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod.
Nob, the city of the priests, he puts to the sword — men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep. Everything.
But one of Ahimelech’s sons — Abiathar — escapes and flees after David.
Abiathar tells David that Saul has killed the priests of YHWH.
David says to Abiathar, “I knew that day when Doeg the Edomite was there that he would certainly tell Saul. I am responsible for the deaths of every person in your father’s house.
Stay with me. Do not be afraid — the man who seeks your life seeks mine. You will be safe with me.”
David is told that the Philistines are attacking Keilah and plundering the threshing floors.
He inquires of YHWH: “Shall I go and attack these Philistines?” YHWH says to David, “Go. Attack them and save Keilah.”
But David’s men say, “We are already afraid here in Judah — how much more if we go to Keilah against the Philistine armies?”
David inquires of YHWH a second time. YHWH answers, “Go down to Keilah — I will give the Philistines into your hand.”
So David and his men go to Keilah, fight the Philistines, drive off their livestock, and strike them with a great blow. David saves the people of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech fled to David at Keilah, he brought the ephod with him.
Saul hears that David has come to Keilah and says, “God has handed him over to me — he has shut himself in by entering a walled city with gates and bars.”
Saul summons all the troops to march on Keilah and besiege David and his men.
David learns that Saul is plotting harm against him and says to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod here.”
David says, “O YHWH, God of Israel — your servant has heard that Saul is coming to Keilah to destroy the city because of me.
Will the men of Keilah hand me over to him? Will Saul come down as I have heard? O YHWH, God of Israel, please tell your servant.” YHWH says, “He will come down.”
David says, “Will the men of Keilah hand me and my men over to Saul?” YHWH says, “They will hand you over.”
So David and his men — about six hundred of them — leave Keilah at once and go wherever they can. When Saul is told that David has escaped from Keilah, he abandons the campaign.
David stays in the wilderness strongholds, in the hill country of Ziph. Saul searches for him every day, but God does not give David into his hands.
David is at Horesh in the wilderness of Ziph, and he can see that Saul has come out to seek his life.
Jonathan, Saul’s son, rises and goes to David at Horesh. He strengthens David’s hand in God.
He says to him, “Do not be afraid — my father Saul’s hand will not find you. You will be king over Israel, and I will stand at your side. My father Saul knows this too.”
The two of them make a covenant before YHWH. David stays at Horesh, and Jonathan goes home.
The Ziphites go up to Saul at Gibeah and say, “Is David not hiding among us, in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon?
Come down whenever your heart desires, O king, and we will hand him over to you.”
Saul says, “May YHWH bless you for taking pity on me.
Go now and investigate further. Find out exactly where he is and who has seen him there — I am told he is very cunning.
Locate all the hiding places he uses, then come back to me with reliable information and I will go with you. If he is in the land I will hunt him down among all the thousands of Judah.”
They set out and go ahead of Saul to Ziph. David and his men are in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men go searching. David is warned and goes down to the rock and stays in the wilderness of Maon. Saul hears and pursues him into that wilderness.

Saul moves along one side of the mountain, David and his men along the other. David is pressing hard to get away from Saul. As Saul and his men begin to close in and surround David and his men to capture them,
a messenger arrives for Saul: “Come quickly — the Philistines have raided the land.”
So Saul breaks off the pursuit and turns to meet the Philistines. That place is named the Rock of Escape.
David goes up from there and lives in the strongholds of En-gedi.
When Saul returns from pursuing the Philistines, he is told that David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.
Saul takes three thousand chosen men from all Israel and goes to look for David and his men near the Rocks of the Wild Goats.
He comes to the sheepfolds along the way, where there is a cave. Saul goes into the cave to relieve himself. David and his men are sitting in the far recesses of the cave.

David’s men say to him, “This is the day YHWH was speaking of when he said, ‘I will give your enemy into your hand — do with him as you see fit.’” David rises and quietly cuts off the corner of Saul’s robe.
But afterward David’s heart strikes him because he has cut off the corner of Saul’s robe.
He says to his men, “YHWH forbid that I should do such a thing to my lord — the anointed of YHWH — by raising my hand against him. He is the anointed of YHWH.”
With these words David restrains his men and will not let them rise against Saul. Saul gets up, leaves the cave, and goes on his way.
Then David rises, goes out of the cave, and calls after Saul: “My lord the king!” Saul looks back, and David bows with his face to the ground and pays homage.
David says to Saul, “Why do you listen when people say, ‘David is out to harm you’?

With your own eyes you can see today that YHWH put you in my hands in the cave. Some told me to kill you — but I spared you. I said, ‘I will not raise my hand against my lord, for he is the anointed of YHWH.’

Look, my father — look at the corner of your robe in my hand. I cut it off but did not kill you. You can know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in me. I have not sinned against you, even though you are hunting my life to take it.
May YHWH judge between me and you. May YHWH avenge me on you — but my hand will not be against you.
As the old proverb says: ‘From the wicked comes wickedness.’ But my hand will not be against you.
After whom has the king of Israel come out? Who are you pursuing? A dead dog! A single flea!
May YHWH be the judge and decide between us. May he look into my cause and defend it — and deliver me from your hand.”
When David finishes speaking, Saul says, “Is that your voice, my son David?” And Saul weeps aloud.
He says to David, “You are more righteous than I — you have treated me well, while I have treated you badly.
You have shown me today what you have done for me: YHWH gave me into your hands, and you did not kill me.
When a man finds his enemy, does he let him go away safely? May YHWH reward you well for what you did to me today.
And now I know for certain that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hand.
Swear to me by YHWH that you will not cut off my descendants after me, and that you will not wipe out my name from my father’s house.”
David gives Saul his oath. Then Saul goes home, but David and his men go back up to the stronghold.
Samuel dies. All Israel gathers and mourns for him and buries him at his house in Ramah. Then David rises and goes down to the wilderness of Paran.
There is a man in Maon whose property is at Carmel. He is very wealthy — three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. He is shearing his sheep at Carmel.
The man’s name is Nabal, and his wife’s name is Abigail. The woman is discerning and beautiful; the man is harsh and badly behaved — a Calebite.
David hears in the wilderness that Nabal is shearing his sheep.
He sends ten young men and says to them, “Go up to Carmel, find Nabal, and greet him in my name.
Say this: ‘Peace to you, peace to your house, peace to all that is yours.
I hear that you are shearing. Your shepherds have been with us and we treated them well — they lost nothing the whole time they were in Carmel.
Ask your own young men and they will confirm it. Receive my men kindly, for we have come on a feast day. Please give whatever you can spare to your servants and to your son David.’”
David’s young men come and say all this to Nabal in David’s name, and then they wait.
Nabal answers David’s servants, “Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are plenty of slaves these days who break away from their masters.
Am I to take my bread and my water and the meat I’ve slaughtered for my shearers and give them to men who come from I don’t know where?”
David’s men turn back, go to David, and report all of this.
David says to his men, “Every man strap on his sword!” They all strap on their swords. David straps on his sword too. About four hundred men go up with David, and two hundred stay with the baggage.
But one of Nabal’s young servants tells Abigail his wife, “David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, and he hurled insults at them.
Yet those men were very good to us. We suffered no harm, and we lost nothing the whole time we were out in the fields with them.
They were a wall around us, day and night, the whole time we were with them keeping the sheep.
Now think carefully about what you should do, for harm is certain to come on our master and his whole household. He is such a good-for-nothing that nobody can say a word to him.”
Abigail moves quickly. She takes two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five dressed sheep, five seahs of roasted grain, a hundred raisin cakes, and two hundred fig cakes, and loads them on donkeys.
She says to her servants, “Go ahead of me — I’ll follow.” She tells her husband Nabal nothing.
As she rides down the mountain on her donkey, David and his men come toward her — and she meets them.
David had been saying, “I guarded everything this man has in the wilderness for nothing — not a thing of his went missing — and he has repaid good with evil.
May God do so to David’s enemies and more, if by morning I leave alive a single male of all that belongs to him.”
When Abigail sees David, she dismounts quickly from her donkey and falls before David on her face, bowing to the ground.
She falls at his feet and says, “My lord, let the guilt be mine alone. Please let your servant speak to you — hear what your servant says.
Let my lord pay no attention to this worthless man Nabal. His name says it all — Nabal is his name, and folly is in him. But I your servant did not see the young men you sent, my lord.

Now, my lord — as YHWH lives and as you live — YHWH himself has kept you from bloodguilt and from taking vengeance with your own hand. May your enemies and all who seek harm for my lord become like Nabal.
Accept this gift your servant has brought you, my lord, and let it be given to the young men who follow you.
Please forgive your servant’s presumption. YHWH will certainly build my lord a lasting house, because my lord fights the battles of YHWH, and no evil will be found in you as long as you live.

Even if someone rises to pursue you and to seek your life, the life of my lord will be bound up in the bundle of the living in the care of YHWH your God. But the lives of your enemies he will hurl away as from the hollow of a sling.
And when YHWH has done for my lord all the good he has promised and has made you prince over Israel,

this will not be a cause of stumbling or a burden on your conscience — that you shed blood without cause or saved yourself by your own hand. And when YHWH has dealt well with my lord, remember your servant.”
David says to Abigail, “Blessed be YHWH, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today!
Blessed be your good judgment, and blessed be you — for you have kept me today from bloodguilt and from taking vengeance with my own hand.
For as YHWH the God of Israel lives — who restrained me from harming you — if you had not come quickly to meet me, not one male belonging to Nabal would have been left alive by morning.”
David receives what she has brought him and says to her, “Go home in peace. I have listened to your voice and granted your request.”
When Abigail comes back to Nabal, he is holding a feast in his house like a king’s feast. His heart is merry within him, for he is very drunk. She says nothing to him until morning light.
In the morning, when the wine has gone out of Nabal, his wife tells him everything. His heart dies within him and he becomes like a stone.
About ten days later YHWH strikes Nabal, and he dies.

When David hears that Nabal is dead he says, “Blessed be YHWH who has avenged the insult I suffered at Nabal’s hand and kept his servant from wrongdoing. YHWH has brought Nabal’s evil back on his own head.” Then David sends word to Abigail to ask her to be his wife.
David’s servants come to Abigail at Carmel and say to her, “David has sent us to you to take you to him as his wife.”
She rises and bows with her face to the ground and says, “Your servant is ready to be a servant — to wash the feet of my lord’s servants.”
Then Abigail hurries and rises, mounts her donkey, and sets out with five of her young women. She follows David’s messengers and becomes his wife.
David also takes Ahinoam of Jezreel as his wife. Both become his wives.
Saul has given his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish, who is from Gallim.
The Ziphites come to Saul at Gibeah and say, “Is David not hiding on the hill of Hachilah, east of Jeshimon?”
So Saul rises and goes down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to search for David there.
Saul camps on the hill of Hachilah beside the road east of Jeshimon. David is staying in the wilderness and he sees that Saul has followed him there.
He sends out scouts and learns exactly where Saul has camped.

David goes and finds the place where Saul is lying. He sees where Saul sleeps, with Abner son of Ner, commander of the army, at his side. Saul is lying inside the camp, and the army is encamped around him.
David says to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down into the camp with me to Saul?” Abishai says, “I will go with you.”
So David and Abishai go to the army by night. Saul is lying asleep inside the camp, his spear stuck in the ground at his head. Abner and the army are lying around him.
Abishai says to David, “God has given your enemy into your hand today. Let me pin him to the ground with one thrust of the spear — I won’t need a second.”
David says to Abishai, “Do not kill him. Who can raise his hand against the anointed of YHWH and be guiltless?
As YHWH lives, YHWH himself will strike him — or his day will come to die, or he will go down in battle and perish.
YHWH forbid that I should raise my hand against the anointed of YHWH. But take the spear at his head and the water jar, and let us go.”

So David takes the spear and the water jar from beside Saul’s head and they slip away. No one sees it, no one knows, no one wakes up — for they are all asleep, because a deep sleep from YHWH has fallen over them.
David crosses to the other side and stands far off on top of a hill, with a great distance between them.
He calls out to the army and to Abner son of Ner: “Abner! Are you not going to answer me?” Abner shouts back, “Who are you, calling out to the king?”
David says, “Are you not a man? And who in Israel is like you? Then why have you not guarded your lord the king? Someone came in to destroy the king your lord.

This is not good, what you have done. As YHWH lives, you deserve to die — you have not guarded your lord, the anointed of YHWH. Now look — where is the king’s spear? Where is the water jar that was at his head?”
Saul recognizes David’s voice and says, “Is that your voice, my son David?” David says, “It is my voice, my lord the king.”
“Why does my lord pursue his servant?” David says. “What have I done? What evil is in my hands?

Now please, my lord the king — hear your servant out. If YHWH has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering. But if men have done it, may they be cursed before YHWH, for they have driven me away from my share in YHWH’s inheritance, as if saying, ‘Go and serve other gods.’
Do not let my blood fall to the ground away from the presence of YHWH. The king of Israel has come out to hunt down a single flea, like someone stalking a partridge in the mountains.”
Saul says, “I have sinned. Come back, my son David — I will not harm you again, because you held my life precious today. I have acted foolishly and made a terrible mistake.”
David answers, “Here is the spear, O king. Let one of your men come across and get it.
YHWH repays every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness. He gave you into my hands today, but I would not raise my hand against the anointed of YHWH.
Just as your life was precious to me today, may my life be precious to YHWH, and may he rescue me from every trouble.”
Saul says to David, “Blessed are you, my son David. You will accomplish much and surely succeed.” David goes on his way and Saul returns home.

David says to himself, “One day I will be destroyed by Saul’s hand. The best thing I can do is escape to Philistine territory. Then Saul will give up searching for me throughout Israel, and I will slip out of his reach.”
So David rises and crosses over with his six hundred men to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David settles with Achish at Gath — he and his men, each man with his household. David has his two wives: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, the widow of Nabal.
When Saul is told that David has fled to Gath, he stops searching for him.
David says to Achish, “If I have found favor in your eyes, let me be given a place in one of the outlying towns, where I can live. Why should your servant live in the royal city with you?”
That day Achish gives him Ziklag. This is why Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.
The time David lives in Philistine territory is a year and four months.
David and his men go up and raid the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites — ancient inhabitants of the land stretching toward Shur and on toward Egypt.
Whenever David strikes the land he leaves no man or woman alive, taking sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing before returning to Achish.
When Achish asks, “Where did you raid today?” David says, “The Negeb of Judah,” or “The Negeb of the Jerahmeelites,” or “The Negeb of the Kenites.”
David leaves no man or woman alive to bring word to Gath, reasoning, “Lest they report what we have actually done.” This is his practice all the time he lives in Philistine territory.
Achish trusts David completely, thinking, “He has made himself utterly repugnant to his own people Israel. He will be my servant forever.”
In those days the Philistines muster their forces for war against Israel. Achish says to David, “You understand that you and your men are marching with me into battle.”
David says to Achish, “Good. You will see what your servant can do.” Achish says to David, “Then I will make you my personal bodyguard for life.”
Now Samuel is dead. All Israel has mourned for him and buried him at Ramah, his own city. And Saul has expelled the mediums and the spiritists from the land.
The Philistines gather and come and camp at Shunem. Saul musters all Israel and they camp at Gilboa.
When Saul sees the Philistine army, he is afraid — his heart trembles violently.
He inquires of YHWH, but YHWH does not answer him — not by dreams, not by Urim, not by prophets.
Then Saul says to his servants, “Find me a woman who consults the dead, so that I can go and inquire through her.” His servants say, “There is a woman at En-dor who consults the dead.”
Saul disguises himself, putting on different clothes, and goes to her by night with two men. He says, “CConsult a spirit for me. Bring up the one I name.”
The woman says to him, “You know what Saul has done — he has expelled the mediums and spiritists from the land. Why are you laying a trap for my life to get me killed?”
Saul swears to her by YHWH: “As YHWH lives, no punishment will come to you for this.”
The woman says, “Whom shall I bring up?” He says, “Bring up Samuel.”
When the woman sees Samuel, she cries out at the top of her voice. She says to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!”
The king says to her, “Do not be afraid. What do you see?” The woman says to Saul, “I see a divine being coming up out of the earth.”
“What does he look like?” he asks. She says, “An old man is coming up, wrapped in a robe.” Saul knows it is Samuel. He bows with his face to the ground and pays homage.

Samuel says to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” Saul says, “I am in desperate straits — the Philistines are making war on me, and God has turned away from me and answers me no more, not by prophets, not by dreams. So I have called on you to tell me what to do.”
Samuel says, “Why do you ask me, when YHWH has turned from you and become your enemy?
YHWH has done exactly what he declared through me: he has torn the kingdom from your hand and given it to your neighbor David.
Because you did not obey the voice of YHWH and did not execute his fierce wrath against Amalek, YHWH has done this to you today.
And more: YHWH will give both Israel and you into the hands of the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. YHWH will give the army of Israel into Philistine hands.”
Saul falls full length on the ground, overcome with terror at Samuel’s words. There is no strength left in him — he has eaten nothing all day and all night.
The woman comes to Saul and sees that he is completely undone. She says, “Your servant obeyed you. I put my life in my hands and did what you asked me.
Now please — let your servant set a little food before you. Eat, so you will have strength for the journey.”
He refuses: “I will not eat.” But his servants, together with the woman, press him, and he listens to their voices. He rises from the ground and sits on the bed.
The woman has a fattened calf at her house. She quickly slaughters it, takes flour, kneads it, and bakes unleavened bread.
She sets it before Saul and his servants, and they eat. Then they rise and go away that same night.
The Philistines assemble all their forces at Aphek, while the Israelites camp by the spring at Jezreel.
As the Philistine lords march past by hundreds and thousands, David and his men are marching at the rear with Achish.

The Philistine commanders ask, “What are these Hebrews doing here?” Achish says, “This is David, who served Saul king of Israel. He has been with me for over a year now, and since he came over to me I have found no fault in him.”

But the Philistine commanders are furious with him. They say, “Send this man back to the place you assigned him. He must not go down to battle with us — he might turn against us in the fighting. What better way to win back his master’s favor than with the heads of our own men?
Is this not the David they sang about in their dances:
‘Saul has struck down his thousands,
and David his ten thousands?’”

So Achish calls David and says, “As YHWH lives, you have been reliable, and I would gladly have you march with me in the campaign — I have found nothing wrong with you since the day you came to me. But the lords do not approve of you.
Go back in peace, so that you do nothing to displease the Philistine lords.”
David says to Achish, “But what have I done? What have you found against your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I should not go and fight the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish answers David, “I know you are as blameless in my eyes as an angel of God. Nevertheless, the Philistine commanders have decided you must not go up with us to the battle.
Rise early in the morning — you and the servants of your lord who came with you — and go as soon as it is light.”
So David and his men rise early to return to Philistine territory. The Philistines go up to Jezreel.
On the third day David and his men reach Ziklag. The Amalekites have raided the Negeb and attacked Ziklag — they have stormed and burned it
and carried off everyone in it, women and all, young and old. They killed no one but drove them off and went on their way.
When David and his men arrive at the city they find it burned to the ground, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive.
David and the people with him weep aloud until they have no more strength to weep.
David’s two wives have been taken captive — Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
David is in desperate straits. The people speak of stoning him, for all of them are bitter in soul over their sons and daughters. But David strengthens himself in YHWH his God.
David says to Abiathar the priest, son of Ahimelech, “Bring me the ephod.” Abiathar brings the ephod.
David inquires of YHWH: “Shall I pursue this raiding party? Will I overtake them?” YHWH answers, “Pursue — you will certainly overtake them and rescue everyone.”
David sets out with his six hundred men and comes to the Besor ravine, where some stay behind.
David and four hundred men press on. Two hundred stay back — they are too exhausted to cross the ravine.
They find an Egyptian in the open country and bring him to David. They give him bread to eat and water to drink,
and a lump of pressed figs and two clusters of raisins. When he has eaten his spirit revives, for he has had neither food nor water for three days and three nights.
David asks him, “Who do you belong to? Where are you from?” He says, “I am an Egyptian boy, slave to an Amalekite. My master abandoned me when I fell sick three days ago.
We had raided the Negeb of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negeb of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag.”
David says, “Can you lead me down to this raiding party?” He says, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or hand me back to my master, and I will lead you down.”
He leads them down. The Amalekites are spread out all over the landscape — eating, drinking, and celebrating over the great plunder they have taken from the land of the Philistines and from Judah.
David strikes them from twilight until the evening of the next day. Not one of them escapes except four hundred young men who ride off on camels.
David recovers everything the Amalekites have taken. He rescues both his wives.
Nothing is missing — not young, not old, not sons, not daughters, not a piece of plunder, not a thing that had been taken. David brings everything back.
He also captures all the flocks and herds. The men drive the livestock ahead and say, “This is David’s plunder.”
David comes to the two hundred men who were too exhausted to follow him and had been left at the Besor ravine. They come out to meet David and the people. David greets them warmly.

But some of the wicked and worthless men among those who had gone with David speak up: “Since they didn’t come with us, we won’t share the plunder with them. Let each man take his wife and children and go.”
David says, “No, my brothers — you must not do this with what YHWH has given us. He has preserved us and given this raiding party into our hands.
Who would agree with your plan? The share of the man who goes into battle shall be the same as the share of the man who stays with the supplies — they share alike.”
From that day on David makes this a fixed rule and practice for Israel, and it holds to this day.
When David comes to Ziklag he sends portions of the plunder to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, “Here is a gift for you from the plunder of YHWH’s enemies.”
He sends to those in Bethel, Ramoth of the Negeb, Jattir,
Aroer, Siphmoth, Eshtemoa,
Racal, the cities of the Jerahmeelites, the cities of the Kenites,
Hormah, Bor-ashan, Athach,
Hebron, and all the places where David and his men had roamed.
The Philistines fight against Israel, and the men of Israel flee before them. Many fall slain on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines press hard after Saul and his sons. They strike down Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul’s sons.
The battle is fierce around Saul. The archers find him, and he is badly wounded by their arrows.

Saul says to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run me through — before these uncircumcised men come and abuse me.” But his armor-bearer is terrified and will not do it. So Saul takes his own sword and falls on it.
When his armor-bearer sees that Saul is dead, he too falls on his sword and dies with him.
So Saul dies, along with his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men — together, on that day.

When the Israelites on the other side of the valley and beyond the Jordan see that the Israelite army has fled and that Saul and his sons are dead, they abandon their towns and flee. The Philistines come and occupy them.
The next day, when the Philistines come to strip the slain, they find Saul and his three sons lying on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head, strip off his armor, and send word throughout Philistine territory — carrying the news to their idols’ temples and to the people.
They put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth and hang his body on the wall of Beth-shan.
When the people of Jabesh-gilead hear what the Philistines have done to Saul,
all their fighting men rise and travel through the night. They take the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan and come to Jabesh, where they burn them.
They take their bones and bury them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fast seven days.
After the death of Saul, when David returns from striking down the Amalekites, he stays two days at Ziklag.
On the third day, a man comes from Saul's camp with his clothes torn and dust on his head. When he reaches David, he falls to the ground and bows down.
David asks him, "Where do you come from?" He says, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."
"What happened?" David asks. "Tell me." He says, "The people have fled from the battle, and many have fallen and are dead. Also Saul and Jonathan his son are dead."
David asks the young man who brings him the news, "How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?"
The young man answers, "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, with the chariots and horsemen closing in on him.
He turned around and saw me and called out to me. I answered, 'Here I am.'
He asked, 'Who are you?' I said, 'I am an Amalekite.'
He said to me, 'Stand over me and kill me — agony has seized me, yet my life still lingers in me.'
So I stood over him and killed him, for I was certain he could not live after he had fallen. I took the crown from his head and the armlet from his arm and have brought them here to my lord."
Then David seizes his own clothes and tears them, and so do all the men who are with him.
They mourn and weep and fast until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of YHWH and for the house of Israel, because they have fallen by the sword.
David asks the young man who brought him the news, "Where are you from?" He answers, "I am the son of a resident foreigner — an Amalekite."
David says to him, "How is it that you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy YHWH's anointed?"
Then David calls one of the young men and says, "Go — strike him down." The young man strikes him, and he dies.
David says to him, "Your blood is on your own head, for your own mouth testified against you, saying, 'I killed YHWH's anointed.'"
David chants this lament over Saul and Jonathan his son,
and he instructs that it be taught to the people of Judah. It is written in the Book of Jashar. He says:
Your beauty, O Israel, is slain upon your high places!
How the mighty have fallen!
Tell it not in Gath;
proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon,
lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice,
lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.
You mountains of Gilboa —
let there be no dew or rain upon you,
no fields of firstfruits.
For there the shield of the mighty was defiled,
the shield of Saul, never anointed with oil.
From the blood of the slain,
from the fat of the mighty,
the bow of Jonathan did not turn back,
and the sword of Saul returned not empty.
Saul and Jonathan — beloved and lovely!
In life and in death they were not divided.
They were swifter than eagles;
they were stronger than lions.
You daughters of Israel, weep for Saul,
who clothed you in scarlet and luxury,
who put ornaments of gold upon your garments.
How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle!
Jonathan is slain upon your high places.
I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan —
you were very dear to me.
Your love to me was extraordinary,
surpassing the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen,
and the weapons of war have perished!
After this, David inquires of YHWH: "Shall I go up into one of the cities of Judah?" YHWH says to him, "Go up." David asks, "Where shall I go?" He says, "To Hebron."
So David goes up there with his two wives — Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
David also brings up the men who are with him, each one with his household, and they settle in the towns of Hebron.
Then the men of Judah come and anoint David king over the house of Judah. When they tell David that it was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul,
