David sends messengers to them and says, "May you be blessed by YHWH, because you showed this steadfast love to Saul your lord and buried him.
Now may YHWH show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I also will do good to you, because you have done this.
Now therefore let your hands be strong and be valiant, for Saul your lord is dead, and the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
But Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, takes Ish-bosheth son of Saul and brings him over to Mahanaim.
He makes him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin — over all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul is forty years old when he begins to reign over Israel, and he reigns two years. But the house of Judah follows David.
The time that David is king in Hebron over the house of Judah is seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul go out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and the servants of David go out and meet them at the pool of Gibeon. The two companies sit down — one on this side of the pool, the other on the far side.
Abner says to Joab, "Let the young men arise and compete before us." Joab says, "Let them arise."
They arise and cross over by number — twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.
Each man seizes his opponent by the head and drives his sword into his opponent's side, and they fall down together. So that place is called Helkath-hazzurim — which is at Gibeon.
The battle is very fierce that day, and Abner and the men of Israel are beaten before the servants of David.
The three sons of Zeruiah are there — Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel is as swift of foot as a wild gazelle.
Asahel pursues Abner, and as he runs he does not turn to the right or to the left from following Abner.
Abner looks behind him and says, "Is it you, Asahel?" He answers, "It is I."
Abner says to him, "Turn aside to your right or to your left — seize one of the young men and take his spoil." But Asahel refuses to turn aside.
Abner says again to Asahel, "Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift my face to your brother Joab?"

But he refuses to turn aside. So Abner strikes him in the belly with the butt of his spear, and the spear comes out through his back. He falls there and dies on the spot. And all who come to the place where Asahel fell stand still.
But Joab and Abishai pursue Abner. As the sun goes down they come to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The men of Benjamin rally behind Abner and form a single company, standing on the top of a hill.
Abner calls out to Joab: "Shall the sword devour forever? Do you not know that the end will be bitter? How long before you tell your people to turn back from pursuing their brothers?"
Joab says, "As God lives, if you had not spoken, the men would not have stopped pursuing their brothers until morning."
So Joab blows the trumpet, and all the men halt. They pursue Israel no more and fight no longer.
Abner and his men march through the Arabah all that night. They cross the Jordan, march the whole morning, and come to Mahanaim.
Joab returns from pursuing Abner. When he gathers all the people together, nineteen of David's servants are missing, besides Asahel.
But the servants of David have struck down of Benjamin and of Abner's men three hundred and sixty who perish.
They take Asahel and bury him in the tomb of his father at Bethlehem. Joab and his men march all night, and daybreak finds them at Hebron.
There is a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. David grows stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grows weaker and weaker.
Sons are born to David at Hebron. His firstborn is Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel.
His second is Chileab, by Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. The third is Absalom son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur.
The fourth is Adonijah son of Haggith; the fifth is Shephatiah son of Abital;
and the sixth is Ithream, by David's wife Eglah. These are born to David in Hebron.
While the war continues between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner is making himself very strong within the house of Saul.
Now Saul had a concubine named Rizpah daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth says to Abner, "Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?"

Abner is very angry at these words. "Am I a dog's head from Judah?" he says. "To this day I have shown steadfast loyalty to the house of Saul your father — to his brothers and his friends — and have not handed you over to David. And now you charge me with a fault over a woman!
God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David exactly what YHWH has sworn to him —
to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and establish the throne of David over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."
Ish-bosheth cannot answer Abner another word, because he fears him.
Abner sends messengers to David on his own behalf, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make your covenant with me, and my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you."
David says, "Good — I will make a covenant with you. But one thing I require: you shall not see my face unless you bring Michal, Saul's daughter, when you come."
David also sends messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, saying, "Give me my wife Michal, for whom I paid the bridal price of a hundred Philistine foreskins."
Ish-bosheth sends and takes her from her husband Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband walks behind her as far as Bahurim, weeping as he goes. Then Abner says to him, "Go back." And he turns and goes home.
Abner speaks with the elders of Israel: "For some time now you have been wanting David as king over you.
Now act on it. For YHWH has promised David: 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from all their enemies.'"
Abner also speaks with Benjamin, then goes to tell David at Hebron all that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin think good to do.
When Abner and twenty men come to David at Hebron, David makes a feast for Abner and the men with him.

Abner says to David, "Let me go and gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you and that you may reign over all your heart desires." So David sends Abner away, and he goes in peace.
Just then the servants of David arrive with Joab from a raid, bringing much spoil. Abner is no longer with David at Hebron, for David has sent him away and he has gone in peace.
When Joab and all the army with him arrive, he is told, "Abner son of Ner came to the king, and the king sent him away, and he has gone in peace."
Joab goes in to the king and says, "What have you done? Abner came to you. Why did you let him go? He is gone.
You know that Abner son of Ner came to deceive you — to learn your movements and everything you are doing."
Joab leaves David's presence and sends messengers after Abner. They bring him back from the cistern of Sirah. David knows nothing about it.
When Abner returns to Hebron, Joab draws him aside at the gate to speak with him privately — and there drives a sword into his belly. And he dies, for the blood of Asahel his brother.
When David hears of it afterward, he says, "I and my kingdom are guiltless before YHWH forever for the blood of Abner son of Ner.

Let it fall on the head of Joab and on all his father's house. May the house of Joab never lack one who has a running sore or a skin disease, or who holds a spindle, or who falls by the sword, or who lacks bread!"
So Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death in the battle at Gibeon.
Then David says to Joab and all the people with him, "Tear your clothes and put on sackcloth and mourn before Abner." And King David follows the bier.
They bury Abner at Hebron. The king lifts up his voice and weeps at Abner's grave, and all the people weep.
The king chants this lament for Abner:
"Should Abner die as a fool dies?
Your hands were not bound;
your feet were not fettered.
As one falls before sons of treachery,
so you fell."
And all the people weep over him again.
Then all the people come to persuade David to eat while it is still day. But David swears: "God do so to me and more also if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!"
All the people take notice, and it pleases them — as everything the king does pleases all the people.
So all the people and all Israel understand that day that the king had no part in the killing of Abner son of Ner.
The king says to his servants, "Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?
And I am weak today, though anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are harder than I am. May YHWH repay the evildoer according to his wickedness!"
When Ish-bosheth son of Saul hears that Abner has died at Hebron, his hands go slack, and all Israel is shaken.
Now Saul's son had two men who led raiding bands. One was named Baanah and the other Rechab — sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, a Benjaminite. (Beeroth is counted as part of Benjamin,
for the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have been living there as sojourners to this day.)

(Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was crippled in both feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and fled, and in the panic of her flight he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.)
The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite — Rechab and Baanah — set out and arrive at the house of Ish-bosheth at the heat of the day, while he is taking his noon rest.
They come into the inner part of the house as if to fetch wheat, and strike him in the stomach. Then Rechab and Baanah his brother slip away.
They had come into the house while he lay on his bed in his chamber, struck him and killed him, and cut off his head. Taking his head, they travel by way of the Arabah through the night

and bring the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron. They say to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. YHWH has avenged my lord the king this day on Saul and on his offspring."
But David answers Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite: "As YHWH lives — who has redeemed my life from every adversity —
when someone told me, 'Saul is dead,' thinking he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag. That was the reward I gave him for his news.
How much more, when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house, on his own bed — shall I not require his blood at your hand and rid the earth of you?"

David commands his young men, and they kill them. They cut off their hands and feet and hang them beside the pool at Hebron. But they take the head of Ish-bosheth and bury it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron.
Then all the tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron and say, "Look — we are your bone and your flesh.
In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led Israel out and brought it back in. And YHWH said to you, 'You shall shepherd my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.'"
So all the elders of Israel come to the king at Hebron. King David makes a covenant with them there before YHWH, and they anoint David king over Israel.
David is thirty years old when he begins to reign, and he reigns forty years.
At Hebron he reigns over Judah seven years and six months. At Jerusalem he reigns over all Israel and Judah thirty-three years.

The king and his men march to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, who live in the land. They say to David, "You will never get in here. The blind and the lame will drive you back." — meaning, 'David cannot come in here.'
But David takes the stronghold of Zion — that is, the city of David.

David says that day, "Whoever strikes the Jebusites, let him reach the water shaft to attack the lame and the blind — those who are David's enemies." That is why they say, "The blind and the lame shall not enter the house."
David lives in the stronghold and calls it the city of David. He builds all around it, inward from the Millo.
David keeps growing greater, for YHWH the God of hosts is with him.
Hiram king of Tyre sends envoys to David, with cedar timber and carpenters and masons. They build David a palace.
And David knows that YHWH has established him as king over Israel and has exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
After he comes from Hebron, David takes more concubines and wives in Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters are born to him.
These are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
When the Philistines hear that they have anointed David king over Israel, they all come up to search for him. But David hears of it and goes down to the stronghold.
The Philistines have come and spread themselves out in the Valley of Rephaim.
David inquires of YHWH: "Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?" YHWH says to him, "Go up — I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand."
David comes to Baal-perazim and strikes them down there. He says, "YHWH has broken through my enemies before me like a bursting flood." So that place is called Baal-perazim.
They abandon their idols there, and David and his men carry them away.
The Philistines come up once more and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
When David inquires of YHWH, he says, "Do not go up — circle around behind them and come against them opposite the balsam trees.
When you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move quickly, for then YHWH has gone out before you to strike down the army of the Philistines."
David does as YHWH commanded him and strikes down the Philistines from Geba all the way to Gezer.
David again gathers all the chosen men of Israel — thirty thousand.
David and all the people with him set out from Baale-judah to bring up the ark of God, which is called by the name of YHWH of hosts, who is enthroned above the cherubim.
They place the ark of God on a new cart and bring it out of the house of Abinadab, which is on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, are guiding the new cart
with the ark of God on it, while Ahio walks before the ark.
David and all the house of Israel are celebrating before YHWH with all kinds of instruments — lyres, harps, tambourines, castanets, and cymbals.
When they come to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reaches out his hand to the ark of God and steadies it, for the oxen stumble.
The anger of YHWH is kindled against Uzzah, and God strikes him down there for his irreverence, and he dies beside the ark of God.
David is angry because YHWH has broken out against Uzzah. That place is called Perez-uzzah to this day.
David is afraid of YHWH that day and says, "How can the ark of YHWH ever come to me?"
He is not willing to bring the ark of YHWH into the city of David. David takes it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite.
The ark of YHWH remains in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite for three months, and YHWH blesses Obed-edom and all his household.

It is told to King David: "YHWH has blessed the household of Obed-edom and everything belonging to him, because of the ark of God." So David goes and brings up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with great rejoicing.
When those carrying the ark of YHWH have taken six steps, David sacrifices an ox and a fattened animal.
And David dances before YHWH with all his might. David is wearing a linen ephod.
So David and all the house of Israel bring up the ark of YHWH with shouts of joy and the blast of the ram's horn.
As the ark of YHWH enters the city of David, Michal daughter of Saul is looking through the window. She sees King David leaping and spinning before YHWH and despises him in her heart.
They bring in the ark of YHWH and set it in its place inside the tent David has pitched for it. David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings before YHWH.
When David finishes offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blesses the people in the name of YHWH of hosts
and distributes to all the people — the entire multitude of Israel, men and women alike — a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins. Then all the people leave for home.

David returns to bless his own household. But Michal daughter of Saul comes out to meet him and says, "How the king of Israel honored himself today — uncovering himself in front of the servant girls of his servants like some worthless fellow who shamelessly exposes himself!"
David says to Michal, "It was before YHWH, who chose me above your father and all his house and appointed me as prince over Israel — the people of YHWH. I will dance before YHWH.
I will debase myself even more than this — and be low in my own eyes. But by those servant girls you just spoke of — they will honor me."
And Michal daughter of Saul has no child to the day of her death.
Now when the king is settled in his palace and YHWH has given him rest from all his surrounding enemies,
the king says to Nathan the prophet, "Look — I am living in a palace of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent."
Nathan says to the king, "Go, do everything that is in your heart, for YHWH is with you."
But that very night the word of YHWH comes to Nathan:
"Go and tell my servant David: 'Thus says YHWH — Are you the one who will build me a house to dwell in?
I have not lived in a house from the day I brought Israel up from Egypt until this day. I have been moving about in a tent and a tabernacle.

In all the places where I have traveled with all the people of Israel, did I ever speak a word to any of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, asking, "Why have you not built me a house of cedar?"'
"Now therefore you shall say this to my servant David: 'Thus says YHWH of hosts — I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel.
I have been with you wherever you went. I cut off all your enemies before you. And I will make your name as great as the names of the greatest men on earth.
I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them there, so that they may dwell in their own place and be disturbed no more. Violent men shall afflict them no more, as in former times
from the days I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, YHWH declares to you that YHWH himself will build you a house.
When your days are fulfilled and you lie down with your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you — one who will come from your own body — and I will establish his kingdom.
He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod as men use it, with blows as sons receive —
but my steadfast love will not leave him, as I withdrew it from Saul, whom I removed from before you.
Your house and your kingdom shall stand firm before me forever. Your throne shall be established forever.'"
In keeping with all these words and this entire vision, Nathan speaks to David.
Then King David goes in and sits before YHWH and says: "Who am I, Lord YHWH, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?
And yet this is a small thing in your eyes, Lord YHWH. You have also spoken of your servant's house for a great while to come. Is this the charter for all humanity, Lord YHWH?
What more can David say to you? You know your servant, Lord YHWH.
For the sake of your word and according to your own heart you have brought about all this greatness, making it known to your servant.
Therefore you are great, YHWH God — for there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our own ears.

And who is like your people Israel — the one nation on earth that God went to redeem as a people for himself, making himself a name, doing great and awesome deeds for them, driving out nations and their gods from before your people, whom you redeemed from Egypt?
You established your people Israel as your own people forever. And you, YHWH, became their God.
And now, YHWH God, confirm forever the word you have spoken about your servant and about his house. Do as you have promised.
Let your name be magnified forever — let men say, 'YHWH of hosts is God over Israel,' and let the house of your servant David be established before you.
For you, YHWH of hosts, God of Israel, have revealed this to your servant, saying, 'I will build you a house.' Therefore your servant has found the courage to pray this prayer to you.
And now, Lord YHWH — you are God. Your words are true. You have promised this good thing to your servant.

Now may it please you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you. For you, Lord YHWH, have spoken, and with your blessing let the house of your servant be blessed forever."
After this, David strikes down the Philistines and subdues them, taking control of Metheg-ammah from Philistine hands.

He also strikes down Moab and measures them with a cord, making them lie down on the ground. Two cord-lengths he measures for death, and a full cord-length for life. So Moab becomes subject to David and pays tribute.
David then strikes down Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as Hadadezer moves to restore his power at the Euphrates River.
David captures from him seventeen hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers. He hamstrings all the chariot horses but keeps back enough for a hundred chariots.
When the Syrians of Damascus come to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David strikes down twenty-two thousand of them.
David puts garrisons in Aram-Damascus, and the Syrians become subject to David and bring tribute. YHWH gives David victory wherever he goes.
David takes the gold shields carried by Hadadezer's officials and brings them to Jerusalem.
From Tebah and Berothai — cities of Hadadezer — King David takes a great quantity of bronze.
When Toi king of Hamath hears that David has broken the whole army of Hadadezer,

he sends his son Joram to King David to greet him and congratulate him on fighting Hadadezer and defeating him — for Hadadezer had been an enemy of Toi. Joram brings with him objects of silver, gold, and bronze.
King David dedicates these to YHWH, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued —
from Edom, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and from the plunder of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David wins further fame on his return from striking down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
He puts garrisons throughout all Edom, and all the Edomites become subject to David. YHWH gives David victory wherever he goes.
David reigns over all Israel. He administers justice and righteousness to all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah is over the army. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud is recorder.
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar are priests. Seraiah is secretary.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada is over the Cherethites and the Pelethites. And David's sons serve as priests.
David asks, "Is there anyone still left of the house of Saul, that I may show him covenant love for Jonathan's sake?"
There is a servant of the house of Saul named Ziba. They summon him to David. The king asks, "Are you Ziba?" He says, "Your servant is he."
The king asks, "Is there no one left of the house of Saul that I may show the covenant love of God to him?" Ziba says to the king, "There is still a son of Jonathan — he is crippled in his feet."
The king asks, "Where is he?" Ziba says, "He is in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar."
King David sends and brings him from the house of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar.
When Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, comes to David, he falls on his face and bows down. David says, "Mephibosheth!" He answers, "Here is your servant."

"Do not be afraid," David says to him, "for I will surely show you covenant love for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore all the land of your grandfather Saul to you, and you shall eat at my table always."
He bows and says, "What is your servant, that you should give notice to a dead dog such as I am?"
Then the king summons Ziba, Saul's servant, and says to him, "Everything that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master's grandson.

You and your sons and your servants shall work the land for him and bring in its produce, so that your master's grandson will have food to eat. But Mephibosheth your master's grandson shall always eat at my table." (Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.)
Ziba says to the king, "Your servant will do exactly as my lord the king commands." So Mephibosheth eats at David's table, like one of the king's own sons.
Mephibosheth has a young son named Mica. All who live in Ziba's house become Mephibosheth's servants.
Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem, for he always eats at the king's table. He is lame in both his feet.
After this, the king of the Ammonites dies and his son Hanun reigns in his place.

David says, "I will show loyalty to Hanun son of Nahash, as his father showed loyalty to me." So David sends his servants to console him for the loss of his father. But when David's servants arrive in the land of the Ammonites,

the Ammonite princes say to Hanun their lord, "Do you really think David is honoring your father by sending men to console you? Has he not sent his servants to search through the city, to spy it out and overthrow it?"
So Hanun seizes David's servants, shaves off half the beard of each, cuts their garments off at the hips, and sends them away.
When David is told, he sends men to meet them, for the men are deeply humiliated. The king says, "Stay at Jericho until your beards have grown back, then come home."

When the Ammonites see they have become a stench to David, they send and hire twenty thousand Syrian foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, plus the king of Maacah with a thousand men, and twelve thousand men from Tob.
When David hears of it, he sends Joab and the entire army of fighting men.
The Ammonites come out and take up battle positions at the city entrance, while the Syrians of Zobah, Rehob, Tob, and Maacah position themselves separately in the open field.
Joab sees that he faces battle both in front and behind. He selects the best troops of Israel and deploys them against the Syrians.
The rest of the army he places under the command of his brother Abishai and deploys them against the Ammonites.
He says, "If the Syrians are too strong for me, you come and help me. If the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come and help you.
Be strong, and let us fight with courage for our people and for the cities of our God. And may YHWH do what is good in his eyes."
Joab advances with his men against the Syrians, and they flee before him.
When the Ammonites see that the Syrians have fled, they too flee before Abishai and retreat into the city. Joab then returns from the fight against the Ammonites and comes back to Jerusalem.
When the Syrians see they have been routed by Israel, they regroup.
Hadadezer sends and brings out the Syrians from beyond the Euphrates. They march to Helam, with Shobach the commander of Hadadezer's army leading them.
When it is reported to David, he musters all Israel, crosses the Jordan, and comes to Helam. The Syrians take up their positions against David and engage him in battle.
But the Syrians flee before Israel. David strikes down seven hundred of their charioteers and forty thousand horsemen, and strikes down Shobach the commander of their army, who dies there.

When all the kings who were vassals of Hadadezer see they have been defeated by Israel, they make peace with Israel and become subject to them. After that, the Syrians are afraid to help the Ammonites anymore.

In the spring of the year — the season when kings march out to war — David sends Joab, and his officers and all Israel with him. They lay waste to the Ammonites and besiege Rabbah. But David remains in Jerusalem.
One evening David rises from his couch and walks on the roof of the palace. From the roof he sees a woman bathing, and the woman is strikingly beautiful.
David sends someone to inquire about the woman. He is told, "She is Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam — the wife of Uriah the Hittite."
David sends messengers and takes her. She comes to him, and he lies with her. (She has just completed her purification.) Then she returns to her house.
The woman conceives. She sends word to David: "I am pregnant."
David sends word to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." Joab sends Uriah to David.
When Uriah arrives, David asks how Joab is, how the army is, and how the war is going.
Then David says to Uriah, "Go down to your house and wash your feet." Uriah leaves the palace, and a gift from the king follows after him.
But Uriah sleeps at the entrance of the palace with all the king's servants. He does not go down to his house.
When they tell David, "Uriah did not go down to his house," David asks Uriah, "You have just come from a journey — why did you not go home?"

Uriah says to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah are living in field tents, and my lord Joab and my lord's servants are camping in the open country. Should I then go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As you live, as you yourself live — I will not do this thing."
David says to Uriah, "Stay here today as well, and tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah remains in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invites him to eat and drink, and makes him drunk. But in the evening Uriah goes out again to lie down on his couch with the king's servants. He does not go down to his house.
In the morning David writes a letter to Joab and sends it by the hand of Uriah.
He writes in the letter: "Put Uriah in the front of the fiercest fighting and then pull back from him, so that he is struck down and dies."
So while Joab is besieging the city, he assigns Uriah to the position where he knows the strongest defenders are.
When the men of the city come out and fight Joab's forces, some of the king's servants fall. Uriah the Hittite also dies.
Joab sends a full report of the battle to David.
He instructs the messenger: "When you have finished giving the king the full account of the battle,
if the king's anger rises and he asks you, 'Why did you advance so close to the city to fight? Did you not know they would shoot from the wall?

Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? Was it not a woman who threw a millstone on him from the wall at Thebez, and he died? Why did you go so close to the wall?' — then say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well.'"
The messenger sets out and arrives and tells David everything Joab has sent him to say.
He says, "The men had us at a disadvantage and came out against us in the open, but we drove them back to the city gate.
Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king's servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well."
David says to the messenger, "Say this to Joab: 'Do not take this badly — the sword devours one and then another. Press your attack on the city and demolish it.' And encourage him."
When Uriah's wife hears that her husband Uriah is dead, she mourns for him.
When the mourning is over, David sends and brings her to his house, and she becomes his wife and bears him a son. But the thing David had done was evil in the eyes of YHWH.
YHWH sends Nathan to David. He comes to him and says: "There were two men in a certain city — one rich and one poor.
The rich man had very many flocks and herds.

But the poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb that he had bought. He raised it, and it grew up with him and with his children. It ate from his portion, drank from his cup, lay in his arms — it was like a daughter to him.

Now a traveler comes to the rich man, and the rich man is unwilling to take from his own flock or herd to prepare a meal for the guest. Instead he takes the poor man's lamb and prepares it for the man who has come to him."
David's anger flares hot against the man. He says to Nathan, "As YHWH lives, the man who did this deserves to die!
He shall restore the lamb four times over, because he did this thing and had no pity."
Nathan says to David: "You are the man! Thus says YHWH, the God of Israel: 'I anointed you king over Israel. I delivered you from the hand of Saul.
I gave you your master's house and your master's wives into your arms. I gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if that had been too little, I would have added as much more.

Why have you despised the word of YHWH, to do what is evil in his sight? You have struck Uriah the Hittite down with the sword — you have taken his wife for yourself and killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now therefore the sword will never leave your house, because you despised me and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite as your own.'

Thus says YHWH: 'I will bring evil against you out of your own house. I will take your wives before your very eyes and give them to one who is close to you, and he will lie with your wives in the open daylight.
For you did it in secret, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'"
David says to Nathan, "I have sinned against YHWH." Nathan says to David, "YHWH has also taken away your sin — you will not die.
However, because you have utterly scorned YHWH by this deed, the son who is born to you shall die."
Then Nathan goes home. And YHWH strikes the child that Uriah's wife bore to David, and the child becomes gravely ill.
David fasts for the child and pleads with God. He goes and lies all night on the bare ground.
The elders of his household stand over him and try to raise him from the ground, but he refuses, and he will not eat with them.

On the seventh day the child dies. David's servants are afraid to tell him, for they say, "Look — while the child was still alive we spoke to him and he would not listen. How can we tell him the child is dead? He may do something drastic."
But David notices his servants whispering among themselves and understands that the child is dead. He asks his servants, "Is the child dead?" They answer, "He is dead."

Then David gets up from the ground. He washes and anoints himself and changes his clothes. He goes into the house of YHWH and worships. Then he comes to his own house and asks for food. They set it before him, and he eats.
His servants say to him, "What is this you have done? You fasted and wept for the child while he was alive, but now that the child is dead you get up and eat?"
He says, "While the child was still alive I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows — perhaps YHWH will be gracious to me and the child will live.'
But now he is dead. Why should I go on fasting? Can I bring him back? I will go to him — but he will not return to me."
Then David comforts his wife Bathsheba. He goes in to her and lies with her, and she bears a son. He calls his name Solomon. And YHWH loves him
and sends word through Nathan the prophet, so that he calls the child Jedidiah — beloved of YHWH — for YHWH's sake.
Meanwhile Joab fights against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captures the royal city.
Joab sends messengers to David and says, "I have fought against Rabbah and have taken its water supply.
Now gather the rest of the troops and besiege the city and take it — otherwise I will take it, and it will be called by my name."
So David gathers all the army and marches to Rabbah, and fights and takes it.

He takes the crown from the head of their king — it weighs a talent of gold and has a precious stone in it — and it is placed on David's head. He brings out an enormous amount of plunder from the city.

He brings out the people there and sets them to work with saws and iron picks and iron axes, and puts them at the brick kilns. He does this to all the cities of the Ammonites. Then David and all the army return to Jerusalem.
Amnon and Tamar
After these things, Absalom son of David has a beautiful sister whose name is Tamar, and Amnon son of David loves her.
Amnon is so tormented over his sister Tamar that he makes himself ill—for she is a virgin, and it seems impossible to Amnon to do anything against her.
But Amnon has a friend whose name is Jonadab son of Shimeah, David's brother, and Jonadab is a very shrewd man.
He says to him, "Why are you, the king's son, so haggard morning after morning? Will you not tell me?" Amnon says to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."

Jonadab says to him, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill. When your father comes to see you, say to him, 'Let my sister Tamar come and give me bread to eat, and prepare the food in my sight, so that I may see it and eat it from her hand.'"

So Amnon lies down and pretends to be ill. When the king comes to see him, Amnon says to the king, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, so that I may eat from her hand."
Then David sends home to Tamar, saying, "Go to your brother Amnon's house and prepare food for him."
So Tamar goes to her brother Amnon's house, where he is lying down. She takes dough and kneads it and makes cakes in his sight and bakes them.
Then she takes the pan and empties it out before him, but he refuses to eat. Amnon says, "Have everyone go out from me." So everyone goes out from him.
Then Amnon says to Tamar, "Bring the food into the chamber, so that I may eat from your hand." And Tamar takes the cakes she has made and brings them into the chamber to Amnon her brother.
But when she brings them near him to eat, he seizes her and says to her, "Come, lie with me, my sister."
She answers him, "No, my brother, do not force me, for such a thing is not done in Israel. Do not do this outrageous thing.
As for me, where could I carry my shame? And as for you, you would be as one of the outrageous fools in Israel. Now therefore, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you."
But he will not listen to her, and being stronger than she is, he forces her and lies with her.
Then Amnon hates her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hates her is greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon says to her, "Get up and go."
But she says to him, "No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me." But he would not listen to her.
He calls the young man who served him and says, "Put this woman out of my presence and bolt the door after her."
Now she is wearing a long robe with sleeves, for thus the virgin daughters of the king are dressed. So his servant puts her out and bolts the door after her.
And Tamar puts ashes on her head and tears the long robe she is wearing. She lays her hand on her head and goes away, crying aloud as she goes.

And her brother Absalom says to her, "Has Amnon your brother been with you? Now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother; do not take this to heart." So Tamar lives, a desolate woman, in her brother Absalom's house.
When King David hears of all these things, he is very angry, but he will not grieve the spirit of his son Amnon, because he loves him, for he is his firstborn.
But Absalom speaks to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hates Amnon because he has violated his sister Tamar.
Absalom's Revenge
After two full years Absalom has sheepshearers at Baal-hazor, which is near Ephraim, and Absalom invites all the king's sons.
Absalom comes to the king and says, "Behold, your servant has sheepshearers. Please let the king and his servants go with your servant."
But the king says to Absalom, "No, my son, let us not all go, lest we be burdensome to you." He pressed him, but he would not go, and he blessed him.
Then Absalom says, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." And the king says to him, "Why should he go with you?"
But Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.
Absalom commands his servants, "Mark when Amnon's heart is merry with wine, and when I say to you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Do not fear; have I not commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant."
So the servants of Absalom do to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king's sons arose and each mounted his mule and fled.
While they are on the way, news comes to David, "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one of them is left."
Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants who were standing by tore their garments.

But Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother, answered and said, "Let not my lord suppose that they have killed all the young men the king's sons, for Amnon alone is dead. For by the command of Absalom this has been determined from the day he violated his sister Tamar.
Now therefore let not my lord the king so take it to heart as to suppose that all the king's sons are dead, for Amnon alone is dead."
But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, many people were coming from the road behind him by the side of the mountain.
And Jonadab said to the king, "Behold, the king's sons have come; as your servant said, so it has come about."
And as soon as he had finished speaking, behold, the king's sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly.
But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.
So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years.
And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.
Joab's Stratagem
Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king's heart went out to Absalom.

So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman. He said to her, "Please pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil but behave like a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead.
Go to the king and speak thus to him." So Joab put the words in her mouth.
When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and paid homage and said, "Save me, O king."
And the king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She answered, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead.
Your servant had two sons, and they quarreled with one another in the field. There was no one to separate them, and one struck the other and killed him.

And now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the man who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed.' And so they would quench my coal that is left and leave to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth."
Then the king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you."
And the woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless."
The king said, "If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me, and he shall never touch you again."

Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood kill no more, and my son not be destroyed." He said, "As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground."
Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."

And the woman said, "Why then have you planned such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this verdict the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring his banished one home again.
We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.

Now I have come to say this to my lord the king because the people have made me afraid, and your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his servant.
For the king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy both me and my son together from the heritage of God.'
And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God to discern good and evil. The LORD your God be with you!"
Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." And the woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."

The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered and said, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right hand or to the left from anything that my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; it was he who put all these words in the mouth of your servant.
In order to change the course of things your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God to know all things that are on earth."
Absalom Returns to Jerusalem
Then the king said to Joab, "Behold now, I grant this; go, bring back the young man Absalom."

And Joab fell on his face to the ground and paid homage and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your sight, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant."
So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
And the king said, "Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence." So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence.
Now in all Israel there was no one so much to be praised for his handsome appearance as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.
And when he cut the hair of his head—he cut it at the end of every year, because it was heavy on him, and when he cut it he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels by the king's weight—
there were born to Absalom three sons and one daughter. The daughter's name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.
So Absalom lived two full years in Jerusalem, without coming into the king's presence.
Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. And he sent a second time, but Joab would not come.
Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there; go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.
Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"

Absalom answered Joab, "Behold, I sent word to you: Come here, that I may send you to the king to ask why I came from Geshur. It would be better for me to still be there. Now let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death."
Then Joab went to the king and told him, and he summoned Absalom. So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.
Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel · 15:1–12
After this Absalom gets himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.

Absalom rises early and stands by the road to the gate. Whenever anyone has a case to bring before the king for judgment, Absalom calls to him and asks, "What city are you from?" When he says he is from such-and-such a tribe in Israel,
Absalom says to him, "Look — your claims are good and right, but the king has no one deputized to hear you."
Then Absalom says, "If only I were made judge in the land! Everyone with a dispute or a cause could come to me, and I would give them justice."
And whenever someone approaches to bow down before him, Absalom reaches out his hand and takes hold of him and kisses him.
Absalom does this to every Israelite who comes to the king for judgment. So Absalom steals the hearts of the men of Israel.
At the end of four years Absalom says to the king, "Please let me go to Hebron and fulfill the vow I made to YHWH.
For your servant made a vow while I lived at Geshur in Aram, saying, 'If YHWH brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship him in Hebron.'"
The king says to him, "Go in peace." So Absalom gets up and goes to Hebron.
But Absalom sends spies throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, "As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, say: Absalom is king in Hebron!"
Two hundred men from Jerusalem go with Absalom — invited guests who know nothing of what is planned.
While Absalom is offering the sacrifices, he sends for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, from his city of Giloh. The conspiracy grows strong, and the people with Absalom keep increasing.
David Flees Jerusalem · 15:13–29
A messenger comes to David: "The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom."

David says to all his servants in Jerusalem, "Rise — we must flee, or there will be no escape from Absalom. Go quickly, or he will overtake us and bring disaster down on us and put the city to the sword."
The king's servants say to him, "Whatever our lord the king decides, your servants are ready."
The king goes out with all his household following him. He leaves ten concubines to keep the house.
The king goes out with all the people after him, and they halt at the last house.
All his servants pass by him — the Cherethites and the Pelethites and all six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath — passing before the king.
The king says to Ittai the Gittite, "Why are you coming with us? Go back and stay with the new king. You are a foreigner, an exile from your homeland.
You came only yesterday, and shall I today make you wander with us? I do not even know where I am going. Go back, and take your brothers with you. May YHWH show you steadfast love and faithfulness."
But Ittai answers the king, "As YHWH lives, and as my lord the king lives — wherever my lord the king is, whether in death or in life, there also will your servant be."
David says to Ittai, "Go then, march on." So Ittai the Gittite marches on with all his men and all the little ones who are with him.
All the land weeps aloud as all the people pass by. The king crosses the Kidron Valley and all the people move on toward the wilderness.
Zadok is there too, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set the ark of God down until all the people have finished passing out of the city.
The king says to Zadok, "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of YHWH, he will bring me back and let me see it and its dwelling place.
But if he says, 'I take no pleasure in you' — then here I am; let him do to me whatever seems good to him."
The king says also to Zadok the priest, "You are a seer, are you not? Return to the city in peace, you and Abiathar, and both your sons with you — Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan the son of Abiathar.
I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me."
So Zadok and Abiathar carry the ark of God back to Jerusalem and remain there.
David on the Mount of Olives · 15:30–37
David goes up the slope of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he climbs, his head covered and his feet bare. All the people with him cover their heads and weep as they go up.
Someone tells David, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." David says, "O YHWH, please make the counsel of Ahithophel foolishness."
When David reaches the summit where people worship God, Hushai the Archite comes to meet him with his robe torn and dust on his head.
David says to him, "If you come with me you will be a burden to me.
But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king — as I served your father, so I will serve you' — then you can work against Ahithophel's counsel for me.
Zadok and Abiathar the priests are there with you. Whatever you hear from the king's house, tell it to Zadok and Abiathar.
Their two sons are with them — Ahimaaz son of Zadok, and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Send me word through them about everything you hear."
So Hushai, David's friend, arrives in Jerusalem just as Absalom is entering the city.
Ziba Meets the King · 16:1–4

When David passes a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth meets him with a pair of donkeys saddled, carrying two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine.

The king asks Ziba, "What are these for?" Ziba says, "The donkeys are for the king's household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for those who are faint in the wilderness to drink."
"And where is your master's grandson?" the king asks. Ziba says, "He is staying in Jerusalem, for he said, 'Today the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my father.'"
The king says to Ziba, "All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours." Ziba says, "I bow before you. May I find favor in your sight, my lord the king."
Shimei Curses the King · 16:5–14
When King David reaches Bahurim, a man comes out of there cursing as he comes. His name is Shimei son of Gera, of the family of Saul's house.
He throws stones at David and at all the servants of King David, though all the people and all the mighty men are on David's right and on his left.
Shimei curses as he throws: "Get out, get out, you man of blood, you worthless man!
YHWH has repaid you for all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you reign! YHWH has given the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. You are ruined — for you are a man of blood!"
Abishai son of Zeruiah says to the king, "Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head."
The king says, "What does this have to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse — if YHWH has told him to curse David, who is anyone to say, 'Why are you doing this?'"
David says to Abishai and to all his servants, "My own son seeks my life. How much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone. Let him curse, for YHWH has allowed it.
Perhaps YHWH will see my affliction and return to me something good in place of his cursing today."
So David and his men go on the road while Shimei moves along the hillside opposite, cursing and throwing stones and flinging dirt.
The king and all the people with him arrive exhausted at the Jordan, and there they rest.
Absalom Enters Jerusalem · 16:15–23
Now Absalom and all the men of Israel come to Jerusalem, with Ahithophel among them.
When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, comes to Absalom, Hushai says, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"
Absalom says to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?"
Hushai says to Absalom, "No — the one whom YHWH and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his I will be, and with him I will stay.
And besides — whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I served your father, so I will serve you."
Absalom says to Ahithophel, "Give your counsel. What do we do?"

Ahithophel says to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house. All Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of everyone with you will be strengthened."
So they pitch a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom goes in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
Now the counsel Ahithophel gives in those days is as if one consults the word of God. That is how both David and Absalom regard all of Ahithophel's counsel.
Ahithophel's Counsel · 17:1–4
Ahithophel says to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men and set out tonight in pursuit of David.
I will come upon him while he is weary and weak and throw him into a panic. All the people with him will flee. I will strike down the king alone
and bring all the people back to you — as a bride returns to her husband. You seek only one man's life; all the rest will be at peace."
This plan is good in the eyes of Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
Hushai Defeats Ahithophel · 17:5–14
But Absalom says, "Call Hushai the Archite as well. Let us hear what he says."
Hushai comes in to Absalom, and Absalom puts it to him: "This is what Ahithophel has proposed. Shall we do it? If not, you speak."
Hushai says to Absalom, "The counsel Ahithophel has given is not good — not this time."

Hushai says, "You know your father and his men — they are warriors, and their spirits are like that of a bear robbed of her cubs in the field. Your father is an expert in war; he will not spend the night with the troops.
Even now he is hiding in a pit or some other place. And if he falls on your men first, whoever hears of it will say, 'There has been a slaughter among the troops following Absalom.'
Then even a valiant man with the heart of a lion will lose heart entirely — because all Israel knows your father is a mighty man, and that those with him are warriors.
My counsel is this: let all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, be gathered to you — a multitude like the sand by the sea — and you yourself go into battle.
We shall light upon him wherever he may be, settling on him like dew on the ground, and not one man of his will be left — not him, not any of the men with him.
And if he withdraws into a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city and drag it down into the valley until not even a pebble is found there."

Absalom and all the men of Israel say, "The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." For YHWH has ordained to frustrate the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that YHWH can bring disaster on Absalom.
The Message Carried to David · 17:15–22
Hushai says to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Ahithophel gave this counsel to Absalom and the elders of Israel, and I gave this counsel instead.
Now therefore send word at once to David: 'Do not spend the night at the fords of the wilderness — cross over at once, or the king and everyone with him will be swallowed up.'"
Jonathan and Ahimaaz are waiting at En-rogel. A female servant is to go and tell them, and they will carry word to King David, since they dare not be seen entering the city.
But a young man spots them and reports it to Absalom. Both of them leave quickly and come to the house of a man in Bahurim who has a well in his courtyard, and they go down into it.
The man's wife takes a covering and spreads it over the mouth of the well and scatters grain on it, and no one knows anything about it.

When Absalom's servants come to the woman at the house and ask, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" the woman says, "They crossed over the brook." They search but do not find them, and return to Jerusalem.
After the servants have gone, the men climb up out of the well and go and tell King David. They say to him, "Rise and cross the water quickly — Ahithophel has counseled thus against you."
So David and all the people with him rise and cross the Jordan. By daybreak not one of them is left who has not crossed.
Ahithophel's End · 17:23
When Ahithophel sees that his counsel is not followed, he saddles his donkey and goes home to his own city. He sets his house in order and hangs himself. He dies and is buried in his father's tomb.
Absalom Crosses the Jordan · 17:24–29
David reaches Mahanaim, and Absalom crosses the Jordan with all the men of Israel.
Absalom has set Amasa over the army in place of Joab. Amasa is the son of a man named Ithra the Ishmaelite, who married Abigal daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
Israel and Absalom encamp in the land of Gilead.
When David comes to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, and Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim,
bring beds, basins, and earthen vessels, wheat and barley, flour and parched grain, beans and lentils, honey and curds and sheep and cheese from the herd, for David and the people with him to eat.
They say, "The people are hungry and weary and thirsty in the wilderness."
The Battle in the Forest · 18:1–8
David musters the men who are with him and sets over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds.
David sends out the troops in three divisions: one under Joab, one under Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and one under Ittai the Gittite. The king says, "I myself will go out with you."

But the men say, "You must not go out. If we flee they will not care about us; if half of us die they will not care. But you are worth ten thousand of us. It is better for you to send us help from the city."
The king says, "Whatever seems best to you, I will do." So the king stands at the side of the gate while all the army marches out by hundreds and by thousands.
The king commands Joab and Abishai and Ittai: "Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom." All the people hear the king's orders to each of the commanders about Absalom.
The army goes out into the field against Israel. The battle is fought in the forest of Ephraim.
The forces of Israel are defeated before David's men there, and the loss that day is great — twenty thousand men.
The battle spreads over the whole countryside, and the forest devours more people that day than the sword.
The Death of Absalom · 18:9–18

Absalom happens to encounter David's servants. Absalom is riding his mule, and the mule goes under the thick branches of a great oak. His head catches in the oak, and he is left hanging between heaven and earth while the mule under him goes on.
A man who sees it tells Joab, "I just saw Absalom hanging in an oak."
Joab says to the man, "You saw him! Why did you not strike him to the ground right there? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a belt."

The man says to Joab, "Even if I felt a thousand pieces of silver in my hand I would not stretch out my hand against the king's son — we heard the king command you and Abishai and Ittai: 'For my sake protect the young man Absalom.'
If I had acted treacherously against his life, nothing is hidden from the king, and you yourself would have stood aloof."
Joab says, "I will not waste time like this with you." He takes three javelins in his hand and thrusts them into the heart of Absalom while he is still alive in the oak.
Ten of Joab's armor-bearers surround Absalom and strike him and kill him.
Joab blows the trumpet, and the troops pull back from pursuing Israel, for Joab restrains them.
They take Absalom and throw him into a great pit in the forest and raise over him a very great heap of stones. All Israel flees, each man to his own home.

Now in his lifetime Absalom had taken and set up for himself a pillar in the King's Valley, for he said, "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance." He names the pillar after himself. It is called Absalom's Monument to this day.
The News Comes to David · 18:19–33
Ahimaaz son of Zadok says, "Let me run and carry news to the king — YHWH has delivered him from the hand of his enemies."
Joab says to him, "You are not the one to carry news today. You may carry news another day, but today you carry no news, because the king's son is dead."
Joab says to the Cushite, "Go, tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bows before Joab and runs.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok says again to Joab, "Come what may, let me also run after the Cushite." Joab says, "Why do you want to run, my son? You will have no reward for the news."
"Come what may, I will run," he says. So Joab says, "Run." Ahimaaz runs by the way of the plain and outstrips the Cushite.
David is sitting between the two gates. The watchman goes up to the roof of the gate by the wall, lifts his eyes, and sees a man running alone.
The watchman calls out and tells the king. The king says, "If he is alone, there is news in his mouth." The man draws nearer and nearer.
The watchman sees another man running and calls down to the gatekeeper: "Here comes another man running alone!" The king says, "He also brings news."
The watchman says, "The running of the first looks to me like the running of Ahimaaz son of Zadok." The king says, "He is a good man and comes with good news."

Ahimaaz calls out to the king, "All is well!" He bows before the king with his face to the ground and says, "Blessed be YHWH your God, who has delivered up the men who raised their hand against my lord the king!"
The king asks, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" Ahimaaz answers, "When Joab sent me, there was great commotion, but I did not know what it was."
The king says, "Step aside and stand here." He steps aside and stands still.
The Cushite arrives and says, "Good news for my lord the king! YHWH has delivered you today from all who rose up against you."
The king asks the Cushite, "Is it well with the young man Absalom?" The Cushite answers, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise against you for evil be as that young man is."
The king is shaken. He goes up to the chamber over the gate and weeps. As he goes he says,
"O my son Absalom —
my son, my son Absalom!
Would I had died instead of you —
O Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab Rebukes the King · 19:1–8
Someone tells Joab, "The king is weeping and mourning for Absalom."
So the victory that day turns to mourning for all the people, for they hear that the king is grieving for his son.
The troops slip back into the city that day like men ashamed after fleeing in battle.
The king covers his face and cries aloud, "O my son Absalom! O Absalom, my son, my son!"

Joab goes to the king in the house and says, "Today you have humiliated all your servants — the men who have saved your life today, the lives of your sons and daughters, the lives of your wives and concubines —

by loving those who hate you and hating those who love you. You have made clear today that commanders and servants mean nothing to you. I know now that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, that would please you.

Now therefore rise, go out and speak encouragingly to your servants. I swear by YHWH — if you do not go out, not a man will remain with you this night. That will be worse for you than any disaster that has come on you from your youth until now."
So the king rises and takes his seat in the gate. When the people are told, "The king is sitting in the gate," all the troops come before the king.
Israel Debates David's Return · 19:9–15

Israel has fled, every man to his own home. Throughout all the tribes the people are arguing: "The king delivered us from the hand of our enemies and rescued us from the hand of the Philistines, and now he has fled out of the land because of Absalom.
But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?"

King David sends word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Speak to the elders of Judah and say, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house? The talk of all Israel has reached the king.
You are my brothers, my bone and my flesh. Why are you the last to bring the king home?'
And say to Amasa, 'You are my bone and my flesh. May God do so to me and more also if you are not my army commander in place of Joab from now on.'"
He sways the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, and they send word to the king: "Come back, you and all your servants."
So the king returns and comes as far as the Jordan. And Judah comes to Gilgal to meet the king and bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei, Mephibosheth, and Barzillai · 19:16–40
Shimei son of Gera the Benjaminite, from Bahurim, hurries down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
With him are a thousand men from Benjamin, and Ziba the servant of Saul's house with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rush to the Jordan before the king,
crossing the ford to bring the king's household across and to do whatever he wishes. As the king is about to cross the Jordan, Shimei son of Gera falls down before him
and says to the king, "Let not my lord count it as guilt or remember what your servant did wrongly on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not let the king take it to heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. I have come this day, the first of all the house of Joseph, to go down and meet my lord the king."
Abishai son of Zeruiah answers, "Shall not Shimei be put to death for this? He cursed YHWH's anointed."

David says, "What has this to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should today be an adversary to me? Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? Do I not know that I am today king over Israel?"
The king says to Shimei, "You will not die." And the king gives him his oath.
Mephibosheth the grandson of Saul comes down to meet the king. He has not trimmed his beard or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he returns safely.
When he comes to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king asks him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"
He answers, "My lord the king, my servant deceived me. I said, 'Saddle a donkey for me so I may ride with the king.' For your servant is lame.
He has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like the angel of God — do whatever seems good to you.
All my father's house deserved only death from my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further right do I have to cry to the king?"
The king says to him, "Why do you keep speaking of these things? I have decided: you and Ziba shall divide the land."
Mephibosheth says to the king, "Let him take it all, since my lord the king has come home safely."
Barzillai the Gileadite comes down from Rogelim and goes on with the king to the Jordan to see him off.
Barzillai is very old — eighty years. He has provided for the king during his stay at Mahanaim, for he is a very wealthy man.
The king says to Barzillai, "Cross over with me. I will provide for you beside me in Jerusalem."
Barzillai says to the king, "How many years of life do I have left, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king?

I am eighty years old today. Can I any longer tell what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I any longer hear the voice of singing men and women? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will go a little way over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?

Let your servant turn back and die in my own city near the grave of my father and mother. But here is your servant Chimham — let him cross over with my lord the king. Do for him whatever seems good to you."
The king answers, "Chimham shall cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever you wish. And whatever you ask of me I will do for you."
All the people cross the Jordan, and the king crosses. The king kisses Barzillai and blesses him, and Barzillai returns to his own home.
The king goes on to Gilgal, and Chimham goes with him. All the people of Judah and half the people of Israel escort the king.
The Quarrel Between Judah and Israel · 19:41–43

Then all the men of Israel come to the king and say to him, "Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household across the Jordan — and all David's men with him?"
All the men of Judah answer the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why are you angry about this? Have we eaten at the king's expense? Has he given us any gift?"

The men of Israel answer the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and in David also we have more than you. Why then did you despise us? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the words of the men of Judah are fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
Sheba's Revolt · 20:1–7
A worthless man happens to be there — his name is Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. He blows the trumpet and calls out,

"We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse! Every man to his tents, Israel!" So all the men of Israel desert David and follow Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah hold fast to their king, from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

David comes to his house in Jerusalem, and the king takes the ten concubines he had left to keep the house and puts them in a house under guard. He provides for them but does not go in to them. They are shut up until the day of their death, living as widows.
The king says to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together for me within three days, and be here yourself."
Amasa goes to summon Judah but delays beyond the appointed time.
David says to Abishai, "Sheba son of Bichri will now do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord's servants and pursue him, or he will find fortified cities and escape from us."
Joab's men go out after him, along with the Cherethites and Pelethites and all the mighty men. They leave Jerusalem in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri.
Joab Kills Amasa · 20:8–13

When they are at the large stone in Gibeon, Amasa comes to meet them. Joab is wearing a soldier's garment, and over it a belt with a sword in its sheath fastened at his hip. As he steps forward, it falls out.
Joab says to Amasa, "Is it well with you, my brother?" And with his right hand Joab takes hold of Amasa's beard to kiss him.

Amasa does not notice the sword in Joab's left hand. Joab strikes him with it in the stomach, and his entrails pour out to the ground. He does not strike a second blow, and Amasa dies. Joab and his brother Abishai continue the pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab's young men stands over Amasa and calls out, "Whoever favors Joab and whoever is for David — follow Joab!"
Amasa lies wallowing in blood in the middle of the road. The man sees that all the troops are stopping, and he moves Amasa from the road into the field and throws a garment over him.
Once he is moved from the road, all the men follow Joab in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri.
The Wise Woman of Abel · 20:14–22
Sheba passes through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah, and all the Bichrites assemble and follow him in.

All the men with Joab besiege him in Abel of Beth-maacah. They heap up a siege ramp against the city, and it stands against the outer wall. All the troops with Joab are battering the wall to bring it down.
Then a wise woman calls out from the city, "Listen! Listen! Tell Joab to come here so I can speak with him."
He comes near, and the woman says, "Are you Joab?" He says, "I am." She says, "Listen to what your servant has to say." He says, "I am listening."
She says, "Long ago people used to say, 'Ask your question at Abel' — and they would settle the matter there.
I am one of the peaceable and faithful in Israel. You are trying to destroy a city that is a mother in Israel. Why would you swallow up the inheritance of YHWH?"
Joab answers, "Far be it from me — far be it! I have no desire to swallow up or destroy.

That is not the case. But a man from the hill country of Ephraim, Sheba son of Bichri, has lifted his hand against King David. Give up him alone and I will withdraw from the city." The woman says to Joab, "His head will be thrown to you over the wall."

The woman goes in her wisdom to all the people, and they cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and throw it out to Joab. He blows the trumpet and they disperse from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returns to Jerusalem to the king.
David's Officers · 20:23–26
Joab is in command of the whole army of Israel. Benaiah son of Jehoiada commands the Cherethites and Pelethites.
Adoram is in charge of forced labor. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud is the recorder.
Sheva is secretary. Zadok and Abiathar are priests.
And Ira the Jairite is also David's priest.
The Famine and the Gibeonites · 21:1–14

There is a famine in the days of David — three years, year after year. David seeks the face of YHWH, and YHWH says, "There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death."

The king calls the Gibeonites and speaks with them. The Gibeonites are not of the people of Israel but a remnant of the Amorites. Though Israel had sworn to spare them, Saul had sought to cut them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah.
David says to the Gibeonites, "What shall I do for you? How shall I make atonement, so that you will bless YHWH's inheritance?"

The Gibeonites say to him, "It is not a matter of silver or gold between us and Saul or his house, and it is not ours to put any man to death in Israel." He says, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."
They say to the king, "The man who consumed us and schemed to destroy us — so that we should have no place left anywhere in all the territory of Israel —
let seven of his sons be given to us, and we will hang them before YHWH at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of YHWH." The king says, "I will give them."
But the king spares Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, son of Saul, because of the oath of YHWH that is between them, between David and Jonathan son of Saul.

The king takes the two sons of Rizpah daughter of Aiah, whom she bore to Saul — Armoni and Mephibosheth — and the five sons of Merab daughter of Saul, whom she bore to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

He gives them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hang them on the mountain before YHWH. The seven of them perish together. They are put to death in the first days of harvest, at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Then Rizpah daughter of Aiah takes sackcloth and spreads it on a rock for herself, from the beginning of harvest until rain falls on them from the sky. She does not let the birds of the air touch them by day or the wild animals by night.
David is told what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, has done.

David goes and takes the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hanged them on the day they struck down Saul at Gilboa.
He brings up the bones of Saul and the bones of his son Jonathan, and they gather the bones of those who had been hanged.
They bury the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son in the land of Benjamin at Zela, in the tomb of his father Kish. They do all that the king commands. After that God responds to the plea for the land.
Wars Against the Philistines · 21:15–22
The Philistines go to war against Israel again, and David goes down with his servants. They fight the Philistines, and David grows weary.
Ishbi-benob, who is among the descendants of the Rapha, whose spear weighs three hundred shekels of bronze and who is armed with a new sword, intends to strike David down.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah comes to his aid, strikes the Philistine, and kills him. Then David's men swear to him: "You will never go out with us to battle again, so that you do not quench the lamp of Israel."
After this there is another battle with the Philistines at Gob. Sibbecai the Hushathite strikes down Saph, who is among the descendants of the Rapha.
There is another battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite strikes down Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear is like a weaver's beam.

There is still another battle at Gath, where there is a man of great stature who has six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot — twenty-four in number — and he too is descended from the Rapha.
When he taunts Israel, Jonathan son of Shimei, David's brother, strikes him down.
These four are born to the Rapha in Gath, and they fall by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.
David's Song of Deliverance · 22:1–51
